The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                              Paper I



             The (3, 4, ∞) family of complex structures on S 6 :
                periods, moduli and the ends of the disc
                               AI-produced research     17 November 2026

                                               Abstract
          For the standard marked (3, 4, ∞) family, the admissible parameter is 0 < |w| < 216,
      where w = exp(−πic), and Xc ≃ Xc0 exactly when c0 − c ∈ 2Z. We determine its normalized
      periods, sharp norm bound, integral monodromy, cohomology, real forms, special fibres and
      arithmetic specializations. The specified affine family has no proper analytic filling at zero
      after any finite parameter cover; the circle |w| = 216 is a natural boundary for proper flat
      extensions. The construction is credited to Claude and Alpöge and to Engel; the standard
      classification, tangent cohomology, Kuranishi germ and automorphisms are credited to Du,
      Guo, Kusakabe and Xie, version 1. Complete independent derivations accompany the period,
      integral, analytic and arithmetic calculations. This writing and its proof comparisons are
      AI-produced by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, ChatGPT Pro mode, effort Pro), 17 November 2026;
      the verification record distinguishes complete readings, source checks and rerun certificates.
      No human has checked the mathematics. A literal global coefficient atlas and an unconditional
      transcendence claim remain in a separate final part.


1     Result
1.1   Statement
We use the marked construction and orientation conventions of Section 2. The standard family
has the parameter domain and equivalence relation
               3
        =c <     log 6,     w = e−πic ,      0 < |w| < 216,       Xc ≃ Xc0 ⇐⇒ c0 − c ∈ 2Z.
               π
The norm maximum is sup Dpart = −(3/π) log 6, attained only at the order-four base point. The
monodromy group is the explicit index-twelve kernel of Theorem 7.1. The complete Hodge
and Bott–Chern tables are in propositions 8.9 and 10.3; in particular h1,1 = h2,2 = 2 and
h1,2 = h2,1 = 1. The tangent dimensions are (1, 1, 1, 0), the reduced Kuranishi germ is a smooth
line, and Aut(Xc ) = C∗ . The no-filling and boundary assertions, with their exact hypotheses,
are theorems 21.58 and 22.3. For instance c = 0 gives w = 1 in the parameter disc, whereas c + 2
gives the same biholomorphism class.
    That this family contradicts Campana et al. (2020, Corollary 2.3) is due to Claude and
Alpöge (2026, Section 1.2 and Theorem 10.5). Paper II, Propositions 5.1 and 13.2, gives the
general analysis and replacement criteria; Paper III, Theorems 2.4 and 6.52 and Corollary 7.32,
gives the map, framing and manifold results. No conditional arithmetic statement is used to
establish the complex family or its parameter disc.

1.4     Proof map
The root charts, affine origins and cusp fan fix the actual compact family. The period lattice
gives the finite norm obstructions and the even-shift classification. Theta identities, analytic
inequalities and separately rerun interval bounds determine the disc. Root-curve direct images
and the logarithmic cotangent sequence give the cohomology and deformation results. At zero
the obstruction is the radial class of the actual affine origins; at the outer circle the intrinsic
multiple fibre has an Albanese invariant with a natural boundary. Arithmetic proofs retain all
hypotheses and error estimates. The construction and credited re-derivations appear in the
appendices; Appendix R gives the complete source-label, proof and verification concordance.

parameter sets, so a fixed compact real parallelepiped proves properness and the    lattice quotient
is holomorphic. At the cusp write Z = sB0 + C(tc , c) with B0 = −1            0 1 . On a compact
                                                                                 0
parameter disc C is uniformly bounded; shrink the cusp radius until k(−2π Im C)/ log |tc |k < 1/2.
The effective logarithmic lattice is then within 1/2 of the unimodular B0 , uniformly. Reduce
its logarithmic valuation modulo the effective logarithmic lattice to a bounded parallelogram.
Choose a height-one triangle containing that reduced valuation. Its barycentric coordinates are
nonnegative and sum to one; the corresponding three unimodular cone characters therefore have
modulus at most one. This puts the point in the closed unit polydisc of that cone. Only finitely
many triangles meet the fixed bounded parallelogram, uniformly on the parameter compactum.
Boundary orbits have the same representatives by translating their height-one components to
these triangles. Thus every orbit has a representative in this finite union of cone polydiscs. Those
closed polydiscs times a compact parameter set form a compact surjective representative set.
This proves properness at the cusp and proper discontinuity by the same uniform lower bound
on nonzero lattice translations. The quotient charts are open subsets of a fixed smooth toric
variety times the parameter disc, so projection to the parameter is a submersion. The explicit
overlap maps are jointly holomorphic. These local families agree after shrinking cusp radii, and
glue over P. The coherent 2Z action is properly discontinuous because its action on P is. Local
inverse logarithms for w = e−πic identify the quotient family with these proper local families. 3.3
gives pairwise non-biholomorphic fibres.

3.4   Albanese invariants and the derivative of the deformation
Proposition 3.5. With κj (c) = κpart
                                j    + c, the Albanese elliptic curves of the reduced finite fibres
are
               Alb(S1 ) = C/(Z + κ1 (c)Z),       Alb(S2 ) = C/(Z + 12 κ2 (c)Z).
Writing J(q) = q −1 + 744 + 196884q + · · · , their invariants are
                                         part                                part
                       j1 (w) = J(e−2πiκ1 w2 ),       j2 (w) = J(e−πiκ2 w).

These are convergent formulas because the displayed nome moduli are below one. Outside the
explicitly defined countable exceptional set in the proof, equality of both Albanese invariants forces
c0 − c ∈ 2Z. Thus the generic Albanese invariants recover the parameter modulo its exact period
subgroup, independently of the centralizer calculation.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.2; proposition 3.3.

Proof. In the product covers of 3.2 the invariant holomorphic one-forms are exactly the multiples
of dξ: the moving factor is multiplied by a primitive third or fourth root. Integration thus
identifies the Albanese with the quotient of the fixed line by the fixed-coordinate projections of
every deck translation. These are, respectively,

             Z + κ1 Z + 23 Z + κ31 Z = 13 Z + κ31 Z,       Z + κ2 Z + 12 Z + κ42 Z = 12 Z + κ42 Z.

Multiplication by three and two gives the stated maps of complex tori. In particular the Albanese
computation includes the kernel of the product isogeny and the affine quotient, rather than just
its fixed eigenspace. Using the positive-imaginary representatives −κ1 and −κ2 /2 in the standard
modular j-series gives the formulas. At sufficiently small nome J is injective: 1/J(q) = q + O(q 2 )
has nonzero derivative at zero. Thus j2 alone distinguishes parameters within a sufficiently
small punctured subdisc when both parameters lie there. For the full generic assertion put
x = −κ2 (c)/2 and d∗ = κpart
                           1   − κpart
                                   2 , so −κ1 (c) = 2x − d∗ . The independently certified interval
in cd_special_intervals.py gives −0.2 < Im d∗ < −0.1; in particular it is nonzero. Equality
of the two elliptic invariants at c, c0 gives matrices M, N ∈ PSL2 (Z) with x0 = M (x) and

                                      N (2x − d∗ ) = 2M (x) − d∗ .

Define the exceptional set to be the c ∈ P obtained from roots of these equations for all pairs
for which the two rational functions are not identical. Each equation has at most two roots
after clearing denominators, so this is a countable, explicitly specified set. For a pair giving an
identity, let C(x) = 2x − d∗ . Then N = CM C −1 . The real matrix M preserves both the real
circle R ∪ {∞} and C −1 (R ∪ {∞}), the parallel line with imaginary part Im d∗ /2 together with
infinity. Their unique intersection is infinity, so M fixes infinity. An element of PSL2 (Z) fixing
infinity is x 7→ x + b, b ∈ Z, and then N (y) = y + 2b. It follows that c0 − c = −2b. This proves
the generic necessity with its actual exceptional set; 3.3 proves the necessity also on that set.

Proposition 3.7. The non-isotriviality argument of Viaclovsky, (Viaclovsky, 2026a, Proposition
4.7), follows for the present family from 3.6 and 3.1. The cited countability argument proves
local non-isotriviality and positive Kuranishi dimension; the computation in 3.6 additionally
proves nonzero derivative at every admissible parameter. The arithmetic method of Yang, (Yang,
2026, Lemmas 6.6–6.9 and Proposition 6.15), specializes to the same centralizer, finite-norm and
collar-gluing operations after replacing his displayed matrices by A1 , A2 ; those replacements are
evaluated in 3.3 and 3.4.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Viaclovsky, 2026a, Proposition
4.7); proposition 3.6; proposition 3.1; (Yang, 2026, Lemmas 6.6–6.9 and Proposition 6.15);
proposition 3.3; proposition 3.4.

Proof. On a fixed ordinary fibre, the three last periods remain fixed and span C2 , whereas the
first changes by δe. A marked complex-linear identification fixing those three periods must be
the identity, so the marked period map is nonconstant. The set of integral markings of one
torus is countable. A holomorphic nonconstant map from a disc has uncountable image; hence
the unmarked fibre family is locally non-isotrivial. 3.1 transfers this to total spaces. This is
exactly the implication used in the cited Proposition 4.7, whose statement and proof we have
read. A nonconstant classifying map gives positive dimension of its local target. It does not by
itself determine the derivative at the base point, as the explicit holomorphic map z 7→ z 2 has
nonconstant image and derivative zero at zero. 3.6 computes the derivative here.
    Yang’s cited lemmas use an integral commuting lattice map, an affine fibre lift, normalization
of the root base change, and a norm-lattice defect. We have exhibited the respective maps and
norm equations for the present matrices. His Proposition 6.15 obtains 6/r from the first-column
scaling and its order-six norm image. Here the first-column scaling is one and the two computed
norm images impose parity, yielding two. The common proof operations transfer through these
explicitly stated matrix substitutions; no conclusion about one family is inferred merely from the
label of the other. His nonzero absolute Kodaira–Spencer conclusion is obtained in the present
setting by the explicit computation and intrinsic-pencil transfer above.

4.3   Higher multiplicities
Proposition 4.8. Let k, l be positive integers with gcd(3k, 4l) = 1, and put m1 = 3k, m2 = 4l.

ε1 = ε, ε2 = ε0 . Two such members are biholomorphic precisely when their multiplicity pair agrees
and, for some a ∈ {1, −1} and integer n = c0 − c,
   p0 = ap,    rj0 ≡ arj   (mod mj ),   nr10 ≡ as1 − s01   (mod k),   nr20 ≡ as2 − s02   (mod 2l).
The congruences on rj0 already follow from p0 = ap. For fixed discrete vectors and cusp collar the
identification subgroup is 2klZ. For fixed admissible u and this multiplicity pair, all the stated
sphere translation data give exactly 2kl isomorphism classes, permuted in one cycle by a circuit
of u about zero.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 3.2; proposition 3.3;
proposition 4.5.

Proof. We first recover the base for these sphere members without using the degree-two canonical
pencil. A biholomorphism F : X → X 0 gives g = f 0 F . Since H 2 (S 6 , R) = 0, the closed form
g ∗ ωFS is exact. Restrict to a regular torus T and wedge with a flat Kahler form on T . Stokes’
theorem gives integral zero, while the integrand is nonnegative and strictly positive wherever
dg|T 6= 0. Thus g is constant on each regular fibre. The image of (f, g) is a compact analytic
curve whose projection to B has degree one; its normalization gives a holomorphic h : B → B
with g = hf . Apply the same construction to F −1 to see that h is an automorphism. The
three homological local monodromy orders are three, four and infinity, independently of k, l;
their intertwining maps under F therefore fix each special point. Hence h = 1. The nonreduced
fibre multiplicities now force equal k, l. This is the full reduction in the read Proposition 4.7 of
Viaclovsky’s paper, written here with its exact maps.
     The root model of degree m1 is the pullback of the degree-three model by s 7→ sk , and
likewise at the other point. Its linear action remains A1 or A2 , while its root generator has order
mj . The primitive invariant coordinate rj /mj proves freeness of every nonidentity power. The
normalization and deck-commutation arguments of 3.2 and 3.3 apply to these root covers without

5.3   The rank-three period quotient
Proposition 5.6. At every point with D = 0, T > 0, the real-linear map Π : R4 → C2 has rank
three. Write µ = a0 τ + b0 , a0 , b0 ∈ R, and put
                               k = (1, −6a0 , −6b0 , 6a0 Re µ − Re β).
Its real kernel is Rk. The subgroup ΠZ4 is discrete exactly when k ∈ Q4 . In that case it is a
rank-three lattice in a real hyperplane and its quotient in C2 is a noncompact complex Lie group.
In every other case the topological quotient C2 /ΠZ4 is non-Hausdorff.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.


                                                 27
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                            Paper I


Proof. The real matrix, with output order (Re ζ1 , Im ζ1 , Re ζ2 , Im ζ2 ), is

                                    6 Re µ Re τ 1 0
                                                          
                                  6 Im µ     T      0 0
                                   Re β Re µ 0 1 .
                                                          

                                     Im β Im µ 0 0

Its last three columns are real-linearly independent because T > 0. Its determinant is T D, so at
zero determinant the rank is exactly three. Substitution gives the displayed kernel, including
its signs. If the image subgroup is discrete, it is a lattice of rank at most three in its real span.
The homomorphism Z4 → ΠZ4 therefore has a nonzero kernel, forcing the displayed kernel
vector with first coordinate one to be rational. Conversely a rational line has a primitive integral
generator extendable to a basis of Z4 . The remaining three basis images are a real basis of the
image hyperplane and hence generate a discrete lattice. Its quotient leaves one unbounded real
direction. Finally a non-discrete finitely generated subgroup of this real hyperplane cannot be
closed: a closed subgroup is a product of a real vector group and a discrete group, and a nonzero
real vector group is uncountable. A quotient topological group is Hausdorff exactly when its
identity subgroup is closed. This proves the last assertion.

Proposition 5.7. The unique degenerate base point at the actual admissibility boundary is t = 1.
The boundary constants c = x + i(3/π) log 6 give

                                   kerR Π = R(1, 3, −3, −x − 3/2).

For rational x + 3/2 = m/n in lowest terms, the quotient is a finite holomorphic quotient of
Ei × C∗ , with a covering of degree four. For irrational x + 3/2, the closure of the period subgroup
is generated by the real line R(0, 1) and the two periods (i, (1 − i)/2), (1, 0). Its Hausdorff quotient
is a real manifold homeomorphic to R × (S 1 )2 .

Remark 5.8 (Local boundary obstruction). The local compactification obstruction at the actual
boundary is localized at the order-four fibre over t = 1. The proposed extension would require a
compact complex-space replacement of the rank-three quotient in 5.7, over a neighbourhood of
one boundary parameter, with a proof that it extends the original cyclic filling and its overlap
with the ordinary torus family. Both rational and irrational values of x + 3/2 are included in the
exact quotient description. The naive quotients cannot be central fibres of a proper complex-space
family: for rational x + 3/2 they are noncompact, and for irrational values they are non-Hausdorff.
5.9 supplies a further obstruction to preserving a holomorphic Weierstrass Albanese model in this
parameter. These prove failure of the stated specific replacements. The unique base-fibre location


                                                  28
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                             Paper I


and exact local period obstruction are thereby determined. The general proper holomorphic
extension is excluded by lemma 22.2 and theorem 22.3, which recovers the intrinsic divisor in a
hypothetical extension.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 5.7; proposition 5.9;
lemma 22.2 and theorem 22.3.

Proposition 5.9. On its half-plane of definition, the j-invariant of Alb(S2 ) has no meromorphic
continuation across any point of the line Im c = (3/π) log 6. In particular the rank-three quotient
at t = 1 cannot be replaced by a Weierstrass family of elliptic Albanese curves whose coefficients
are holomorphic in the same parameter across that line.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; section 3.4; proposition 5.1.

Proof. The explicit Albanese lattice in 3.4 is Z + (κ2 /2)Z, with κ2 = c + 3/2 − i(3/π) log 6
by 5.1. A positive-imaginary modulus is z = −κ2 /2, so the invariant is j(z). At a reduced
rational r = a/b on the real boundary, choose an integral determinant-one modular matrix with
bottom row (b, −a). Its value at r + iy has imaginary part 1/(b2 y). The convergent Fourier
expansion j = q −1 + 744 + O(q) therefore gives growth of order exp(2π/(b2 y)) as y ↓ 0. A
meromorphic function at r is bounded by a fixed power of 1/y, so continuation there is impossible.
A meromorphic continuation near an irrational real point would also continue the same function
near some rational real point in that neighbourhood, which has just been excluded. The affine
change from c to z transfers this obstruction to the stated line. A Weierstrass family with
holomorphic coefficients has a meromorphic j-invariant, expressed as the quotient of its cubic
invariants, so it cannot supply the indicated continuation. This obstruction concerns the stated
Albanese construction; it does not silently assume that every possible compact threefold filling
preserves an Albanese model of its special surface.

6.2   Compact curves and surfaces
Proposition 6.8. For a standard-twist member Xc with underlying manifold S 6 , every compact
irreducible complex curve lies in one fibre of f , and every compact irreducible complex surface is
one of the reduced fibres.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The given diffeomorphism with S 6 implies H 2 (Xc ; Z) = 0. For a compact irreducible
curve C, let ν : C  e → C ,→ Xc be its normalization map. The holomorphic map f ν has
deg(f ν) OP1 (1) = 0, since its Chern class is pulled back from the zero class on Xc . A nonconstant
         ∗

holomorphic map of compact Riemann surfaces has positive degree: a regular value has a positive
number of preimages, all with positive local multiplicity. Therefore f ν, and hence f |C , is constant.
     An irreducible surface Z in the smooth threefold is an effective Cartier divisor. If its image
were all of B, a general smooth fibre would meet it in a nonempty effective divisor D whose line
bundle is OXc (Z)|RFt . Its integral RChern class is zero. Choose a flat Kähler form ω on the torus
Ft . The equality Ft c1 (D) ∧ ω = D ω has left side zero and right side positive, a contradiction.
Thus Z lies in a single fibre. Each reduced fibre is irreducible of dimension two, so containment
forces equality. This uses the full map into Xc , not a transfer of a vanishing claim from its
normalization.

Proposition 6.9. There is no rational curve in Xc \ Wc . There are elliptic curves outside all
three special fibres, in particular in each of the two smooth fibres Ft± . All curves in Wc are
precisely the images of irreducible algebraic curves in dP6 under its finite normalization map.
Distinct curves have the same image only for the three paired boundary lines. All curves in a
bielliptic fibre Sj are images of irreducible curves in its finite product cover.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.8; proposition 6.1;
theorem 5.10.

Proof. By 6.8 every curve is vertical. A holomorphic map from P1 into a torus lifts to its
vector-space universal cover, since P1 is simply connected, and its coordinate functions are
constant by compactness. Thus a smooth torus fibre contains no rational curve. A map from

                                                  34
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


P1 into a bielliptic surface lifts through its finite unramified torus cover by the same covering
criterion; the lifted map is constant. These arguments prove the first assertion, including possibly
singular rational images. 6.1 gives an embedded connected elliptic kernel in each Ft± , proving
the second.
    For the third assertion let η : dP6 → Wc be the finite normalization morphism. Each
component of the inverse image of a compact curve is compact and one-dimensional and maps
onto that curve, because finite maps have zero-dimensional fibres. It is algebraic in the projective
surface dP6 . Conversely its image is a compact analytic curve by properness. Away from the
conductor, η is a biholomorphism, so two distinct curves can have the same image only when
both lie in the conductor; its identifications are exactly the three opposite pairs computed
in 5.10. This is also an explicit algebraic parametrization: the curves of dP6 are the three
exceptional lines and strict transforms of irreducible plane curves under the blow-up of the three
coordinate points. Their homogeneous equations and their three multiplicities specify the strict
transforms. The finite-product cover statement for Sj follows from the identical proper-image
and finite-preimage argument applied to its unramified morphism Ej × Fj → Sj ; curves in the
product are algebraic.

Theorem 6.10. The following descriptions give all compact irreducible curves of Xc . In Wc
and Sj they are exactly the images described in 6.9. In a smooth fibre of algebraic dimension
zero there are none. In a smooth fibre of algebraic dimension one they are exactly the translates
of its unique elliptic kernel Kt . In an abelian fibre they are exactly the translates of elliptic
subtori, together with the irreducible zero divisors of the positive Appell–Humbert theta sections
described below. These descriptions, 6.6, and 6.8 constitute a classification including every smooth
exceptional fibre and every compact irreducible surface.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 6.9; theorem 6.6;
proposition 6.8; section P.7.
   This is the effective line-bundle criterion for compact complex tori in the present lattice. A
complete re-derivation is given in Appendix P.7.

Lie algebras and their bracket span sl2 . They generate the connected algebraic group SL2 . A
subgroup containing the entire unipotent kernel and surjecting onto this Levi quotient is the
entire vector stabilizer. Its dimension is 3 + 3 = 6. This reasoning uses equations over Q, so
proves the rational assertion as well as the real assertion.

Theorem 7.4. The set O is the largest Γ-invariant open subset of D on which the action is
properly discontinuous. It is also the largest such open subset for PZ . Each sign region is a
complex manifold in the analytic topology, and its quotient by either discrete group is a Hausdorff
complex analytic orbifold.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (5).


                                                38
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                       Paper I


Proof. Let PR be the real symplectic group preserving the real line Re. We first prove properness
on each sign region. For a fixed J, the form hJ (v, w) = ψ(v, Jw) + iψ(v, w) is a nondegenerate
Hermitian form of signature (1, 1) on the complex vector space (ΛR , J), with the convention
conjugate linear in the first entry. When qe (J) 6= 0, the complex line Ce is nondegenerate and
its Hermitian orthogonal complement is a complex line of the opposite sign. Normalize e by a
positive real scalar and choose a unit vector in this complement. Comparing these two Hermitian
bases for two complex structures with the same sign gives a real symplectic map preserving Re
and conjugating one complex structure to the other. Thus PR is transitive on each sign region.
    An element of the stabilizer of J inside PR is complex linear and sends e to re for a real
nonzero r. Preservation of qe (J) gives r2 = 1. On the complementary complex line it acts by
an element of U (1). The stabilizer is consequently the compact group {±1} × U (1). Each sign
region is therefore a homogeneous space of PR with compact stabilizer L. Local sections of
PR → PR /L, and a finite cover of a compact subset K, give a compact subset C of PR mapping
onto K. Every element carrying a point of K back into K belongs to CLC −1 , which is compact.
This proves properness. Restricting a proper action to a closed discrete subgroup gives the
required finite-intersection condition. Both Γ and PZ are closed discrete matrix groups. The two
sign regions are disjoint invariant open-and-closed subsets of O, so the same finite-intersection
condition holds on their union. Proper actions by discrete groups have finite stabilizers and
Hausdorff quotients; their holomorphic local finite-group quotient charts supply the asserted
analytic orbifolds.
    It remains to prove maximality, which requires more than one bad point. The real vector
stabilizer Pe,R acts transitively on D0 = {J : qe (J) = 0}. Here is a direct comparison map. In
the Hermitian space just described, e is a nonzero null vector. Choose v with hJ (e, v) = 1, and
replace v by v − 12 hJ (v, v)e. This preserves hJ (e, v) = 1 and makes v null. The ordered complex
basis (e, v) has Gram matrix 01 10 . The complex-linear map between two such bases fixes e and
preserves h, hence its imaginary part ψ. As a real map it belongs to Pe,R and conjugates the two
complex structures.
    The subgroup Pe,Q is dense in Pe,R . For the unipotent coordinates in (5) this is density of
Q3 in R3 . For SL2 one may approximate a, b, c by rational numbers in the chart a 6= 0 and set
d = (1 + bc)/a; translates of that chart cover the group. Hence

                                       {rJ0 r−1 : r ∈ Pe,Q }

is dense in D0 . Put R0 = g(T 6 , 0, −1), so R012 = R and (R0 − I)2 = 0. At rJ0 r−1 the
nonzero rational nilpotent L = r(R0 − I)r−1 commutes with the complex structure and satisfies
L2 = 0. Choose a positive integer d clearing its denominators. The matrix I + dL and its
inverse I − dL are integral, symplectic, and fix e; this follows either by conjugating the identity
(I + s(R0 − I))t Ω(I + s(R0 − I)) = Ω or by expanding it. The twelfth power of I + dL lies in
Γ, because Pe,Z /Γ ∼= Z/12. It has infinite order and fixes rJ0 r−1 . Thus points with infinite
Γ-stabilizer are dense in D0 .
    Every open neighborhood in D of any point of D0 therefore contains a point with infinite
stabilizer. An open set on which the action is proper cannot meet D0 . This proves the largest-
open-set assertion for Γ. The same points have infinite PZ -stabilizer, so it proves that assertion
for the full parabolic as well.

8.4   Ordinary relative differentials and the correction at the cusp
Proposition 8.11 (All local modules needed to distinguish degrees one and two). Let R =

                          Ω1R/C{t} = R3 /R(y, x, 0) ≃ (x, y) ⊕ R,
and
                       Ω2R/C{t} ≃ (x, y) ⊕ R/(x, y),       Ω3R/C{t} ≃ R/(x, y).
For t = xyz, Ω1 = R3 /R(yz, xz, xy) is torsion-free of rank two and is not free at the triple point.

                               ∧dt                          Ru ⊕ Rv
                0 → T → Ω2 −−→ I → 0,           T =                       ,   IT = 0,
                                                       (xu, y(u − v), zv)

and Ω3 = R/I. Finally, for t = sm in R = C{s, y1 , y2 },

                                 Ω1 = R2 ⊕ R/(sm−1 ) ds,
                                                             2
                                 Ω2 = R dy1 ∧ dy2 ⊕ R/(sm−1 ) ,
                                 Ω3 = R/(sm−1 ) ds ∧ dy1 ∧ dy2 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The degree-one presentation is the quotient by dt; higher degrees are its exterior powers. At
a double point the transverse quotient R2 /R(y, x) maps isomorphically to (x, y) by (a, b) 7→ xa−yb
after an immaterial change of sign of one basis vector. More explicitly one may use (a, b) 7→ xa−yb
with relation (y, x); its kernel is precisely that relation, since x, y are relatively prime. In degree
two, with basis A = dx ∧ dy, B = dx ∧ dz, C = dy ∧ dz, the relations are xA = yA = 0,
yB + xC = 0. This gives the displayed torsion summand and the ideal (x, y); wedging once more
gives R/(x, y).
    At the triple point the map from ordinary to logarithmic relative one-forms sends (a, b, c) to
(xa − zc, yb − zc). Its kernel is precisely R(yz, xz, xy): the two equations imply c = xyh, a = yzh,
b = xzh by relative primality of the coordinates. Thus it injects into R2 , proving torsion-freeness.
Its fibre at the maximal ideal has dimension three although its rank is two, so it is not free. The
same minimal-generator argument works at the double locus.
    In degree two, wedging with dt is the row (xy, −xz, yz) in the basis (A, B, C). Its syzygies
are generated freely by u = (z, y, 0) and v = (0, y, x). To check generation, an equation
xyA − xzB + yzC = 0 implies x | C, say C = xC1 ; then yA = z(B − yC1 ) implies A = zA1 ,
B = y(A1 + C1 ). Thus the syzygy is A1 u + C1 v. The three relations from dt ∧ (dx, dy, dz) are
−xu, y(u − v), zv, proving the stated presentation of the kernel. The ideal I kills it by those
relations. Conversely the quotient I is torsion-free, so this kernel is exactly the torsion of Ω2 .
The presentation immediately gives Ω3 = R/I. All matrix identities have also been checked over
Z[x, y, z] by the supplied exact program. For t = sm the sole degree-one relation is msm−1 ds = 0;
m is a unit and taking exterior powers gives the three formulas.

Proposition 9.2 (The relative cohomology comparison). Fix the period family and cusp filling.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. We construct the comparison at every point. Over B \ Σ the two families are identified,
and a translation acts trivially on H q (F, OF ) and H q (F, Ω1F ) for a complex torus F . For the
second assertion, translation fixes the invariant holomorphic one-forms, V          and the first follows
either from invariant Dolbeault forms or the exterior algebra H • (F, OF ) = • H 1 (F, OF ). These
are statements about the induced maps on cohomology, including their holomorphic variation.
      At a point with original order d = 3 or 4, let fe : T → ∆z be the smooth proper torus model
with coarse coordinate q = z d . The new model is its pullback by z = se , where m = de, followed
by the free cyclic quotient of order m. Smooth proper base change identifies the higher direct
images upstairs with the pullbacks of those for T . The relative logarithmic cotangent bundle
upstairs is precisely Ω1T /∆z pulled back: the base logarithmic direction is killed in the quotient
defining E 0 . The derivative of a translation contributes only a multiple of ds; it consequently
acts on this quotient as ordinary translation on relative forms.
      Average over the cyclic action and choose holomorphic eigenframes. If a frame for H q (O) or
H q (Ω1 ) has character ζd−a , 0 ≤ a < d, its original invariant extension is z a O∆q . On the order-m
cover its character is ζm    −ea , and its invariant extension is sea O
                                                                        ∆q = z O∆q . Taking invariants
                                                                               a

is exact in characteristic zero; hence this equality is an equality of the extensions inside the
common punctured-disc bundle, not only an equality of their ranks or degrees. A translation
twist induces the identity on the cohomology just used and changes none of these lattices. This
proves the comparison at both finite points, including the full nonreduced fibres.
      At the cusp the relative logarithmic forms have the global toric frame d log x1 , d log x2 ,
modulo d log q. A toric gluing has the form xi 7→ ci (q)q bi xi and therefore changes d log xi by
(qc0i /ci +bi )d log q. It induces the identity on the relative logarithmic quotient. The structure-sheaf

comparison is also the identity on the normalization cochain complex. This verifies the cusp

    The logarithmic cotangent exact sequences are isomorphic on the smooth base, so their
connecting maps agree there under these comparisons. Their source and target sheaves are locally
free by the local calculations in Part A and the eigenframe calculation above. A holomorphic map
between vector bundles on a reduced curve which is zero on a dense open set is zero everywhere.
Thus the connecting maps agree globally.

9.3   Finite fundamental groups and universal covers
Proposition 9.6 (Connected cyclic covers and the cusp comparison). For an admissible (3, 4)
member with n = |12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 | > 1, let π : Y → X be the universal cover and g = f π. It is a
finite etale holomorphic map of degree n. Every fibre of g is connected; its finite reductions are
bielliptic, its multiplicities are 3, 4, and its cusp Wn normalizes to a disjoint union of n copies of
dP6 . The pullback maps induce isomorphisms

                           Rq f∗ OX ≃ Rq g∗ OY ,        Rq f∗ EX ≃ Rq g∗ EY .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 9.8; proposition 9.2.

Proof. We first derive the fundamental-group presentation from the fillings. The smooth family
over the punctured base has zero section, so its fundamental group is Λ o hx, yi, where x, y are
the analytic peripheral generators fixed by the root-deck convention and act by A1 , A2 . On a
finite filling the lifted affine generator has mj th power translation by vj : its mj translations add
to vj because Aj vj = vj . Thus filling the normal disc imposes x3 = tv1 and y 4 = tv2 , with the
signs fixed by the clockwise convention on the first page.
    The toric covering space of the cusp tube is simply connected. Indeed its dense torus has
cocharacter lattice Z3 ; a loop may be perturbed into that torus, and the normal discs of the three
rays (0, 1), (e1 , 1), (e2 , 1) kill a basis of this lattice. This argument applies also to the infinite
fan, since a compact loop and a homotopy meet only finitely many of its locally finite charts.
The same conclusion holds for the small tube: if a loop in |tc | <  bounds a disc in the toric
space, the torus action (x1 , x2 , tc ) 7→ (x1 , x2 , atc ) for a sufficiently small positive a moves that
compact disc into the tube, and the scaling homotopy of its boundary stays in the tube. The
cusp quotient therefore has fundamental group Λ/Λtor , and its toric meridian bounds the normal
disc at fixed x1 , x2 . A translated collar makes this meridian tµ y −1 x−1 , where γ(µ) = l0 . Van
Kampen consequently kills Λtor and imposes xy = tµ .
   The normal closure of Λtor in the fibre lattice is ker γ: it contains ŵ, δ̂ and A1 ŵ + ŵ = û,
and all these relations lie in ker γ. The remaining generator c, the image of γ̂, is central because

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


γAj = γ. The presentation is thus hc, x, y | c central, xy = cl0 , x3 = cl1 , y 4 = cl2 i. Eliminating

regular-fibre lattice, containing c, generates the entire group Z/n. The same is true of each

Proposition 10.1 (The complete Frölicher differential in terms of h). For a compact complex
threefold with (21) and the complex de Rham cohomology of S 6 , the Frölicher spectral sequence
satisfies E1 6= E2 = E∞ . Its only nonzero d1 ranks are

                  rank d0,1
                        1 = 1,        rank d1,1
                                            1 = h,          rank d1,2
                                                                  1 = h,      rank d2,2
                                                                                    1 = 1.

In particular its two middle rows are exact.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (21).

Proof. Here E1p,q = H q (X, ΩpX ) and dr : Erp,q −→ Erp+r,q−r+1 are complex-linear. For r = 2, any
source in the two middle rows has target in one of (2, 0), (3, 0), (3, 1) or outside the table, except
the source (0, 2), which is zero. Sources in row q = 3 outside (3, 3) are zero, and (3, 3) has no
target. For r = 3 the only possible targets inside the table have sources (0, 2) or (0, 3), both zero.
For r > 3 there is no arrow inside the table. A zero term remains zero on subsequent pages.
Hence E2 = E∞ .
    The filtration on HdRk (X; C) has no nonzero associated graded term for 1 ≤ k ≤ 5. Every

middle term of E2 therefore vanishes. Consequently

              0 −→ C −→ Ch+1 −→ Ch −→ 0,                     0 −→ Ch −→ Ch+1 −→ C −→ 0

are exact, giving the stated ranks. The first rank is one, so E1 cannot equal E2 .

The totals are (1, 0, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1) and (1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 0, 1), respectively.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.9; Stelzig (2021, Theorem
3); proposition 10.1; Stelzig (2021, Proposition 6(1)); equation (23).

Proof. We apply the structure theorem for bounded double complexes over a field, Stelzig (2021,
Theorem 3), to the actual algebraic double complex (A•,• (X), ∂, ∂).
                                                                   ¯ The word bounded refers
to the bidegrees, not to the dimensions of the spaces of smooth forms, so that theorem applies
here. It gives a direct-sum decomposition by isomorphisms of double complexes into squares and
zigzags. An odd zigzag has one-dimensional total cohomology. All odd zigzags in intermediate
total degree are therefore excluded by b1 = · · · = b5 = 0. An odd zigzag of length greater than
one would have at least two vertices of its cohomological total degree. The extreme diagonals
p + q = 0 and p + q = 6 contain just one bidegree each, so the remaining odd zigzags are exactly
one dot at (0, 0) and one at (3, 3).
    An even zigzag of length 2r contributes a nonzero dr to one of the two Frölicher spectral
sequences. 10.1 and complex conjugation exclude r ≥ 2 in both sequences. Thus the remaining
summands are arrows. The horizontal arrows, with their multiplicities, are

                                      source target multiplicity
                                       (0, 1) (1, 1)           1
                                       (1, 1) (2, 1)           h                               (23)
                                       (1, 2) (2, 2)           h
                                       (2, 2) (3, 2)          1.

The vertical arrows are their reflections in p = q, with the same multiplicities. The correspondence
with spectral-sequence ranks is Stelzig (2021, Proposition 6(1)); alternatively one computes
column cohomology on each horizontal arrow directly.
    We now evaluate the displayed definitions, rather than use a formula for the dimensions.
On an arrow, the source is killed by neither the outgoing differential nor its total differential,
whereas its target is closed under both. There is no composite ∂ ∂. ¯ Hence the target contributes
one dimension to Bott–Chern cohomology, and the source contributes one dimension to Aeppli
cohomology. On a square, only the top right corner is closed under both operators, and it is
the image of ∂ ∂¯ from the bottom left corner. The other three corners of the square are images
of ∂ or ∂,
         ¯ while the bottom left corner is not in ker ∂ ∂. ¯ Thus a square contributes to neither
cohomology. A dot contributes once to each. These computations commute with direct sums,
including the possibly infinite sum of squares. Counting the sources and targets in (23) and its
reflection gives (22).

Proposition 10.9 (Metric obstructions that do not require h). The threefold X admits no
balanced, strongly Gauduchon, Kähler, locally conformally Kähler, or Hermitian-symplectic
metric.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let θ = f ∗ ωF S . It is a nonzero semipositive exact real (1, 1) form. If ω were balanced,
the real four-form ω 2 would be closed and X θ ∧ ω 2 > 0, because the integrand is positive on
                                             R

the regular locus. Exactness of θ and Stokes’ theorem give zero, a contradiction.
    More generally, if ω were strongly Gauduchon, write ∂ω 2 = ∂u     ¯ with u ∈ A3,1 . The real
four-form Ω = ω − u − ū is closed. Bidegrees give θ ∧ Ω = θ ∧ ω , so the same argument applies.
                 2                                                2

Kähler metrics are balanced. If dω = ` ∧ ω with a closed real Lee form `, then b1 = 0 gives ` = dv,
and d(e−v ω) = 0, excluding locally conformally Kähler metrics. Finally any symplectic two-form
on X is exact because b2 = 0. Its cube has nonzero integral for its symplectic orientation,
whereas an exact cube has zero integral. Thus X is not symplectic and in particular admits no
Hermitian-symplectic metric.

Proposition 10.10 (Gauduchon metrics with specified Chern–Ricci form). There exists a

Gauduchon metric ω with [ω 2 ]A = [ω02 ]A and
                                          RicCh (ω) = πf ∗ ωF S .                                   (29)
This Ricci form is semipositive and has rank one at regular points of f . No Chern–Ricci-flat
Hermitian metric exists on X.

Székelyhidi et al. (2017, Theorem 1.3); section P.11.
   This is the application of Gauduchon (1985, Theorem 2) and Székelyhidi et al. (2017,

the asserted four dimensions.

Proposition 11.4 (Local complexes and every noncusp torsion length). Let z ∈
                                                                           / Z. At a regular
resonance t∗ in (D.15), with A = C{t − t∗ }, the two stalks are

       (R1 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))t∗ = (A/(t − t∗ ))2 ,      (R2 f∗ (TX ⊗ Mz ))t∗ = A/((t − t∗ )2 ).   (D.18)

At p1 , write z = n + k(3β1 + 4 − 2ρ), k 6= 0, when this is possible. Both coarse stalks are killed
by t and have length 1 + n , with n as in 11.1. At p2 , write z = n + k(2β2 + 3 − 3i), k 6= 0,

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 11.1; proposition 8.7.

Proof. We first give the comparison that turns the local calculation into a computation of the
sheaves. On a simply connected disc of smooth torus fibres, including a finite root cover, retain
the real marking and the holomorphic period matrix. Translation by Π(s)v, for fixed v ∈ R4 , is
holomorphic on the total family. After subtracting the integer cocycle of a resonance, the line
bundle has constant lattice multipliers. Multiplying the lifted real translation by its constant
factor of automorphy makes the lattice act as the identity and gives a genuine compact real torus
action on the line bundle. The same action acts on the tangent bundle by differentiation. It
commutes with the full Dolbeault differential.
    Averaging over this compact torus projects the relative Dolbeault complex onto its invariant
part. Choose the lift so that the central trivial line has trivial character. On every nonzero
Fourier character, the relative Dolbeault symbol is exterior multiplication by a nonzero covector;
contraction by a dual covector is a contracting homotopy. After shrinking the disc, these
nonzero covectors have a uniform positive lower bound for bounded Fourier frequency and
grow linearly for unbounded frequency, because the real period matrices and their inverses stay
bounded. The homotopies therefore preserve smooth Fourier series, with all derivatives, and are
uniform on compact subsets of the disc. The tangent extension is triangular with respect to its
vertical and horizontal parts; its nilpotent off-diagonal term is treated by the finite homological
perturbation series, so every nonzero Fourier complex is still contractible. Thus averaging is a
quasi-isomorphism, not merely a fibrewise dimension comparison.
    The chain-level comparison can be written without an unspecified holomorphic gauge. Write
the normalized period matrix as [Z(s), I] and use the real coordinates ζ = Z(s)x + y, with
x, y ∈ R2 /Z2 . Set

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 11.1; proposition 11.2;
proposition 11.4; question T.3.

Proof. The support assertions and all stalks were proved in 11.2–11.4. The direct image in
degree zero is zero for a nonintegral twist: it has generic rank zero and is torsion-free, since
multiplication by a nonzero base function is injective on the bundle on the smooth integral total
space. The support of either higher coherent direct image is a proper closed analytic subset of
the compact curve, and hence is finite. This proves finiteness of Rz as well as the absence of
an accumulation at the special values. If two integer tuples at a marked fibre represented the
same trivialized line, their difference would be an integral real class in H 1,0 , which is zero. Thus
there is no multiplicity from duplicate tuples. Formula (D.26) follows by the decomposition of a
finite-support sheaf into its local modules. Its global sections have dimension equal to its length
and its H 1 is zero, so Leray gives (D.25).
    To clarify the word generic, the global closed form Gγ in T.3 defines a holomorphic line bundle
on X × C by the integrable operators ∂¯ − 2πizGγ . Proper coherent base change for the projection
to C makes each cohomology-dimension threshold an analytic subset. A real noninteger z has no
resonance by (D.17) and (D.16), so the generic values are attained. All possible exceptional values
were shown to form a countable set. Thus each actual threshold exceeding a generic dimension is
a proper analytic subset of a complex curve and is locally discrete. Some indexed resonances,
namely the two invisible order-four congruences, produce no jump; (D.25) distinguishes them.
    This is an explicit countable description of the jump loci in the Picard coordinate, rather
than a generic assertion. It can also be indexed algebraically on the elliptic surface. If a regular
fibre has torsion section P of exact order rt , choose its marked relation qt τ + rt µ = pt . Its full
resonance lattice is                                          
                                      Z + 6qt µ(t) + rt βc (t) Z.
Every regular resonance arises this way. The underlying values t are exactly the non-special
roots of the division polynomials ψN (P ), N ≥ 2. The nonintegral lattice points contribute
two to Jz for each distinct such fibre. The finite-point lattices have the congruence weights
already stated. The script d_division_polynomials.py evaluates the polynomials exactly for
2 ≤ N ≤ 12; for example the first nonconstant regular factors are 5t − 32, 89t2 + 4736t − 4096
and 11t2 − 6016t + 8192. These computations specify an executable enumeration of the resonance
loci without inventing decimal values for the unspecified parameter c.
    As an independent index check, c1 (X) = c2 (X) = c1 (M ) = 0 in integral cohomology, so the
degree-six Riemann–Roch integrand for the actual twisted tangent bundle is c3 /2. Its integral is
one. Both (D.13) and (D.25) have alternating sum one. The index is used here to verify the
completed sheaf calculation, not to select its lengths.

Source and re-derivation of the tangent theorem. The tangent cohomology (1, 1, 1, 0)
and the smooth one-dimensional Kuranishi germ are theorems of Du, Guo, Kusakabe, and Xie,
arXiv:2610.00250v1, Section 6 (Du et al., 2026a). The invariant run re-derived these results after
reading that paper. The present proof prints the root-base calculation, its local comparisons,
and the additional coarse direct images and all Picard twists. Version 2 (Du et al., 2026c) does
not contain the deformation section; this does not alter the credit for the version 1 theorems.

Proof. The precise Albanese lattices in proposition 3.5 are verified by projecting all translations

                      √ Thus the positive-imaginary period representatives are −κ1 and −κ2 /2.

    The identity q2 = iw/216 in Proposition 22.1 has factor 1/2 precisely because of the Albanese

boundary points. The existence criterion and exact 2Z identification are theorems 3.8 and 5.5;
the latter is also Theorem 1.4 (label p2:thm:exact-period) of Du et al. (2026b). Its hypotheses
specify precisely the retained period family, affine finite twists and cusp collar. They coincide
with the marked family Xc ; the normalization differs only by the fixed choice of the particular
solution, which does not alter parameter differences. Version 2 drops that theorem; we infer no
mathematical conclusion from this omission.
    The Fourier expansion for J converges for 0 < |q| < 1 and has a simple pole at q = 0. The
inverse image under q = −w2 /483 is the claimed punctured disc and the pole has order two. The
inequality 216 < 483/2 is equivalent to 27 < 64. At every nonzero point on the larger boundary
the map to q is locally biholomorphic. A continuation there would continue J through the unit
circle, contradicting the rational-cusp argument proved in Proposition 22.1. The phrase “up to
the radius” therefore means the open punctured disc, not holomorphy on its bounding circle or
at its central pole.

d0 = d¯0 in C/Z, hence d0 has a real representative. Composing the reflection with translation by
−d0 /2 makes its square the identity. Necessity and sufficiency for an involution follow.

Proof. The division polynomial ψn (Pt ) is a nonzero rational polynomial in t. To check
nonvanishing for every n, a hypothetical torsion identity would express the elliptic logarithm as

Statement C.5. For a CM curve, the Coates–Wiles theorem, in the form Rubin (1999, Theorem
10.1), says that a nonzero central Hecke L-value forces the Mordell–Weil group over the CM
field to be finite. For a nonmaximal CM order first pass to an isogenous curve with maximal
order; ranks and L-functions are unchanged. Since L(E/K, s) = L(E/Q, s)2 for the CM field
K, nontorsion therefore forces L(E, 1) = 0. This proves the needed central vanishing also in the
two sign-+1 cases. The functional equation then forces L0 (E, 1) = 0 for those two curves. The
positive first or second derivatives just evaluated prove exactly the asserted analytic ranks.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Gross and Zagier, 1986); Gross (1991,
Theorem 1.3); Jetchev et al. (2008, Theorem 1.1).

Proof. Gross–Zagier’s theorem applies because each curve is modular and L(Ei , 1) = 0. CM
modularity follows from its Hecke-character theta series. Their Theorem I.7.3, in the opened
original preprint (Gross and Zagier, 1986), gives a rational point R and a nonzero rational factor
relating L0 (E, 1) to its canonical height times the real period. Changing their period convention
to the full real period changes that factor only rationally. As L0 (Ei , 1) > 0, R has infinite order.
Primitivity gives R = mPi + T , m 6= 0, T torsion; its height is m2b        h(Pi ). This proves (43),
including positivity.
    The rank-one Gross–Zagier–Kolyvagin implication asserts rank one and finite Tate–Shafarevich
group when the central zero is simple. One can use Kolyvagin’s Heegner-point theorem as stated
in Gross (1991, Theorem 1.3), together with the nonzero Gross–Zagier Heegner height; a modern
primary research statement of the rank conclusion is Jetchev et al. (2008, Theorem 1.1). The
hypotheses are satisfied separately by the positive derivative and exact sign in each of the nine
rows. The two remaining rows have analytic rank two, and this implication makes no assertion of
a height formula or of finiteness of their Tate–Shafarevich groups. In particular it cannot express
the second derivative in terms of the height of P alone: the rank-two regulator involves a second
independent point and their height pairing.

The scope of Rubin’s theorem. The applicable ordinary CM results concern a prime p at
which E has good ordinary reduction, equivalently p splits in the CM field. One precise opened
formulation of Rubin’s rank-one formula is Bertolini et al. (2012, Theorem 1): for a curve over Q
with CM by the maximal order, an ordinary prime prime to the conductor, and a simple central
zero, an appropriate Katz p-adic L-value is, up to a nonzero algebraic factor, the square of a
formal logarithm of a nontorsion rational point divided by a p-adic period. Its input is analytic
rank one, already verified here. It is a p-adic identity; it does not identify the real exponential
exp b
    h(P ) as algebraic.
    For the p-part of the real leading-term formula, a modern precise version is Castella (2025,
Theorem A). In addition to analytic rank one it requires full CM, abelian torsion field over the
CM field, p - 6hK , splitting of p, conductor prime to p, and that the different of K divide the
Hecke conductor exactly. For the maximal odd-discriminant cases here, the latter follows from
the exponent two of the ramified prime in the rational conductor. The nonmaximal cases of
discriminant −12 and −28 can be passed through a 2-isogeny at p > 3. The discriminant −16
case requires care: the direct application of this version has a different-conductor hypothesis at
2 that fails, and we do not claim that this particular formulation proves its full leading-term
formula. Rubin’s original ordinary main-conjecture paper is (Rubin, 1991); its bibliographic
record was checked, but its complete theorem text was not available in the opened publisher
copy, so no additional hypothesis-free claim is based on it here.
    In particular these ordinary-prime statements
                                                √ do not prove that the 3-primary part of Sha
has order 9 for the last curve: 3 is inert in Q( −163) and also excluded from the stated p > 3
hypotheses. 13.10 proves the corresponding analytic quotient to be exactly 9 by a separate
denominator argument. The identification with the actual Tate–Shafarevich group remains a
separate arithmetic question in that row.

is surjective. Since p is odd and unramified in K, this also proves that the conductor contains

remains true for D = −3 because |d| > 1.

Proposition 14.9 (the correctly normalized equidistribution). Let Dn be the divisor, with
intersection multiplicity, of parameters t ∈ P1 \ {0, 1, ∞} for which nPt = O. Then

                       n2              1                                1
            deg Dn =      + O(1),         [Dn ] −→ mP ,                     [Dn ] −→ 12mP
                       12              n2                            deg Dn
weakly as n → ∞ through indices for which Dn 6= 0. For any nonrepeating sequence of individual
algebraic torsion parameters, their Galois-orbit probability measures likewise converge to 12mP .
Thus the probability limit requires the factor 12.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; DeMarco and Mavraki (2020, Theorem
1.1 and Corollary 1.2); proposition 13.4; proposition 14.8.

Proof. We apply DeMarco and Mavraki (2020, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2). Their hypotheses
are a number field, a smooth projective base curve, an elliptic surface and a rational section of
nonzero generic canonical height. Here they are Q, P1 , the displayed rational elliptic surface,
and P , whose generic height for (O) is 1/12 by 13.4. At a torsion specialization the canonical
height is zero. Corollary 1.2 consequently gives convergence of every nonrepeating sequence of
Galois-orbit probability measures.
    The limiting measure is the curvature of the height metric divided by the degree of its line
bundle. In our normalization, 14.8 computes the curvature as mP , and 13.4 computes that degree
as 1/12. Hence the probability measure is 12mP . This division by the degree is essential: a
measure of mass 1/12 cannot be a weak limit of probability measures. The source’s informal
description of the pullback current is interpreted with this normalization.
    For completeness, the passage from individual orbits to the full division divisor does not
require uniformity of the equidistribution theorem in n. The surface height formula, with our
half-self-pairing convention, reads
                                                        1
                                                                     contrv (Q).
                                                             X
                            hO (Q) = χ(OE ) + (Q · O) −
                            b
                                                        2        v

Here χ = 1, and the finitely many fibre corrections are bounded as Q = nP varies, because they
depend only on its component. Since b   hO (nP ) = n2 /12, it follows that (nP · O) = n2 /12 + O(1).
Removing the singular fibres changes this by O(1): the local intersection at each such fibre is
bounded as n varies in characteristic zero. One can see this in the formal group after a fixed
multiple enters it; multiplication by a nonzero integer is a local analytic isomorphism over the
residue field C. Thus deg Dn = n2 /12 + O(1).
    At any fixed smooth torsion parameter t0 , of exact order d, the multiplicity in Dn is zero
unless d | n, and is constant when d | n. Indeed the formal parameter of nP = [n/d](dP ) has first
term (n/d) times that of dP , with nonzero constant coefficient. Fix a continuous test function
and ε > 0. Corollary 1.2 implies that all but finitely many distinct Galois orbits of torsion
parameters have average within ε of the limiting integral; otherwise a countersequence would
violate it. The total weighted contribution of the finitely many exceptional orbits is bounded
independently of n, by the multiplicity observation. Divide by deg Dn and let n → ∞. This
proves the probability convergence for Dn , and the degree asymptotic proves the unnormalized
version.

16 Periods, compact subgroups, and the transcendence question
We use a Weierstrass equation over Q and its invariant differential. Its period lattice is Λ =

extend η : Λ → C real-linearly to C. The discriminant in this section is the discriminant of this
equation, equivalently of the lattice in the specified differential. The quantity N is independent
of changing this algebraic equation and differential.

16.1    The conditional theorem and its exact conjectural input
We use Grothendieck’s period conjecture in the form stated as Conjecture 1.1 of Bertolin et al.
(2022): for a motive M over Q, the field generated by its periods over Q has transcendence degree
dim Gmot (M ). Only 1-motives occur below. We also use their Construction 3.4 and Lemma 3.5:
if B is the smallest abelian subvariety generated by the point and extension data, and Z(1) is
the central torus constructed from the Weil-pairing bracket and the remaining algebraic lift, then
                       dim Gmot (M ) = dim Gmot (A) + 2 dim B + dim Z(1).                       (84)
The bracket is described explicitly in their Section 6.1. Their Table 2 corrects the table in the
paper they discuss; the dependent nondeficient case has unipotent dimension three. We now
verify which case occurs here.
Proposition 16.3 (the motivic groups needed on the diagonal). Let P be nontorsion and let R
be any algebraic lift above P in GP . Put MR = [Z → GP ], 1 7→ R. Its connected motivic group
is, after a choice of Levi subgroup, the semidirect product of Gmot (E) and the three-dimensional
Heisenberg group attached to H1 (E) and its principal polarization. Its dimension is 5 for CM
and 7 without CM.
    For a non-real embedding put M = MR ⊕ MR . If E and Ē are not isogenous, its dimension
is 13. If they are isogenous, choose an isogeny φ : Ē → E of degree d and write Q = φ(P̄ ). Let r
be the dimension over F = End(E) ⊗ Q of the span of P, Q, modulo torsion. Then
                               case     dim B dim Z            dim Gmot (M)
                          r = 2, E CM     2     2                    8
                        r = 2, E not CM   2     2                    10
                          r = 1, E CM     1   1+e                  5+e
                        r = 1, E not CM   1   1+e                  7 + e.

                                                 123
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


Here e is either zero or one: it is zero precisely when the algebraic lift in the one-dimensional
quotient of the two central tori by the bracket torus is torsion. This criterion is independent of
the choices made modulo isogeny. In the real case we use the single motive MR ; no extra quotient
torus is necessary.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (84).

Proof. All curves, polarizations, points, and lifts are algebraic over Q, as required by Construction
3.4 and Lemma 3.5. For MR the smallest abelian subvariety containing (P, P ) is the diagonal
B = E, since P is nontorsion. If ψ is the polarization pairing, the bracket on this diagonal is

                           [(x, x), (y, y)] = ψ(x, y) − ψ(y, x) = 2ψ(x, y).

It is nonzero and spans Q(1). Hence Z 0 = Z = Gm ; there is no deficient or Ribet exception,
including for CM. The pure group is GL2 without CM and ResF /Q Gm for the imaginary quadratic
CM field. Their dimensions are four and two. This proves the single-motive assertion, including
its Lie bracket and Levi action: the action on the centre is the polarization multiplier.
    For the direct sum only the two diagonal central coordinates occur. If the two elliptic curves
are not isogenous, they cannot be CM conjugates. The pure group is {(g1 , g2 ) ∈ GL22 : det g1 =
det g2 }, of dimension seven. The point data generate E × Ē, and the two brackets are independent,
giving 7 + 4 + 2 = 13.
    If the curves are isogenous, transport the second polarized factor through φ. Its polarization
pairing becomes ψ/d. The smallest abelian subvariety has dimension r. For r = 2, independent
variation in its two factors makes the two diagonal brackets span both central coordinates; thus
Z 0 = Z = G2m . The unipotent group is the product of two Heisenberg groups, with the same
pure group acting on both standard factors. For r = 1, after multiplying the points by a common
integer we may write Q = aP , a ∈ F × . The bracket image is the one-dimensional line with
proportional central coordinates
                                                       aa†
                                       (1, c),    c=       > 0,                                   (85)
                                                        d
where † is the Rosati involution. On an elliptic curve aa† is a positive rational number: a square
in the non-CM case and the positive field norm in the CM case. Construction 3.4(3) adds a
further central direction exactly when the image of the algebraic lift in the quotient torus is
nontorsion. This is the integer e above. The unipotent Lie algebra is the Heisenberg algebra,
with one additional central Tate line when e = 1. Formula (84) proves every entry of the table.
This description computes the group even when the lift contributes a Kummer factor; specifying
only the span of P, Q would not determine that last factor.

Proposition 16.4 (conditionally: transcendence of the local norm). Assume Grothendieck’s
period conjecture for 1-motives over Q. For every algebraic parameter t 6= 0, 1 at which Pt is
nontorsion, N (Pt ) is transcendental. More generally the conclusion holds for every nontorsion
algebraic point on an elliptic curve over Q. The weaker named Relative Semi-abelian Conjecture
4.7 of Bertolin et al. (2022), restricted to the groups and algebraic lifts used in this proof, already
suffices.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Bertolin et al. (2022); proposition 16.2;
equation (82); Bertolin et al. (2022, Remark 4.13); equation (85); equation (87); equation (86).

Proof. Suppose N (P ) is algebraic. Statement 16.2 supplies an algebraic lift R = (P, r) in GP (C)c ,
and its conjugate supplies a lift R̄ in GP̄ (C)c . Let v denote the logarithmic coordinate in (82).
Put
            K0 = Q entries of the full de Rham–Betti period matrix of GP × GP̄ .
                                                                                    


                                                 124
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


Here “full” includes the integrals of differentials of the second kind, hence the quasi-periods ηj , as
well as the periods ωj , the third-kind periods κj , and 2πi. It is the matrix ΩG in their Definition
2.4, not merely the lattice in the Lie algebra of the semi-abelian variety. This field contains u, ζ(u)
and their complex conjugates. Indeed it contains the pure periods, 2πi, and κj = ζ(u)ωj − ηj u;
the determinant of the two equations for u, ζ(u) is, up to sign, ω1 η2 − ω2 η1 = −2πi. This is also
the observation of Bertolin et al. (2022, Remark 4.13). The real-linear expression for η(u) is

                                       (uω̄2 − ūω2 )η1 + (ūω1 − uω̄1 )η2
                              η(u) =                                       .                      (86)
                                                 ω1 ω̄2 − ω̄1 ω2
The denominator is nonzero. Thus uη(u) and its conjugate belong to K0 . The compact equation
χ(R) = 0 becomes the algebraic relation over K0

                              v + v̄ = uζ(u) + ūζ(u) − uη(u) − ūη(u).                           (87)

Complex conjugates here are coordinates of the conjugate 1-motive. They are not being treated
as rational functions of un-conjugated periods without justification.
    Consider the period torsor of M over the period torsor of G = GP × GP̄ . The kernel of the
corresponding motivic groups is its weight −2 vector group Lie Z, of dimension dim Z. There
is no weight −1 kernel: the point coordinates are exactly the extension coordinates under the
polarization, so BQ = 0. More explicitly, projection of the smallest abelian variety B to the
variety generated by the extension coordinates is an isogeny, since B is the graph of the same
point data in the two factors. It therefore induces an isomorphism on the weight −1 graded Lie
algebras. The motive [0 → G] has only weights −1 and −2, and its unipotent Lie algebra has
no weight −2 graded piece. Thus the entire kernel is exactly W−2 Lie Gmot (M); no additional
abelian direction or unaccounted logarithm remains in the fibre. After evaluating the base
periods, the fibre is an affine torsor over K0 under that vector group. Translation in its two
central coordinates changes (v, v̄) by 2πi(c1 , c2 ), with the signs fixed by using a positive Tate
loop for each motive. The linear functional c1 + c2 is nonzero on this central group. It is nonzero
on the whole plane when dim B = 2, and when dim B = 1 it is already nonzero on the bracket
line (85), because 1 + c > 0.
    Consequently (87) cuts a proper affine hyperplane in the period-torsor fibre. It forces the
relative transcendence degree of the actual periods over K0 to be at most dim Z − 1. The
pure-base period torsor has dimension dim Gmot (G), so the total transcendence degree is at most
dim Gmot (M) − 1. This contradicts the asserted period conjecture. For real data the single
motive suffices: conjugation acts on its Betti realization over Q, and the same equation has a
nonzero coefficient on its one central direction. One can also double the point and lift into the
identity component, choose u, ω1 real, and read the relation directly as

                                     ω1 v − ω1 uζ(u) + η1 u2 = 0.

Doubling preserves the equivalence of algebraicity of N by the division formula and its algebraic
nonzero factors.
    For the weaker conjectural input, Conjecture 4.7 asserts relative transcendence degree at
least 2 dim BQ + dim Z. All Ri used here are algebraic, BQ = 0, and the generalized logarithms
add exactly the central coordinates to K0 . Thus it contradicts the same hyperplane relation
directly. Proposition 4.12 of that paper derives Conjecture 4.7 from the generalized period
conjecture; in our case the field of definition is algebraic, so the ordinary period conjecture is
enough. The weaker Conjecture 4.9, formulated using arbitrary algebraic translates, gives a zero
lower bound at an algebraic point and does not by itself yield this conclusion. Linear relations
among 1-periods are also insufficient: after clearing the denominator in (86), the prohibited
relation is polynomial, not a linear relation with algebraic coefficients.

16.2    CM theta normalization and further unconditional deductions
The holomorphic theta normalization proposed for the CM interpolation approach differs from
the norm occurring in the stated problem. We make that distinction explicit, including the
finite-character ambiguity in the multiplication law.
Proposition 16.6 (the exact CM multiplication law). Let E/Q have complex multiplication by
an order O, and use an algebraic invariant differential. Write A = area(Λ) and

               div(Fα ) = 2[α]∗ (O) − 2d(O),          Fα (expE z) = α2 z 2−2d (1 + O(z 2 )).

For αΛ ⊂ Λ, the exponential multipliers of θ(αz)/θ(z)d cancel because αᾱ = d. Its remaining

give F1+i = 2i℘. The unsquared quotient has a simple zero at the nonzero point in ker(1 + i)
and a simple pole at O, which is not a principal divisor on E; its square is the rational function
just displayed.

Neither formula excludes algebraicity of N (P ): transcendence of one complex factor does

finite-order interpolation approach supplies only the rank-two set Ou; it does not meet the
proposed rank-greater-than-four criterion. The derivative approach would need the algebraicity
of θ0 (u)/θ(u) = ζ(u) − s2 u, which 16.7 excludes. Replacing the norm by the holomorphic theta
value would therefore change the problem precisely by the factor in (89).
    The related independence theorem of Reyssat (1982, Corollary 2) says that two of eiπu/ω1 , s(u)
and s0 (u) are algebraically independent, where s(z) = σ(z)e−η1 z /(2ω1 ) . For real u, hypothetical
                                                                    2


algebraicity of N (P ) makes s(u) algebraic, so the conclusion instead forces independence of eiπu/ω1
and ζ(u) − η1 u/ω1 ; it yields no contradiction. The periodic-functional-equation theorem reported
in Waldschmidt (1988a, p. 15-05) assumes algebraic q = eiπτ , whereas this q is transcendental
for imaginary quadratic τ by Gelfond–Schneider. These specific checked applications therefore
do not decide the metric norm; their source scopes and the larger CM independence tuples are
recorded separately.
    We also tested an additive-extension route. Bost and Künnemann (2009, Theorem 3.1.2)
proves that an algebraic point of the universal vector extension of an abelian variety which lies in
its maximal compact subgroup at one complex embedding is torsion. The theorem’s hypotheses
require an algebraic point of the vector extension, equivalently an algebraic line bundle with an
algebraic connection having unitary monodromy. 16.2 supplies only an algebraic point in one
fibre of a multiplicative extension. It does not supply that algebraic connection. Differentiating
a metric value at one algebraic point cannot establish algebraicity of the connection there or
globally. This is the exact missing implication in that attempt.
    Another route uses the Lattès map fE defined by x(2Q) = fE (x(Q)). Its canonical height
is b
   hfE (x(P )) = 2bhO (P ). For rational parameters C.6 therefore makes algebraicity of N (P )
equivalent to algebraicity of exp(b  hfE (x(P ))). Nguyen (2023, Theorem 1.4 and Corollary 1.6)
settle the corresponding multiplicative-height problem for nonintegrable polynomials using
Böttcher coordinates in the basin of infinity. They do not apply to fE . Indeed an elliptic
duplication Lattès map has no exceptional point: the inverse images of any point contain the

                                                128
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


images of all successive division points of an elliptic point, an infinite set. A polynomial has the
exceptional point ∞, so no conjugate of fE is polynomial. The Julia set is the whole sphere and
the required basin of infinity is absent. This checks the failed hypothesis, rather than treating a
theorem for polynomials as a theorem for all rational maps.
    We also checked the arithmetic algebraicity criterion of Xie (2024, Theorems 1.3 and 2.3).
Besides sufficiently rapid height-normalized approximation by points in a fixed number field,
it requires the analytic germ to be formally defined over that field. This hypothesis fails for
the compact leaf in 16.9: its tangent has the proved transcendental slope c = ζ(u) − η1 u/ω1 . A
smooth formal germ defined over Q has an algebraic tangent; algebraic translations, coordinate
changes and isogenies preserve this obstruction. Assuming N (P ) algebraic supplies an algebraic
point on the leaf and its integer multiples, but not an algebraic formal germ. Attempting to force
convergence by successive division also loses the fixed-number-field hypothesis: if [2]n Qn = Q
with all Qn ∈ E(K) for one number field, then b     hO (Qn ) = 4−nbhO (Q) > 0. The Qn are distinct
with bounded ample height, contrary to Northcott finiteness. The full hypothesis audit and the
opened preprint are retained in the records.

A current source whose theorem text remains unchecked. The publisher’s abstract
for Pham (2025) announces complex and p-adic linear-independence results for semiabelian
varieties and applications to Weierstrass sigma functions. We opened its metadata, abstract
and reference list, but both the full-HTML link and the publisher’s citation-PDF link returned
the abstract/access page. No accessible author manuscript was located. Consequently we could
not check any theorem statement or its hypotheses. This is a potentially relevant unverified
source: we make no claim either that it settles the Gaussian norm question or that its results are
inapplicable to it.

16.3    The precise nonarchimedean comparison
Proposition 16.8 (with derivation: a nonzero ordinary height). Let E/Q have complex
multiplication by the full ring of integers of an imaginary quadratic field K of class number
one. Assume that its functional-equation sign is −1, and let p > 3 be a prime of good ordinary
reduction, pOK = pp∗ . For a nontorsion P ∈ E(Q) the p-adic height and the cyclotomic p-adic
height of P over K, in the normalization of Agboola and Howard (2006, Appendix A), are nonzero.
In particular this applies to

                       E : y 2 + y = x3 − 38x + 90,    P = (0, 9),     p = 5.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Agboola and Howard (2006, Appendix
A); Agboola and Howard (2006); section P.17; proposition 16.6; Bertrand (1995, Theorem 2.1);
proposition 16.3; proposition 16.4; Bertrand (1995, Theorem 3.1); Bost and Künnemann (2009);
proposition 16.2.
    The nonvanishing theorem is reproduced in Rubin’s Appendix A, Theorem A.1 and Lemma A.2
of Agboola and Howard (2006); the exact hypotheses and application are retained. A complete
re-derivation is given in Appendix P.17.
    The comparison explains the missing step in an attempted archimedean adaptation. The
ordinary p-adic sigma construction uses a holomorphic quadratic correction. In the CM
normalization the corresponding complex holomorphic function is θ of 16.6, whereas the real
metric also contains exp(−π|u|2 /(2A)). Theorem A.1 supplies no identity between the ordinary
p-adic height and that real factor. Transferring the conclusion would require precisely such a
new argument; replacing the real factor by the holomorphic CM correction does not preserve the
norm being asked about.


                                                129
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                            Paper I


    There is also a definite limitation on the maximal-compact approach. Bertrand (1995,
Theorem 2.1) constructs nontrivial multiplicative extensions of polarized abelian varieties with
nontorsion algebraic points in their maximal real compact subgroup. Its hypotheses include an
endomorphism not fixed by the Rosati involution and a nontorsion rational point over a real
number field. The construction uses a base point related to the extension class by a Rosati-
antisymmetric endomorphism. It cannot be replaced by a theorem saying that every algebraic
compact point of every multiplicative extension is torsion. For our diagonal class, an equality
N P = f (P ) with N > 0 and f + f † = 0 would force P torsion: N − f has no zero eigenvalue,
since (N − f )† (N − f ) = N 2 − f 2 is positive. In the elliptic case this is simply a nonzero isogeny.
The diagonal positivity used in 16.3–16.4 is therefore essential, but these counterexamples neither
prove nor refute the desired unconditional diagonal statement. The additive result in Bertrand
(1995, Theorem 3.1), and its higher-dimensional extension in Bost and Künnemann (2009),
requires a point in a vector extension, a hypothesis not furnished by 16.2.

Proof. The torus is the maximal connected affine subgroup of Gq . Consequently every

   The difference between the given endomorphism and [n] has image in the torus and is trivial
on the torus. It therefore factors through an algebraic-group homomorphism E → Gm . This

                                                 130
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


homomorphism is zero, since a morphism from the proper connected curve E to the affine
