additional ambiguity from Hom(E, Gm ), and the endomorphism is exactly [n]. Conversely all
integer multiplications exist. This proves the first assertion.
    For the concrete curve, the tangent slope at P is −2, giving 2P = (4, −2). Its discriminant
is −193 and ψ2 (P ) = 2 · 9 + 1 = 19. The division identity in C.4 therefore gives the asserted
formula for N (Q), so replacing P by Q preserves algebraicity of the norm. This doubling also
places the base point in the identity component of the real elliptic group without any component
assumption. In the chosen differential the Weierstrass coordinates are (℘, ℘0 ) = (x, 2y + 1), with
g2 = 152, g3 = −361. The negative discriminant means that the real cubic has one real root.
Along (0, ω1 /2), ℘ decreases from +∞ to that root and ℘0 < 0. Since ℘0 (u) = 2(−2) + 1 = −3,
the indicated real logarithm of Q exists.

                                   (ω1 , ζ(u)ω1 − η1 u) = ω1 (1, c).

and real u, ω1 make c real.
    Suppose c were algebraic. Then `c would be an algebraic Lie subspace. Dividing the nonzero
period ω1 (1, c) by a sufficiently large positive integer gives a vector in `c whose exponential is a
nonzero torsion point of GQ , hence an algebraic point. The analytic subgroup theorem (Huber
and Wüstholz, 2023, Theorem 6.1) supplies a positive-dimensional connected algebraic subgroup
with Lie algebra contained in `c . Its dimension is one, and its projection to E is nontrivial. Such
a subgroup must be an elliptic curve E 0 projecting isogenously to E: a connected one-dimensional
affine algebraic group cannot map nontrivially to an elliptic curve. Its inclusion splits the pullback
of GQ to E 0 . The dual of that isogeny would therefore kill the extension class λ(Q), forcing Q
torsion. This contradicts 13.6. We conclude that c is transcendental. In particular the line is not
defined over Q. This argument uses the period vector alone; it does not assume algebraicity of
N (P ).

Proof. Use the principal polarization to identify the two extension classes with Q and βQ. They
are linearly independent over Q modulo torsion: any nonzero m + nβ is an isogeny, so (m + nβ)Q
cannot be torsion. A character of G2m given by (m, n) ∈ Z2 extends to G exactly when the

homomorphism G → Gm to the torus is zero. Such a homomorphism then factors through E
and is zero. This proves the asserted absence of characters. An isogenous semiabelian variety
cannot acquire a nonzero character, because composing it with the isogeny would give a nonzero
character of G.
    The Rosati adjoint of β is −β. Pullback by β sends the ordered extension classes to (−βQ, dQ),
exactly as does pushout by the displayed torus matrix. Equality of these extension classes provides
the endomorphism B. It is unique because Hom(E, G2m ) = 0. Its square induces [−d] on the
torus and on E, so the same uniqueness gives B 2 = [−d]. The map

                              End(G) ⊗ Q −→ End(E) ⊗ Q = Q(β)

is injective: an endomorphism inducing zero on E has image in the torus, and the absence of
characters makes it zero. Its image contains β, hence equals Q(β).

The precise several-variable criteria that were checked. The differential criterion of
Waldschmidt (2009, Theorems 3.6 and 3.7) requires a finite algebraically independent family
whose partial derivatives belong to the polynomial ring generated by that family over one
number field. Algebraic values of the full family then give algebraic values of all iterated partial
derivatives. The second-jet calculation above proves that a family containing H cannot satisfy
both requirements at the hypothesized algebraic orbit points. The issue persists although the
first cancelling direction is algebraic; the direction also varies with α.
     For a criterion without differential equations we opened Waldschmidt (1975, Theorem 1,
p. 24), including its proof and a visual check of the displayed inequalities. For d meromorphic
functions on Cn with growth and arithmetic-size exponents ρ1 , . . . , ρd , a set with cardinality
N `−o(1) in a ball of radius O(N ) and separation at least N −λ−o(1) yields algebraic dependence
under the strict condition
                                            d
                                                                                               (97)
                                            X
                              (d − 1)` >          ρj + 2d(n − 1)(λ + 1).
                                            j=1

The theorem also requires all function values to belong to one number field and bounds on
denominators in the entire representations of the meromorphic functions. We do not silently
discard these hypotheses.
    The natural independent triple here is ℘(z), ℘(w), H(z, w), all of order at most two. The
first two are algebraically independent. If H satisfied a polynomial over C(℘(z), ℘(w)), fix
a generic pair (z, w) and translate only z by mω, with 0 6= ω ∈ Λ. The coefficients of the
polynomial remain constant, whereas the absolute values of its proposed roots H(z + mω, w)
grow as exp(k|ω|2 m2 + O(|m|)). This contradicts the finite set of roots of a nonzero polynomial.
Thus the triple is independent.
    Even granting all the size and denominator bounds with the favorable exponents ρj = 2,
substitution of n = 2, d = 3 and ` = 4 into (97) would require

                                             8 > 12 + 6λ,

which fails even for λ = 0. The actual geometry is less favorable: the  N 4 points obtained
by bounding the four integer coefficients lie in a ball of radius O(N ) in a real plane. Packing
separated discs in that plane gives N 4  N 2+2λ+o(1) , hence λ ≥ 1. Removing the rank-two set
of poles does not change this count. Larger growth exponents only worsen the inequality. This
checks the particular published criterion rather than asserting that every possible multivariable
transcendence method fails. The missing unconditional step in C.7(c) remains the exclusion of
an algebraic value on the diagonal compact leaf.

   The alternative variable-degree theorems of Herblot and Gasbarri require a formal germ over
the residue number field, with additional arithmetic estimates. At a real nontorsion division
point with coordinate z and algebraic g(z),

                                     dg   g(z)          
                                        = 0    ζ(z) − bz .
                                     dx  ℘ (z)

The slope in parentheses is transcendental by the period-line argument of 16.9 applied to that
nontorsion algebraic point. The other two factors are nonzero algebraic numbers. Thus the germ
is not even defined over Q; the required arithmetic-germ hypothesis has not been gained by
passing to division values.

    We also checked the Mahler-functional-equation route against Adamczewski and Faverjon
(2017, Theorem 1.1 and system (1.2)). That theorem requires algebraic Taylor coefficients, a linear
power-map functional system and an algebraic regular argument. The compact normalization here
has the transcendental coefficient b, its elliptic logarithm is transcendental, and its duplication
in the algebraic coordinate is a Lattès map. We have not obtained a representation satisfying
the stated hypotheses; we do not assert that every alternative representation is impossible. The
entropy identity of Einsiedler et al. (2001, Theorem 5.1) uses a sequence of transformations built
from the denominators of x(2n Q), with scale 4n . It does not identify the height with the entropy
of a single finite-dimensional algebraic automorphism, and supplies no algebraic value for its
exponential.
    The period-refined algebraic-group rank theorem has also been checked in the original
sources (Waldschmidt, 1988b, Theorem 4.1 and Corollary 4.3) (Roy and Waldschmidt, 1993,
main theorem, p. 363). Its coefficient is α(G) = 2 dim G − 2d0 (G) − d1 (G), where d1 counts
multiplicative quotients, not the dimension of the torus subgroup. For the nonsplit GQ of 16.9,
d0 = d1 = 0: a nonzero character on its torus would kill a nonzero integer multiple of the
nontorsion extension class. Thus α(GQ ) = 4. The line `c has no nonzero algebraic vector, has
period rank κ = 1, and the norm hypothesis supplies one independent algebraic-point logarithm
in addition to that period. The theorem allows total rank 3 = (4 − 1) dim `c ; the available rank 2
therefore gives no contradiction. The period rank is exactly one because a second period on this
line would, by Legendre’s relation, force u/ω1 to be rational, contrary to the nontorsion of Q.

Its fixed curve is z0 = z2 = 0. This directly locates the incorrect identification of the family

be interchanged.

      The nonextension above is local and pointwise. It does not contradict extension of the
cohomology class over a cusp neighbourhood. The toric covering has rays (v, 1) for all v ∈
Z2 . Meridians about its toric divisors kill the whole cocharacter lattice: (0, 1) is a ray and
(ei , 1) − (0, 1) = (ei , 0). The toric cover is therefore simply connected. Its free period deck group
is Λ and hence
                                            π1 (N0 ) = Λ = Λ/K.
For the punctured cusp the map to this group kills K and the base meridian. The latter bounds
the disc given by a point of the dense orbit on a central component. Both long-period covectors
extend in integral H 1 , since they kill precisely these relations. In contrast, an extension of θγ to
all of X ≃ S 6 would induce a nonzero map H1 (F ) → Z factoring through H1 (X) = 0, which is
impossible. This last argument is the global cohomological obstruction; it says nothing about
pointwise cusp limits.

Proposition 17.3 (The filled three-dimensional target). For the original data the quotient over
the complement of the cusp disc is the exterior of the (3, 4) torus knot, with the specified Seifert
structure. For general admissible (l0 , l1 , l2 ) the filled quotient is the lens space determined by the
following meridian slopes in one oriented integral torus basis (ρ1 , h):

          µ1 = (3, −l1 ),     µ2 = (−4, 4l0 − l2 ),      det(µ1 , µ2 ) = p = 12l0 − 4l1 − 3l2 .

In the lens-space convention that the second meridian is −q0 µ1 + pλ1 , where det(µ1 , λ1 ) = 1, the
lens parameter satisfies 3q0 ≡ 4 (mod p). In particular the target depends only on the signed
integer p, and is a three-sphere exactly when |p| = 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let P be the three-holed sphere, with oriented boundary meridians ρ0 + ρ1 + ρ2 = 0 and
positive fibre h. The two finite meridian relations are 3ρ1 − l1 h = 0 and 4ρ2 − l2 h = 0; the cusp
solid-torus meridian is ρ0 + l0 h. Eliminating ρ0 gives ρ2 = l0 h − ρ1 on the annulus joining the
finite solid tori, which gives exactly (17.3). Since both slopes are primitive, this is a genus-one
Heegaard splitting. Choose a, b ∈ Z with al1 + 3b = 1 and put λ1 = (a, b). Direct multiplication
gives
                     µ2 = −q0 µ1 + pλ1 , q0 = a(4l0 − l2 ) + 4b, 3q0 − ap = 4.
This proves the claimed lens parameter in a convention fixed by actual meridians, including
orientations. The fundamental group of this gluing is Z/|p|. Admissibility implies gcd(p, 6) = 1,
so the modular inverse of 3 used above exists.
    For (l0 , l1 , l2 ) = (0, 1, −1) the two exceptional-fibre data are (3, 1), (4, −1). They are realized
by the circle action
                                   s · (z1 , z2 ) = (e4is z1 , e3is z2 ) on S 3 ⊂ C2 .
Its invariant map is [z13 : z24 ]; the local circle translation residues are 4−1 = 1 (mod 3) and
3−1 = −1 (mod 4). Removing a regular orbit gives the same two Seifert solid tori and their
product annulus as above. A regular orbit is the (3, 4) torus knot, up to the harmless exchange
of the two coordinates. This identifies the manifold with its peripheral structure; the abstract
presentation hx, y | x3 = y −4 i alone would not have justified that identification.

17.1    The repaired map and its relative uniqueness
Theorem 17.4 (The repaired map and its relative homotopy class). For every admissible
member, there is a smooth map eq : X → Q over B whose restriction outside an arbitrarily small
cusp neighbourhood is the literal circle quotient. For fixed quotient gluing, its homotopy class is
independent of the cusp replacement, provided the replacement maps the cusp neighbourhood into
its designated solid torus and is kept fixed on its outer collar. In particular there is a well-defined
class for the original member X ≃ S 6 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; section 17.

Proof. On the cusp boundary use the product coordinates (q, θγ ) after the specified collar shear.
By (17), the boundary circle class extends to N0 . Since S 1 = K(Z, 1), it has a continuous
representative θ0 : N0 → S 1 . Its restriction to the boundary is homotopic to the given one:
the two maps induce the same homomorphism on π1 of the boundary mapping torus. The
homotopy-extension property for a manifold with boundary changes θ0 on a collar so that it
agrees exactly with θγ there. Relative smooth approximation gives a smooth representative, still
equal on a smaller collar. Then (f, θ0 ) is the required map into D2 × S 1 , and agrees with the

                                                  145
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


finite-filling maps on the overlap. This proves smoothness even at the critical points of f : the
product map is smooth without any submersion assertion.
    The inclusion ∂N0 → N0 surjects on π1 , as (17) explicitly shows. It follows that H 1 (N0 ; Z) →
H 1 (∂N0 ; Z) is injective. Since both spaces are connected, the long exact sequence gives
H 1 (N0 , ∂N0 ; Z) = 0. Two circle replacements agreeing on the boundary therefore have quotient
whose relative H 1 class is zero, hence have a relative homotopy. Keeping the base coordinate
fixed gives the required homotopy of maps into the solid torus. Different choices of the collar
size are compared on a common smaller collar. This proves the assertion.

Proposition 18.1 (Two conjugacy classes of real structures). For a real member the
antiholomorphic involutions have exactly two conjugacy classes under holomorphic automorphisms.
For any fixed involutive splitting σ they are represented by σ and ρ(1/2)σ. Every nonempty fixed
set is a closed connected orientable totally real three-manifold with the mod-two homology of S 3 .
The circle ρ preserves each such fixed set and acts semifreely on it.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 4.10; proposition 4.9;
(Illman, 1972, Theorem 3.1, p. 48); (Knudson, 2004, Theorem 4.1(1)).

Proof. The real comparison of Proposition 4.10 has derivative complex conjugation in the second
period coordinate. It therefore conjugates translation by b ∈ C/Z to translation by b̄. In
multiplicative notation its action is z 7→ 1/z̄. The square of zσ is z/z̄, so it is an involution
exactly for z ∈ R∗ . Conjugation by y ∈ C∗ changes this coefficient to |y|2 z, giving exactly its
two signs. The automorphism computation used here is Proposition 4.9: the integral centralizer
has linear part aI, the cusp and finite norm equations force a = 1 for a self-map, and the global
translation sheaf has H 0 = Ce with integral periods Ze. These are precisely the three steps
needed to identify the full group with C∗ , rather than only its identity component.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                               Paper I


    At a fixed point an antiholomorphic involution has a real three-dimensional fixed tangent
space, and its complexification is the full tangent space. An invariant metric and its exponential
map identify its fixed locus locally with this real subspace. It is therefore a closed totally
real three-manifold. The smooth Z/2 action admits an equivariant triangulation by (Illman,
1972, Theorem 3.1, p. 48); compactness and finite dimension give the finite-dimensional G-CW
hypothesis. Smith’s theorem, in the form of (Knudson, 2004, Theorem 4.1(1)), applies to the
smooth finite action on the sphere and gives the stated mod-two homology. A nonempty three-
dimensional fixed set is consequently connected, and its first mod-two cohomology vanishes; its
orientation class w1 therefore vanishes. On the unit circle 1/z̄ = z, so σ commutes with ρ. Its
stabilizers are inherited from the checked semifree action on X and hence are either trivial or
the whole circle.

Theorem 18.3 (The real three-manifolds). Every nonempty fixed set in Theorem 18.2 is
diffeomorphic to S 3 . Its fundamental group is trivial and its integral homology is (Z, 0, 0, Z). For
negative imaginary w, the restricted circle action is the standard semifree action on S 3 with fixed
circle D2σc . For positive imaginary w, the nonempty real form has a free circle action isomorphic,
up to circle and orientation conventions, to the Hopf action.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 18.2.

Proof. For negative imaginary w both fixed manifolds meet D2 in one circle. Their circle action
is semifree, so the orbit space is a compact orientable surface with boundary. The local quotient
at a fixed circle is the quotient of S 1 × C by scalar rotation on C, hence is a boundary collar. Over
the surface interior the principal circle bundle is trivial because the surface has boundary and
H 2 = 0. Changes of boundary trivialization extend over the attached normal discs by rotation.
Thus the three-manifold is
                                     (B × S 1 ) ∪∂B×S 1 (∂B × D2 ).
If B has genus gB and bB boundary components, van Kampen or its surface handle decomposition
gives first homology Z2gB +bB −1 . Smith’s theorem makes this rank zero. Since bB > 0, we have
gB = 0, bB = 1. The displayed manifold is then ∂(D2 × D2 ) = S 3 , with the indicated circle
action. This derives the smooth recognition from an explicit surface decomposition.
    For positive imaginary w the nonempty real manifold is free under ρ. The two real tori on
t < 1 join at the single real torus over 1. At 0 the odd root comparison is a torus product. At
infinity they are capped by the real neighbourhoods of D1 and D12 . These are solid tori: the
primitive circle in the edge direction collapses and the remaining real circle is their core. In the
outer real-fibre lattice Zhw, di the two cap meridians are w and w − d.
    We check the intervening torus identification. Put B1 = A−1       2 A1 A2 and C = B1 . The two
                                                                          −1                 2

real-arc involutions satisfy R< Rm = B1 , Rm B1 Rm = B1−1 and B13 = I. Moving between the real
root lifts requires B1k Rm B1−k = B1 Rm , so 2k ≡ 1 (mod 3) and k = 2. Thus the actual odd-root
transport is C, not merely an arbitrary matrix conjugating the two reflections. It satisfies
R< = CRm C −1 , and C(u + w) = −w + d. The exchange across the multiplicity-four real torus
is A22 ; after this odd-root transport it is CA22 C −1 , whose restriction to hw, di is w 7→ −w, d 7→ d.
Consequently the meridians, compared on one boundary torus, have determinant of absolute
value one. The resulting genus-one Heegaard splitting is S 3 : primitive meridians intersecting
once can be taken to the two coordinate circles by an integral torus automorphism, giving the
usual two solid tori of S 3 . The free circle d then has Euler number of absolute value one, so the
displayed bundle over S 2 is the Hopf bundle. This proves the integral assertions, beyond the
mod-two information.

Proof. The literal quotient is circle invariant. In a cusp extension θ0 : N0 → S 1 , each orbit circle

Proposition 18.5 (The coherent closing translation). Fix the standard twists and the root

In this section S is the smooth minimal rational elliptic surface with Weierstrass equation

π : S → B is its elliptic fibration, P is the section used in the period dictionary, T = t6P : S → S,
and L = MS = OS (P − O). We use the convention that PS (O ⊕ L) contains the total space of

Proposition 19.1. The quotient
                                 Q = R/{s0 (x) ∼ s∞ (T x) : x ∈ S}
has a compact, reduced complex-space structure. Its normalization is the finite holomorphic map
ν : R → Q. Its singular locus is a copy of S, and its local analytic equation along that locus
is ab = 0, with two further coordinates on S. The induced map Q → B is proper. Its sheaf of
first-order local smoothing parameters is
                         TQ1 = Ext1OQ (ΩQ , OQ ) ≃ L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 ≃ π ∗ OB (1)
on the double locus.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Engel, 2026, Lemma 2.1).

Proof. The two sections of R are disjoint closed submanifolds. The equivalence relation consists
of their two graphs and the diagonal; it is closed in R × R. A quotient of a compact Hausdorff
space by a closed equivalence relation is Hausdorff: for distinct equivalence classes, compactness
gives disjoint saturated neighbourhoods by taking finite subcovers of the complements of the
relation. Thus the displayed quotient is compact and Hausdorff.
    For a coordinate neighbourhood U ⊂ S and frames of L|U and L−1 |T (U ) , the two tubular
coordinate charts are (x, a) at s0 (U ) and (T x, b) at s∞ (T (U )). We give their identification the
ring
                   {(f (x, a), g(x, b)) : f (x, 0) = g(x, 0)} = C{x1 , x2 , a, b}/(ab).
Changes of frame are holomorphic and invertible on each branch and have the same change of
x on their intersection. They therefore glue these hypersurface charts to the inherited charts
off the sections. This constructs the asserted complex space. The direct sum of the two regular
branch rings is the integral closure: an integral element in the total ring of fractions is integral
on each smooth branch, and conversely the two branch idempotents are integral. The resulting
map ν is proper with at most two points in each fibre, and its local ring extension is finite. The
map to B is well defined because πT = π; its properness follows from compactness of Q.
    The conormal presentation for the hypersurface ab = 0 gives Ext1 (Ω, O) = O/(a, b). A change
of normal frames a0 = g(x)a, b0 = h(x)b changes the equation and its smoothing parameter
by gh. Consequently these local modules glue as Ns0 /R ⊗ T ∗ Ns∞ /R = L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 . For this
particular surface, Engel’s Lemma 2.1 states Hom(T ∗ L, L) = π ∗ OB (1) (Engel, 2026, Lemma 2.1).
Its identification applies here with exactly T = t6P and L = O(P − O); there is no replacement
of the translation by its inverse in this normal-bundle calculation. One can recover the degree
in that lemma directly: the bundle has multidegree zero on every fibre, since T preserves every
component; hence it is π ∗ OB (n). Its degree on O is
                   n = (O − P ) · 6P + (P − O) · O = (2 − 2) + (0 − (−1)) = 1.
The section intersections used here are the explicit computations in the proof of that lemma.
This derives the displayed sheaf in the normal-bundle convention of our pushout.

Proposition 19.2. Over S ◦ = S \ S∞ , the pushout in 19.1 is the central fibre of a holomorphic

Proof. Let φ be the section of L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 with divisor S∞ , as in Corollary 2.2 of Engel (2026).
On S ◦ it is nowhere zero. At the pair s0 (x), s∞ (T x) we use the node chart

This equation is invariant under changes of the two line-bundle frames, so it defines a hypersurface

This is exactly the inverse of the contracting bundle map LT x → Lx , aT x 7→ uφx aT x . Thus

of this generator. Every orbit meets the core or an attached collar by contraction, and two

consequently a biholomorphism. At u = 0, (E1) is the pinching chart ab = 0.

to u is −φx 6= 0. The projection to u is flat: its local rings are torsion free over the convergent

form a regular sequence in the regular total local ring: after setting t = t0 , the equation (E1) has

local flatness criterion for a regular base (equivalently its elementary regular-sequence proof)
gives flatness over (t, u). This argument uses smoothness of the surface S, not smoothness of the
Kodaira fibre; it therefore applies at every point of the fibres IV ∗ and III.

Proof. The surface S is smooth and its nodal elliptic fibre has local equation q = zv at its node.
The section φ has a simple zero along that fibre. Thus φ = zv times an invertible holomorphic
function. Absorbing the function in one normal coordinate gives (E2). The convergent power-
series ring C{x, y, z, v, u} is factorial, and u is coprime to xy − uzv. Hence uh ∈ (xy − uzv)

argument uses u − u0 . This proves flatness over the smooth parameter curve. For fixed u 6= 0 the
four first derivatives vanish only at the origin, and the quadratic form xy − uzv is nondegenerate.
This proves the ordinary-double-point assertion by its defining equation.

z and x, respectively. For u 6= 0 the first chart solves for v and the second for y, so both are
smooth. The map is an isomorphism away from the origin in the fixed u-fibre: where the ideal
fails to be visibly principal, the hypersurface equation and one of y, v make it principal. The
fibre over the origin is P1 . The modification is projective over (E2), since it is a closed subspace
of its product with P1 . The first strict-transform equation is coprime to u − u0 in its convergent
power-series ring for every u0 ; the second chart is smooth with free parameter u. Thus flatness
over u persists.
    At u = 0 the first chart has ry = 0. The branch r = 0 maps isomorphically to x = 0 in
the original central fibre. The branch y = 0, together with the second chart, is the ordinary
blow-up of the branch y = 0 in coordinates (x, z, v) along (x, z). This description follows from
the two affine substitutions defining that blow-up and is an identification of normalizations,
not just a birational map. For u 6= 0, the base coordinate in the first chart is q = zry/u and
in the second it is q = xav. Thus the modification also exhibits the triple-coordinate strata
that the cusp filling requires. The substitutions and Jacobian are independently checked in
code/e_degeneration.py.

Remark 19.5 (Local obstruction and the precise gluing requirement). The following local
construction isolates the obstruction to a flat proper filling of the prescribed compact untwisted
family with central fibre exactly Q. The full nonexistence result is proved in lemma 20.8
and theorem 20.9. 19.1 constructs the compact candidate as an actual complex space; 19.2
constructs its smoothing away from infinity, including the two other special fibres; 19.3 computes
the two-parameter germ and a concrete flat modification of it.
    The local requirement identified by this argument is the following analytic gluing problem
at one lift of the node of S∞ . The local model xy = uzv must be replaced by charts whose
restriction to every u 6= 0 is the chosen small resolution of the rank-two Mumford filling,
and these charts must be equivariant under both period generators, with proper quotient and
with central normalization R. The explicit blow-up in 19.3 supplies the required smooth local
general fibre but changes the normalization at u = 0. This particular blow-up does not settle
whether another gluing can preserve that normalization. Thus the local computation alone is
an obstruction to the unmodified plumbing argument. The global virtual-Euler argument in
lemma 20.8 and theorem 20.9 supplies the exclusion. A modified compact limit also requires
an equivariant periodic fan and verification of its quotient near the crossing (u, q) = (0, 0); the
complete fan and quotient data are supplied in propositions 20.1 and 20.3 and theorem 20.4.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; lemma 20.8 and theorem 20.9;
proposition 19.1; proposition 19.2; proposition 19.3; propositions 20.1 and 20.3 and theorem 20.4.

universal cover C of its elliptic base. The resulting union of simply connected ruled pieces, with
simply connected intersections and a tree as incidence graph, is simply connected by van Kampen.
Its deck group is generated by the enlarged lattice of translations on Fj and one step round the
component cycle. The latter conjugates the lattice by the order-three or order-four rotation.

isomorphic groups by reversing the cycle generator.

the incidence matrix is a twisted cycle: its cokernel is coker(Rj − I) and its kernel is zero, because
Rj has no eigenvalue one. The degree-zero incidence matrix contributes an additional Z to
H1 . In degree two the two section classes on a component agree, so the incidence matrix is the
ordinary cycle matrix on their classes. It has kernel Z and primitive image of rank n − 1. Thus
H2 = Zn+1 , H3 = Z2n+1 , and H4 = Zn . Finally coker(R3 − I) = Z/3 and coker(R4 − I) = Z/2.

We write L = OS (P − O), T = t6P , J = L ⊗ T ∗ L−1 = π ∗ OB (1), and R = PS (O ⊕ L). The

Proposition 20.1. For k, l ∈ Z, let Pk,l be the cone defined by hq , hu ≥ 0, khq ≤ y1 ≤ (k + 1)hq
and l(hq + hu ) ≤ y2 ≤ (l + 1)(hq + hu ). These cones and their faces form a fan. Its two period
automorphisms on the cocharacter lattice are

     G1 (y1 , y2 , hq , hu ) = (y1 + hq , y2 , hq , hu ),    G2 (y1 , y2 , hq , hu ) = (y1 , y2 + hq + hu , hq , hu ).

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                                Paper I


The affine chart of P0,0 is

                         U0,0 = Spec C[x, y, z, v, u]/(xy − uzv),         q = zv.

In particular the unsubdivided chart is not a smooth simultaneous model of the cusp.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. At fixed hq , hu ≥ 0, the cone Pk,l cuts out the rectangle

                   khq ≤ y1 ≤ (k + 1)hq ,        l(hq + hu ) ≤ y2 ≤ (l + 1)(hq + hu ).

When hq = 0 the first interval is a point. These rectangles tile their support, and their intersections
are common faces, including this collapsed boundary. This proves the fan assertion. The displayed
integral transformations preserve the fan and have integral inverses.
    For a character (a, b, c, d), the six inequalities of the dual cone are c, a+c, b+c, a+b+c, d, b+d ≥
0. The characters

     x = (0, 1, 0, 0),   y = (0, −1, 1, 1),   z = (1, 0, 0, 0),   v = (−1, 0, 1, 0),   u = (0, 0, 0, 1)

generate its integral monoid. Indeed if b ≥ 0 we subtract bx; if b < 0 we subtract (−b)y. The
remaining character has second coordinate zero and is a nonnegative integral combination of
z, v, u. The sole relation is x + y = u + z + v, and the character of the first base coordinate is
z + v. This proves the coordinate-ring assertion, including normality. The calculation is checked
exactly in code/ab_push_local_checks.py.

                                              T x , a ⊗ b = uφx , kak, kbk < 2r, |u| < }.

On r < kak < 2r identify a point of N with (x, a, u) ∈ C. On r < kbk < 2r identify it with
(T x, b−1 , u) ∈ C. Both identifications are biholomorphisms between open complex spaces; in
the first collar b = uφx /a, and in the second a = uφx b−1 . Their domains are disjoint because
kakkbk < r2 . Changes of frames multiply the equation by units and give the stated bundle-valued
equation, so no choice of frame enters the gluing.
    This gluing is Hausdorff. At either end of a collar, exactly one of its two charts contains
the limiting circle: the core omits kak = r, and the node chart omits kak = 2r; the infinity

                                                    158
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                                 Paper I


collar has the identical property in b. Thus the graph of the identification has no unpaired
pair of limiting points. The two collars in each chart are separated, so there are no additional
chains of identifications. These observations give disjoint saturated neighbourhoods of any two
inequivalent points. Properness is equally concrete. Over a compact subset of B × ∆ , the closed
core 3r/2 ≤ kak ≤ 2/(3r) together with the closed node subspace kak, kbk ≤ 7r/4 is compact
and maps onto the glued space. To see surjectivity, a point outside the smaller core lies on a node
collar, and a node point outside the smaller node subspace lies on the smaller core. Compactness
of S supplies the uniform bound used above. This proves properness of the joint map to (t, u).
    The total node rings are hypersurface rings over the regular two-dimensional local rings of
S. They are Cohen–Macaulay. Every fibre of the joint map has pure dimension two: first fix
t, and then impose xy = uφ on the two line coordinates over the one-dimensional fibre of S.
Consequently t − t0 , u − u0 is a regular sequence in every total local ring. The regular-sequence
flatness criterion over the smooth two-dimensional base proves flatness. On the core the same
conclusion is immediate from flatness of S → B. This includes the nonreduced Kodaira fibres
at 0, 1; smoothness of S, rather than smoothness of those fibres, is what the argument uses.
At u = 0 the node equation is ab = 0, and the two collar maps recover precisely the specified
pinching of the two sections of R.
    For u 6= 0 and t 6= ∞, the equation gives aT x = ax /(uφx ). Hence the resulting quotient is
exactly L× /huφi, where the contracting generator covers T −1 . Every orbit meets a core or a
collar, by the uniform contraction estimate; the displayed comparison identifies exactly its orbit
relation. It is therefore a biholomorphism, not just a meromorphic comparison.
    At the nodal point of S∞ , write q = zv. Absorbing a unit in one line coordinate gives
xy = uzv. At a smooth point of S∞ the equation is xy = uq. For u 6= 0 the latter threefold
is smooth; the former has one nondegenerate quadratic singularity at the origin. There are no
other singularities of a nonzero u fibre.
    For completeness, the relation to the infinite fan quotient is also explicit. In a Tate covering
of a neighbourhood of the I1 fibre use the torus coordinates (Z, W ) of Engel’s Proposition 2.7.
The two periods act as

             (Z, W, q, u) 7−→ (c1 qZ, c2 W, q, u),         (Z, W, q, u) 7−→ (c3 Z, c04 uqW, q, u),

neighbourhood over a sufficiently small bidisc, the fan space maps by a holomorphic covering to

20.2    Two minimal toroidal fillings and further modifications
Proposition 20.3. Among subdivisions with no new rays, the fan in 20.1 has exactly two smooth
period-invariant subdivisions restricting to the chosen A2 triangulation at hu = 0. These are also
all subdivisions which are flat over the original (q, u) bidisc, have reduced u-central divisor, and
retain that boundary triangulation. Without the joint-flatness restriction there are infinitely many
smooth invariant subdivisions retaining that triangulation and having reduced u-central divisor.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 20.1.

Proof. Write the six rays of P0,0 as A = (0, 0, 1, 0), B = (1, 0, 1, 0), C = (0, 1, 1, 0), D = (1, 1, 1, 0),
E = (0, 0, 0, 1), F = (0, 1, 0, 1). The return’s A2 diagonal is BC. A triangular prism has six
triangulations without new vertices. With this bottom diagonal the three possibilities are

                         maximal tetrahedra          left diagonal right diagonal
                       ABCE, BCDE, CDEF                   CE            DE
                       ABCE, BCDF, BCEF                   CE            BF
                       ABCF, ABEF, BCDF                   AF            BF.

Periodicity identifies the left and right faces by A 7→ B, C 7→ D, E 7→ E, F 7→ F ; it
excludes exactly the middle row. Every listed maximal cone has determinant ±1. There
are no missed triangulations: the prism has normalized volume three, all its nondegenerate
four-vertex tetrahedra have normalized volume one, and enumeration of their triples with pairwise
face intersections gives exactly these six possibilities before fixing the bottom. The program
ab_push_fan.py performs this enumeration in rational arithmetic; intersections are tested by all
vertices of the combined barycentric halfspaces.
    For the stronger assertion, a new ray with hq , hu > 0 would give a divisor mapping to the
origin of the two-dimensional base. Its fibre dimension would be three, contradicting joint flatness.
A ray with hu = 0 is excluded by the retained boundary triangulation. On hq = 0, the fan
support has y1 = 0. Reducedness requires the primitive ray to have hu = 1, so it is already one
of the ρl . Thus there are no new rays under the stated three restrictions. Conversely the two
triangulations have all heights zero or one, and every cone maps onto a face of the quadrant with
saturated image. Their local monomial maps are flat and their u divisors reduced.
    If joint flatness is omitted, star-subdivide the orbit of the maximal cone ABCE by its interior
ray v1 = A + B + C + E = (1, 1, 3, 1). Distinct translates have disjoint interiors and distinct
closed torus orbits. These are simultaneous ordinary blow-ups at disjoint points, so the operation
is unambiguously period-invariant. Repeat in the cone ABCvm−1 , where v0 = E. The new ray
is vm = vm−1 + A + B + C = (m, m, 3m, 1). Replacing any basis vector by their sum preserves
determinant one, and every new ray has hu = 1. The boundary triangulations are unchanged.
On the compact quotient this blows up one smooth central point away from the conductor at
each step. There are therefore infinitely many invariant smooth refinements, all reduced over
u = 0, with increasing numbers of rays modulo the period group. They are not jointly flat. An
earlier attempted witness using an orbit of two-faces did not justify compatibility of intersecting
centres; its correction is retained in evidence/ab_push_correction_orbit_stars.md.

Remark 20.5 (counterexample; the literal blow-up shape). The unrestricted request that every
normalized component be a blow-up of R is false. The first maximal-cone star already contributes
a P3 component, which admits no proper bimeromorphic map to R, since such a map would
inject a rank-eleven rational H 2 into a rank-one group. 20.6 gives every normalization by explicit
star charts; 20.7 supplies the terminating blow-up and blow-down algorithm with centres, order,
exceptional bundles and gluing maps. Thus the literal shape is refuted and its general algorithmic
replacement is proved.

    A common-face test is also completely explicit: write each tetrahedron in barycentric
halfspaces, intersect the two finite lists of halfspaces, and enumerate the possible vertices
by solving triples of bounding equations. The intersection is a common face precisely when all its
vertices are common tetrahedron vertices. Since the candidate tetrahedra lie in Pn , pairwise face
intersections and the volume equality imply that they cover the slice. Otherwise their finite closed
union would omit a nonempty relatively open set, which has positive volume. The boundary
tests make the translates agree on every shared face. This proves that every passing collection
gives the claimed invariant fan.
    Conversely, intersect any invariant smooth refinement with Pn . A smooth maximal cone
has four primitive generators with determinant ±1, and its slice is one of the stated tetrahedra.
Finitely many cone orbits give finitely many rays in this prism, hence some maximum height
H. No additional bottom rays are permitted by the boundary condition; every other ray has
the form (A.24a). The resulting collection passes all three tests. Thus the procedure is a finite,
exhaustive search at every height, rather than a restriction to regular triangulations or to new
rays in a chosen orbit. There is no projectivity condition in the tests.
    The finite-orbit condition is necessary for a proper quotient of such a refinement, not an
additional restriction on the requested proper models. Each full-dimensional cone has a closed
torus orbit consisting of one point with q = r = 0. These points form a closed discrete set: an
affine chart of a full-dimensional cone contains exactly its own closed torus orbit. After the
properly discontinuous period quotient the points are indexed by cone orbits and remain closed
and discrete. Infinitely many such orbits would therefore give an infinite closed discrete subset of
a compact central fibre, which is impossible.

         (a, b, k, `),   k, ` > 0,   0 ≤ a < k,     0 ≤ b < k + n`,       gcd(a, b, k, `) = 1.   (A.24c)

necessarily includes each (0, j, 0, 1), 0 ≤ j ≤ n. Indeed an omitted such vector would lie inside a
regular two-cone; writing it in that cone’s integral basis would express its height one as the sum

pure top orbits and H−1 k=1 k(k + n) available mixed orbits.

Proof. The first maximal-cone star in 20.16 produces a normalized component P3 . There cannot
be a proper bimeromorphic holomorphic map P3 → R: between smooth compact oriented
manifolds such a map has degree one, and proper pushforward gives a left inverse to pullback on

    Here is the promised algorithm. Retain all marking data from 20.6: the lattice, the two period
matrices, the original line-bundle units, and the common unsubdivided fan. Strictify the finite
quotient cone complex by the decreasing-dimensional barycentric stars used in 20.18. Record these
operations and do the same for the reference model. Form their common intersection complex.
A regular common subdivision can be found either by toric desingularization or by enumerating
rational subdivisions with increasing primitive-ray bounds and testing their determinants and
common faces. A regular subdivision exists, so the latter enumeration terminates.
    On a finite strict regular complex there are finitely many possible ordinary star blow-ups:
choose a cone of dimension at least two and insert the sum of its primitive basis rays. There are
also finitely many possible inverse moves: choose a ray and test whether its star is exactly the
star created by such a subdivision of a regular cone. Both tests are exact integer calculations.
Require that every intermediate complex remain a subdivision of the marked original complex.
Record face identifications; equality of two marked complexes is a finite rational comparison,
using the period orbit representatives in A.24c and their pure top and pure bottom analogues.
    Enumerate this locally finite graph of moves in increasing path length, discarding repeated
marked complexes. Applied separately to the two proper subdivision morphisms from the
common regular complex, the finite-complex weak-factorization theorem used in 20.18 guarantees
a path, all of whose intermediates are over the corresponding target. Thus the search terminates.
Concatenate the two paths and the recorded strictification paths. This gives a fully specified
finite sequence once the input fan is given. Temporary pure bottom subdivisions may occur; they


                                               165
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


are allowed in a presentation of the birational comparison, and are removed before the prescribed
endpoint is reached.

blow-downs and projective bundles. Independently, the direct star charts avoid running this
search when only a normalization chart or an intersection is required. The mixed-ray components
are complete smooth toric threefolds; a pure top component (0, b, 0, `) is bimeromorphic to
PS (O ⊕ L` ). There is no assertion that all these distinct components are modifications of a single
copy of R.
    Finally D is globally the principal Cartier divisor of the parameter r in a smooth total
space. Its two-term cotangent complex is [OD −−→ ΩY |D ], so its first-order deformation module
                                                   dF

is the cokernel of the gradient. Equivalently, a lifted hypersurface equation F + G is changed
by an infinitesimal coordinate change precisely by a Jacobian term. This argument applies to
nonreduced monomials as well; an ordinary conormal sequence need not be left-exact there.
Absorbing the local unit, or reducing its derivative modulo F , gives (A.25a). A global parameter
makes the normal line trivial, so these Jacobian quotients glue by the canonical hypersurface
presentation. In the reduced case the Jacobian ideal defines the singular scheme, giving the
asserted trivial deformation line there.
    The exact certificate code/ab_push_normalization_algorithm.py executes the star search
on the first two maximal-cone examples, verifies both inverse contractions, and checks all local
multiplicity substitutions with exponents zero, one and two. The finite-complex theorem supplies
termination for arbitrary input; these tests check the explicit local implementation.

20.3    The virtual Euler obstruction and the conjecture
Lemma 20.8. Let Z be a compact reduced local-complete-intersection complex space of pure
dimension n. In any proper flat holomorphic family over a disc with central fibre Z and smooth

                                                      166
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


nearby fibres, their Euler number is

                                       evir (Z) = hcn (TZvir ), [Z]i.

This statement needs no projectivity or Kähler hypothesis.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Levy, 2008, Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and
Section 3.1); (Łojasiewicz, 1964, Section 3, Theorems 1–2); Fantechi and Göttsche (2010).

Proof. Flat deformation preserves the local-complete-intersection property relative to the disc
near Z. Locally this follows by lifting an embedding and its regular sequence of equations;
Nakayama’s lemma and flatness show that their lifts generate the ideal and remain a regular
sequence. Properness allows one to shrink the disc so that these neighbourhoods cover the total
space. The relative cotangent complex is consequently perfect of amplitude [−1, 0]. Its dual
defines a topological complex K-class V on that total space; local finite vector-bundle complexes
define the class by descent, or by stabilization and partitions of unity; the analytic-to-topological
comparison is given in (Levy, 2008, Lemmas 3.1–3.2 and Section 3.1). Its restriction to a smooth
fibre is its tangent bundle, and its restriction to Z is its intrinsic virtual tangent class.
    The compact fundamental cycles of the central and a nearby fibre are homologous in the total
space. More explicitly, the inverse image K of a short closed radial segment [0, ] is compact
and semianalytic. Away from Sing Z it is an oriented real (2n + 1)-manifold with boundary the
nearby fibre and −Zreg , because flatness with smooth fibre implies smoothness of the morphism
at those points. The exceptional set Sing Z has real dimension at most 2n − 2. Triangulate
compatibly with this set and the two endpoints, using (Łojasiewicz, 1964, Section 3, Theorems
1–2). The sum of the oriented top simplices has boundary exactly [X ] − [Z]: no real 2n-simplex
can be supported on that exceptional set. Reducedness and flatness give multiplicity one on
every central component. Pairing the globally defined cn (V ) with these homologous cycles gives
the equality of Chern numbers. Gauss–Bonnet on the smooth compact complex fibre gives its
Euler number. This proves the analytic assertion directly. The algebraic counterpart is Theorem
5.8 and Remark 5.9 of Fantechi and Göttsche (2010); those scheme statements alone would not
justify omitting the analytic comparison above.

Proposition 20.14 (limitation of Clemens–Schmid). The classical Kähler or projective Clemens–

positive q-height then forces a = 0; any ray with positive q- or r-height forces b = 0. Consequently
a stratum of cone dimension d is an actual (C∗ )4−d , with no additional torus quotient. The
induced gluing units only identify different period translates of the stratum. Its compactly
supported Euler number is zero unless d = 4, in which case it is one. Every maximal cone has
both kinds of height, and each has one representative in the interior of the fundamental prism.
Thus the cusp contributes exactly t4 (Σ). Additivity proves the displayed central Euler formula.
    The local total space is smooth, and its parameter is r = z1`1 · · · zs`s times a holomorphic unit,
with `i > 0. Its Milnor fibre has the homotopy type of a finite disjoint union of (S 1 )s−1 . For
s = 1 it consists of `1 contractible pieces; for s ≥ 2 its Euler number is zero. This proves the
pointwise assertion. Off the cusp the one-branch parts are C∗ -bundles over the appropriate parts
of S \ S∞ and have Euler number zero; the double parts have nearby Euler value zero. At the
cusp, positive-dimensional torus strata again contribute zero. A maximal cone with exactly one
positive-r ray must have three bottom rays. Its bottom face is consequently one of the two
prescribed triangles ABC and BCD. Each triangle belongs to exactly one such maximal cone.
Its determinant is the r-height ` of the fourth ray, because the bottom triangle is unimodular.
Smoothness forces ` = 1. Exactly these two points contribute one each. Thus the nearby Euler
integral is two for every output, even when some other components have multiplicity greater
than one.
    For the fundamental group, first choose the reference model obtained by base-changing X + by
u = rn and resolving the surface equation xy = rn along its smooth conductor S. Its normalized
central components are R+ and n − 1 projective-line bundles over S. All are simply connected,
and their double surfaces are copies of the simply connected S. The gluing graph is an n-cycle,
interpreted as the self-gluing circle when n = 1. Van Kampen therefore gives fundamental group
Z for this reference centre.
    Any two fans of 20.6 have the explicit proper common normal modification formed by
intersecting their cones. Resolve this analytic space to a smooth common model; analytic
resolution, including the noncompact version near the compact central set, is supplied by
(Bierstone and Milman, 1995, Theorem 1.6 and its following paragraph). This use of a common
modification is legitimate here because the common fan has already constructed it. It is not an
assumed extension of an arbitrary punctured isomorphism.
    A proper bimeromorphic map F : Y → X between smooth complex manifolds induces an
isomorphism of fundamental groups. To see this directly, choose an analytic A ⊂ X of complex
codimension at least two such that F is an isomorphism outside A. General position gives
π1 (X \ A) ≃ π1 (X), and gives surjectivity of π1 (Y \ F −1 A) → π1 (Y ). Under the common-open
identification, composition with F∗ is the displayed isomorphism to π1 (X). Thus the first map is
also injective, and F∗ is an isomorphism. Apply this argument to both maps from the smooth
common model, after restricting to a sufficiently small parameter disc.
    Finally, each smooth total space retracts to the support of its central divisor, including in
the nonreduced case. The gradient proof in 21.15 applies with the explicit bound for ρ = |r|2

                             k∇ρk ≥ cρ1−1/(2L) ,       L = `1 + · · · + `s .

Theorem 20.18 (integral homology of every toroidal output). Let DΣ be the reduced central
space of an output of 20.6 for u = rn . Write k for its number of pure top ray orbits, m for
its number of mixed ray orbits, and t4 for its number of maximal four-cone orbits. Then every
integral homology group is free, and

                (b0 , b1 , b2 , b3 , b4 , b5 , b6 ) = (1, 1, 8 + k + m, 7,
                                                                 9k + t4 − 2m − 1, 0, k + m).

This includes nonreduced central divisors: the homology is that of their underlying support. The
marked nearby fibre is X(rn ), and its integral monodromy is I + nN in degree three, where N is
the map in 20.12; it is the identity in every other degree. In particular the six nonzero Smith
factors of this degree-three monodromy minus the identity are n, n, n, n, n, 11n.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 20.6; proposition 20.12;
proposition 20.11; (Abramovich et al., 2002, Section 5.6, pp.565–566); (Abramovich et al., 2002,
Theorems 1.6.1 and 2.7.1); (Matsuki, 2000, Section 2, p.2); (Abramovich et al., 2002, Section
5.5); theorem 20.17.

Proof. We first compute a reference centre by its normalization mapping cylinder. Base-change
X + by u = rn and resolve xy = rn along its smooth conductor S. Put N0 = OS (m − F ), using
the lattice notation of 20.11. The normalization consists of R+ and n − 1 copies of PS (O ⊕ N0 ), in
a cycle. The latter assertion follows directly on the surface-resolution charts: if x has transition
function g, the coordinates x/ri have the same transition function, while their complementary
coordinates have transition function g −1 . Only the closing identification is T .
    In the integral mapping-cylinder sequence the degree-two map has domain Ln and target of
rank 11n + 1. Project each intermediate ruled component to S. The resulting n − 1 difference
blocks are integral identity matrices. Eliminate them by integral row and column operations.
The remaining map from L is d+     2 from 20.11, together with n − 1 coordinates a 7→ a(m − F ).
Those coordinates are integral combinations of the three primitive coordinates of d+   2 . Thus the
original degree-two map has primitive image of rank 10(n − 1) + 3, kernel Z7 , and cokernel Zn+8 .
    In degree four, the same elimination uses the n − 1 identity blocks on the fundamental classes
of the bases. The remaining map from Z contains d+      4 , which is primitive by 20.11; the other
entries are the section differences m − F . Hence the degree-four map is injective with primitive
image of rank n, and cokernel of rank 10n + 1. In degree zero it is the incidence map of an
n-cycle. In degree six the normalization contributes one independent fundamental class per
component. Consequently the reference centre has free integral homology and Betti tuple

                                         (1, 1, n + 8, 7, 10n + 1, 0, n).



                                                         175
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


This is also a direct integral calculation of all the maps needed below; it uses no degeneration
theorem.
    We next justify the precise factorization used to compare an arbitrary output with this
reference. On each total space take the toroidal boundary
                                   E = {r = 0} ∪ f −1 (∞) red .
                                                           

In the cusp charts it is the toric boundary, and outside the cusp its nontrivial toroidal charts are
the plumbing charts along S. The unit transition functions preserve monomial ideals. 20.6 gives
a finite cone complex modulo the two periods, with the possible self-identifications of its faces
explicitly retained.
    Make this complex strict by barycentric star subdivisions, in decreasing cone dimension. At
the moment a stratum is blown up, all of its deeper self-intersections have already been separated.
Its closure is therefore smooth, and different translates in the chosen orbit are disjoint. The star
at the sum of the primitive basis generators is the ordinary blow-up of that closure. Repeating
over the finitely many cone orbits gives smooth strict toroidal embeddings. This is the geometric
barycentric subdivision used in (Abramovich et al., 2002, Section 5.6, pp.565–566); its analytic
realization by the same monomial ideals is described in Section 5.5 of that paper. Pure q-strata
are allowed in this preparatory step. Thus we do not assume that strictification preserves the
punctured r-family.
    Intersect the two subdivided fans, and take a regular subdivision, to obtain their explicit
common strict toroidal modification. Apply toroidal weak factorization to each of its two
subdivision maps. The needed theorem is the finite polyhedral-complex factorization by
nonsingular star subdivisions and inverse subdivisions, (Abramovich et al., 2002, Theorems
1.6.1 and 2.7.1). The corrected form for a morphism states that its centres are smooth irreducible
closed strata and that all intermediate complexes map to the target (Matsuki, 2000, Section 2,
p.2).
    There is no invocation here of a general relative analytic weak-factorization theorem. The
complexes in question are finite. The cited combinatorial factorization applies to them; the
analytic subdivision–modification correspondence of (Abramovich et al., 2002, Section 5.5) realizes
each of its finitely many stars by the indicated monomial blow-up. The correspondence respects
the face identifications and the bundle units, so the local analytic blow-ups glue. All intermediate
morphisms are proper over the target of the subdivision map, hence over a sufficiently small r-disc.
They remain smooth, and both parameters remain monomials times units. This gives the required
finite chain of actual analytic blow-ups and blow-downs between the total neighbourhoods.
    We classify the connected centres in this chain. A nontrivial centre has codimension at
least two. For a cone having a positive q-height ray, its period stabilizer is trivial: a power of
a stabilizing element fixes each of its finitely many primitive rays; the positive q-height first
forces the exponent of G1 to vanish and then the exponent of G2 to vanish. The same argument
holds for pure bottom cones. Thus there is no elliptic quotient hidden in those centres. The
normalization of the closure of their torus stratum is the toric variety of its star. If the closed
stratum is smooth, this finite birational normalization map is an isomorphism.
    For a mixed cone the centre is contained in q = r = 0; its star is complete, and it is a compact
smooth toric point, curve, or surface. It has free integral cohomology in even degrees only. For a
pure top centre, the cone must have dimension two. Its stabilizer is precisely hG1 i, and the chart
quotient and the plumbing identification show that its dense open part is the corresponding open
part of S. The compact smooth centre is therefore a surface birational to the rational surface
S. Equivalently, its proper map to the unmodified top stratum is a birational map of smooth
surfaces. It is a smooth rational surface and again has free even cohomology. It need not remain
isomorphic to S after earlier mixed modifications.
    For a pure bottom centre the cone has dimension two or three. Its star gives a smooth toric
surface or curve proper over the r-disc. The induced character r is primitive on its quotient lattice,

                                                176
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


since it was primitive before quotienting by a smooth cone on which it vanishes. Its generic fibre
is therefore connected, and is respectively a complete toric P1 or a point. In the surface case the
ordered two-dimensional fan gives a chain of rational curves as the central support, possibly with
positive multiplicities. In the curve case the support is one point. Monomial gradient retraction,
as in 20.17, shows that the ordinary integral cohomology of the centre is free and even, with
H 0 = Z and H 4 = 0. These centres are not compact; this is why they must be distinguished
from the first two types.
    For any closed smooth complex centre C ⊂ Y of complex codimension c, compact or not, the
integral blow-up splitting is
                                                            c−1
                                                            M
                          H j (BlC Y ; Z) ≃ H j (Y ; Z) ⊕         H j−2a (C; Z).
                                                            a=1

For clarity, this statement requires no Kähler hypothesis. Tubular excision identifies the relative
groups by the integral Thom class; the projective-bundle theorem for the exceptional divisor
supplies the powers of its hyperplane class. Their exceptional Gysin maps, together with pullback
from Y , give the displayed map. The relation that restriction of the exceptional class is minus
the hyperplane class makes the relative matrix triangular with unit diagonal. Proper blow-down
pushforward, defined by Borel–Moore duality, splits the pullback summand. This proves the
splitting also for the noncompact centres just listed.
    It follows that all odd cohomology groups and all torsion are unchanged along the factorization.
Each connected centre adds one to b2 and one to the number of prime boundary components.
Each compact centre adds one to b6 and one to the number of central prime components: in
degree six the only new group is its top cohomology. A pure bottom centre adds neither, because
its H 4 (and, for a curve, its H 2 ) vanishes. The reverse operations subtract the same contributions.
    Consequently b2 minus the number of all boundary ray orbits, and b6 minus the number
of central ray orbits, are invariants of this comparison. Both endpoints have exactly one pure
bottom ray orbit. The reference has n central components and b2 = n + 8, so the arbitrary
output has
                     b2 = 8 + k + m,        b6 = k + m,      (b1 , b3 , b5 ) = (1, 7, 0).
All groups are free by the integral splitting in both directions. The total neighbourhoods
retract onto their central supports by 20.17, and those compact analytic supports have finite
triangulations. The universal coefficient theorem therefore transfers the same freeness and ranks
to integral homology. Finally the independently computed torus-stratum Euler number 11k + t4
of 20.17 gives b4 = 9k + t4 − 2m − 1.
    Every original output, unlike temporary intermediate factorizations, agrees with the marked
family X(rn ) off r = 0. A positive r-loop makes n positive u-loops. Since N 2 = 0, its monodromy
is (I + N )n = I + nN . Multiplication of the already computed integral Smith matrix by n gives
the stated factors.
    The exact program code/ab_push_all_fan_homology.py checks the full reference
normalization maps and their Smith forms at n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12, the blow-up rank increments
for every centre type used here, and the resulting formula on the certified fan families of 20.17.
These finite checks supplement the integral row-reduction and factorization argument for every
fan; they are not a bounded search substituted for it.

to the indicated C∗ -bundle. For a degree-zero line bundle L0 on an elliptic curve, P(O ⊕ L0 ) is a

L0 , L−1

same identity globally. Each nonzero torsion equation therefore has a discrete zero set. Outside
a countable union of such sets, Ps − Os is non-torsion. This disproves the product assertion,
even after an arbitrary fixed finite isogeny of the elliptic factor. The special torsion isogenies at
sj = 0 used in proposition 19.6 remain valid.

21.2    The base-changed cusp fan
Proposition 21.3. For the plain base change u = rn of the untwisted cusp model, the smooth
period-invariant refinements which retain the prescribed bottom triangulation, are jointly flat
over (q, r), and have reduced r-central divisor are indexed by k = 0, . . . , n. In a fundamental
prism write its four bottom rays as A, B, C, D as in 20.3, and put ρi = (0, i, 0, 1) for 0 ≤ i ≤ n.
The maximal cones for the index k are

                   ABCρk ,      BCDρk ,        ABρi ρi+1 (i < k),          CDρi ρi+1 (i ≥ k).

There are thirteen such models for n = 12 and three for n = 2. Each has smooth total space and
a reduced normal-crossings central divisor with n components and no triple locus. Its component
labels over the punctured q-disc are globally Z/n; in particular their monodromy around q = 0 is
the identity.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 20.3; theorem 20.2;
theorem 20.4.

Proof. The map of cocharacter lattices for the base change is

                                   (y1 , y2 , hq , hr ) 7−→ (y1 , y2 , hq , nhr ).

The old top ray indexed by l pulls back to (0, nl, 0, 1). Smoothness on the two-dimensional top
face forces insertion of every primitive ray ρnl+i , 0 < i < n: a skipped interval of length d > 1
would retain lattice index d on that face. Joint flatness excludes any new ray with both base
heights positive, and the fixed bottom excludes new rays of hr = 0. Reducedness permits only
top rays of hr = 1. These are consequently all the rays.
    On the left face ACρ0 ρn , a triangulation with these collinear top vertices has a unique triangle
containing the bottom edge AC. Write its third vertex as ρa . The triangles on either side of
that bridge are then forced. The analogous right face has bridge BDρb . The first period takes
A, C to B, D and fixes every top ray, so periodicity requires a = b = k. The fixed bottom
triangles ABC and BCD must then cone to ρk . The remaining successive top intervals force
exactly the displayed cones, leaving no choice. Conversely those cones have determinant ±1 and
common-face intersections. Their normalized volumes sum to n + 2, the volume of the prism, so
they cover it. The determinant, intersection and volume assertions for both requested exponents
are certified in ab_push_basechange_fan.py using rational arithmetic.
    The period actions are

               G1 : (y1 , y2 ) 7→ (y1 + hq , y2 ),       G2 : (y1 , y2 ) 7→ (y1 , y2 + hq + nhr ).

Thus the choices propagate consistently from the fundamental prism. The proper toric
subdivisions descend by the covering construction of 20.2. Every ray has pure q-height or pure
r-height, so in a regular affine chart q and r are monomials in disjoint sets of coordinates. This
proves joint flatness. All nonzero r-heights equal one, and there are at most two top rays in any
maximal cone; this proves reduced normal crossings and absence of triple points. Properness
follows by descent from the proper toric modification of the base-changed proper cusp model.
    The central components and all their intersection maps are specified by the stars of the ρi .
Modulo the periods their indices are i mod n; adjacent indices meet in the conductor elliptic
surface. Away from the cusp their normalizations are the ruled bundles of the expanded plumbing.
At the unique bridge class the star has both bottom triangles, and gives the nodal-curve blow-up
and small resolution described in 20.4, on the corresponding ruled bundle. This star description
also fixes the gluing when the bridge is on an inserted component. The endpoint choices k = 0, n
are the canonical resolutions of the base changes of the two original models. Intermediate values
are related to them by the successive side flops.

                                                        182
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


    Finally, G1 fixes each index and G2 changes it by n. The units in the cusp periods are single-
valued holomorphic functions of q and do not change a ray label. The toric charts themselves
are defined over q, not a root of q. Hence these labels remain global on the punctured q-disc,
proving the monodromy assertion. Further smooth periodic subdivisions with mixed rays give
infinitely many models flat over r alone, as in 20.3; they are excluded by the stated joint-flatness
condition.

Corollary 21.4 (general plain-cusp normalization). For n = 2 and n = 12, 20.6–20.7 give all
finite-orbit smooth invariant plain-cusp refinements, their proper flat families, normalization
charts, finite blow-up and blow-down presentations, multiplicities and all multiple loci. 20.17–20.19
give their complete integral topology and nearby Euler function. These statements concern the
plain untwisted cusp. They assert no compatibility with the finite logarithmic-transform pieces of
B.1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 20.6; proposition 20.7;
theorem 20.17; proposition 20.19.

Corollary 21.5 (unrestricted toroidal parametrization). For u = r12 and u = w2 , all finite-orbit
smooth invariant subdivisions of the plain cusp fan are obtained by 20.6 with n = 12 and n = 2,
respectively. The construction there gives their proper flat smooth-total-space families, central
multiplicities, normalization charts and all multiple loci. Reducedness is exactly the restriction
` = 1. This is a classification of the plain untwisted cusp models; it does not supply the missing
transition to the finite logarithmic-transform models in B.3.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 20.6.


21.3    The prescribed pieces do not glue
Theorem 21.6 (counterexample to simultaneous gluing). The finite models of 21.1 and any of
the plain u = r12 cusp models of 21.2 cannot be glued to a proper complex space over B × ∆r
with the prescribed central fibres on all three base neighbourhoods. In particular the proposed
simultaneous gluing is false. This conclusion does not rule out a different cusp model of the same
punctured S 6 family.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; section 21.1; section 21.2; theorem 21.2;
proposition 21.3.

Proof. If a further plain cusp refinement changes the top fan, its central fibre over an ordinary
q 6= 0 has additional components or different multiplicities and already cannot agree with the
twelve-cycle model of 21.1 on the overlap. We may therefore assume its top fan is the standard
reduced twelve-cycle. Additional mixed-height rays lie over q = 0 and do not change the following
argument over the punctured base.
     Suppose such a gluing exists and put B ◦ = B \ {0, 1, ∞}. Normalize its reduced central
fibre over B ◦ . In each of the prescribed plumbing charts this is a proper smooth family whose
fibres are the disjoint union of twelve connected ruled surfaces. The charts and their transition
isomorphisms therefore give a locally constant twelve-element set of connected components.
Equivalently, the Stein factor of this normalization is an unramified degree-twelve cover of B ◦ :
the algebra of fibrewise holomorphic functions is locally O12 , since each proper connected ruled
surface has only constant holomorphic functions. This description constructs the cover and
requires no conjecture about components at the missing three points.
     The double curves give the adjacency graph of a twelve-cycle. Thus its transition permutations
lie in the dihedral group D12 , the automorphism group of that graph. We record a peripheral

                                                183
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


permutation by its deck-identification map. Holonomy defined by lifting a clockwise path and
returning its endpoint to the initial root slice uses the inverse permutations throughout; the
relation and the following contradiction are unchanged. At 0 the monodromy is a rotation by
four steps; at 1 it is a rotation by minus three steps, by the explicit root deck maps in 21.2.
Relabelling a cycle can reverse either orientation, but changes these only to ±4 and ±3. At the
cusp the monodromy is the identity by 21.3.
    The peripheral relation in π1 (B ◦ ) is g1 g2 g0 = 1 with the consistently chosen clockwise loops.
In any common labelling, the product of the two finite rotations would therefore have to be the
identity. Its possible rotation numbers are

                       4 + 3,   4 − 3,   −4 + 3,   −4 − 3 ≡ 7, 1, 11, 5 (mod 12).

None is zero. This contradicts the peripheral relation. The four residues and the finite component
cycles are checked exactly by ab_push_finite_decks.py.

Proposition 21.7 (necessary condition only). If a corrected global construction retains the finite
models and a twelve-cycle over B ◦ , then, in the common orientation with finite shifts 4, −3, its
cusp component monodromy must be the twelve-cycle of shift −1. The associated component cover
of B ◦ is connected. Its compact normalization over B has degree twelve, ramification indices
3, 4, 12, and genus three. In this deck convention it is the normalization of

                                                         t4
                                             y 12 =            .
                                                      (t − 1)3
These assertions do not construct the required central complex space.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The peripheral relation gives the remaining rotation as −4 + 3 = −1. The subgroup
generated by 4, −3 is all of Z/12, proving connectedness. The local cycle decompositions have four
cycles of length three, three cycles of length four, and one of length twelve. Filling a punctured-disc
cover by its normal branched cover gives ramification contribution 4(3−1)+3(4−1)+(12−1) = 28.
The Riemann–Hurwitz formula gives 2 − 2g = 24 − 28 = −4, hence g = 3. The displayed
Kummer equation has orders 4, −3, −1 at the three points and hence the same marked cyclic
monodromy. The classification of connected covering spaces identifies its restriction to B ◦ with
the required component cover; normalization gives the compact comparison. Reversing the
transport convention replaces y by y −1 . Only this component cover has been constructed; no
topology is assigned here to a hypothetical threefold above it.

Proposition 21.8 (obstruction to a specified repair). A cyclic cusp-root construction using
a fractional translation by the two cusp periods cannot repair 21.6 while retaining the reduced
Mumford fibre for r 6= 0. More precisely, let q = sd , u = rn , and suppose a cyclic deck generator
has translation d−1 (aG1 + bG2 ) in the additive notation for the two periods. Assume its r-
component shift is integral. Then its r-component shift is nb/d mod n, whereas the multiplicity
of every generic quotient q-component is a positive multiple of
                                                   d
                                                            .
                                               gcd(d, a, b)
A nonzero r-component shift therefore forces a nonreduced q-fibre. In particular a shift −1 mod 12
in this class of constructions forces multiplicity at least twelve.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.6; theorem 20.2.


                                                      184
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


Proof. In the coordinates of 20.2 the two periods have q-valuation vectors (1, 0) and (0, 1);
their r-valuation vectors are (0, 0) and (0, n). After q = sd , the period lattice on the q-central
component indices is dZ2 . A regular toroidal resolution has indices in (Z/d)2 . The proposed
deck generator translates them by (a, b). The order of that translation is d/ gcd(d, a, b), so the
subgroup preserving a component has order h = gcd(d, a, b). Its subgroup fixing a generic point
has some order h0 dividing h; unit factors may make h0 smaller. That isotropy acts on the
normal coordinate s by a primitive h0 th root of unity. The quotient normal coordinate is sh0 ,
and q = (sh0 )d/h0 has multiplicity d/h0 , a positive multiple of d/h. Unit factors cannot decrease
this lower bound.
    Reducedness would require h0 = d, and therefore h = d, so both a, b are divisible by d.
Then nb/d is zero modulo n. If nb/d is relatively prime to n, its order in Z/n is n, which
divides the order d/h of the full component translation; this gives the final lower bound. The
residue calculations and examples for the requested exponents are independently recorded in
ab_push_cusp_root_repair.py. This rules out the specified repair, not a cusp model with a
different geometry or a different comparison to the punctured family.

Corollary 21.10 (exact Mordell–Weil lattice). In the notation of 21.9,

                       E (C(C)) = ZP ⊕ ZR ⊕ ZR0 ,             det NS(E ) = −32.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.9.

Proof. The affine coordinate ring of C is C[a, b]/(b3 − a4 − 1), with unique representatives of
degree at most two in b. The pole orders 3i + 4j of ai bj , 0 ≤ j ≤ 2, are distinct, so cancellation
cannot create functions with pole order one or two at infinity. Consequently

                       H 0 (C, OC (2∞)) = C,         H 0 (C, OC (3∞)) = C ⊕ Ca.

A section disjoint from O therefore has X = x0 , Y = y0 +y1 a for constants x0 , y0 , y1 . Substitution
in the Weierstrass equation forces x0 = y0 = 0 and y12 = 2. Thus the only nonzero sections with
intersection zero with O are P, −P . Every other nonzero section has intersection at least one
with O, and hence height at least 4 − 3 = 1.
    21.9 proves that every section has integral coefficient along P in the rational height
decomposition. The remaining lattice can have index only one, two or four over ZR + ZR0 .
Any proper such overlattice contains a nonzero element of order two modulo this sublattice.
After subtracting an integral combination of R, R0 it is one of R/2, R0 /2, (R + R0 )/2. Each
has height 1/3, contradicting the preceding lower bound. Thus the index is one. The
determinant already computed in 21.9 is the full Néron–Severi determinant. The pole-basis
calculation, coefficient equations and three half-class heights are included in the exact certificate
ab_push_trace_obstruction.py.

Proposition 21.11 (an unramified torsor alternative). Put K = C(t), L = C(C), G =
Gal(L/K) = hσi, and let E/K be the generic elliptic curve of S → B. There is a nonzero class

         ξ ∈ Sha(EL /L)G     whose transgression in      H 2 (G, E(L)) = ZP /12ZP     is 6P.

Here Sha denotes the subgroup of genus-one torsors trivial over the henselian local fields of all
points of C. In particular the trace obstruction of 21.9 does not obstruct all genus-one torsors.
Such a class has a relatively minimal projective genus-one surface V → C, locally isomorphic to
E → C, and an affine lift A : V → V of σ with

                                               A12 = t6P .

This is an existence statement for a possible normalization base, not a construction of a threefold
central fibre or of its smoothing.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.9; (Hochschild and Serre,
1953, Chapter III, Section 4, Theorem 2 and the following remark, pp.129–130); (Cossec et al.,
2024, Lemma 4.7.8); Cossec et al. (2024); (Xiao, 1991, Section 4, equation (4)); (Xiao, 1991,
Sections 3–4); corollary 21.14.

Proof. We use Galois cohomology with its continuous cochains. The five-term Hochschild–Serre
sequence gives
                                                 d
                   H 1 (K, E) −→ H 1 (L, E)G −−2→ H 2 (G, E(L)) −→ H 2 (K, E).

The transgression sequence is (Hochschild and Serre, 1953, Chapter III, Section 4, Theorem 2
and the following remark, pp.129–130); its continuous form follows by passing to finite Galois
quotients for the finitely many values of each continuous cochain. For this complex function field,
H 2 (K, E) = 0, as in (Cossec et al., 2024, Lemma 4.7.8). One can also see this from cd K = 1:
the torsion submodule of E(K) has no second cohomology, and its quotient is a rational vector
space, whose positive continuous cohomology vanishes by averaging on finite quotients.
