The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


     Cyclic group cohomology gives H 2 (G, E(L)) = E(K)/ Trσ E(L). By 21.9 this is Z/12, with
generator the class of P . Hence there is a G-invariant torsor class ξ0 ∈ H 1 (L, E) with d2 ξ0 = 6P .
We next remove all its local ramification without changing this transgression.
    At a place v of B choose a point w of C above it and its decomposition subgroup Gw . The
only nontrivial decomposition groups have orders 3, 4, 12, at 0, 1, ∞ respectively. The component
groups of the original fibres are Z/3, Z/2 and zero. Thus 6P belongs to the identity component
of the local Néron group at every ramified place. Multiplication by the ramification index is
surjective on that identity group over the henselian local field: on the residue group it is surjective
on Ga (C) or Gm (C), and its derivative is invertible; Hensel’s lemma lifts a division point. Choose
such a division point over Kvh . Viewed over Lhw , it is invariant, so its local norm is 6P . The
restriction of the transgression class to H 2 (Gw , E(Lhw )) is therefore zero. For unramified places
the decomposition group is trivial, so the same assertion is automatic.
     Naturality and exactness of the local five-term sequences now show that (ξ0 )w is the restriction
of some ηv ∈ H 1 (Kvh , E). Only finitely many of these classes need be nonzero. The original
elliptic surface is nontrivial, since j = 1728t. Ogg–Shafarevich localization is therefore surjective:
                                                 M
                                  H 1 (K, E) −→     H 1 (Kvh , E) −→ 0.
                                               v∈B

This is the combination of exact sequence (4.7.4) and Theorem 4.7.9 of Cossec et al. (2024); the
same surjectivity and its geometric fibre-twist interpretation are given in (Xiao, 1991, Section 4,
equation (4)). Take a global η with these local values and put ξ = ξ0 − resL/K η. It is locally
trivial at every point of C, remains G-invariant, and has d2 ξ = 6P . It is nonzero because its
transgression is nonzero.
    The standard interpretation of the Weil–Châtelet group represents ξ by a smooth projective
genus-one curve over L; taking its relatively minimal regular model over C gives V . Local
triviality identifies each henselian model with that of EL . Over C the corresponding étale
identifications yield holomorphic identifications over small base discs. Equivalently, V is obtained
by gluing copies of E over these discs by translations by local sections. These translations extend
over the regular I12 model. Thus V is locally isomorphic to E , has smooth total surface, no
multiple fibres, and the same single I12 fibre. Properness and flatness hold locally over the base
and hence globally. This use of torsors and local twists is the one in (Xiao, 1991, Sections 3–4);
it does not assert an explicit equation for the selected torsor.
    The G-invariance of ξ gives an affine isomorphism of its generic fibre covering σ. It extends to
the relatively minimal regular surface: in this particular situation the extension can be checked
on a common resolution. If an exceptional (−1)-curve for one projection is not contracted by the
other, its image is a vertical rational curve and has self-intersection at least −1, since blowing
down only increases self-intersection. On either locally trivial model all vertical rational curves
are components of the I12 fibre, of square −2. Thus every such (−1)-curve is contracted by both
projections and can be removed from the common resolution. Repeating this proves that the
map is an isomorphism. The same argument gives the local comparison with the Jacobian model
used above. Transporting the base by σ changes none of these facts. Write A0 for this lift. Its
twelfth power is translation by a section N ∈ E(L)G = ZP . Choosing the powers 1, A0 , . . . , A11   0
as lifts of G gives the cyclic factor set N b(i + j)/12c. Its cohomology class is precisely the descent
obstruction d2 ξ, so N = (6 + 12m)P for an integer m. Replacing A0 by A = t−mP ◦ A0 gives
A12 = t6P . The finite carry-cocycle identities, its exact order two modulo twelve, and the three
local component checks are recorded in ab_push_torsor_cocycles.py.

Proposition 21.13 (analytic unramified torsors do not evade the Hodge obstruction). Let
V → C be any compact smooth analytic genus-one surface locally isomorphic, as a torsor over
every base disc, to the Jacobian surface E → C of 21.9. Algebraicity or finite order of this
analytic torsor class is not assumed. Then b1 (V ) = 6, and V is Kähler. For every holomorphic
line bundle M on V , the projective bundle PV (O ⊕ M ) is Kähler. Every smooth compact threefold
bimeromorphic to such a bundle satisfies the ∂ ∂-lemma.
                                                ¯
    Consequently the necessary non-∂ ∂ normalization component in 21.18 cannot be obtained
                                       ¯
simply by replacing the projective torsor of 21.11 by a nonalgebraic locally trivial analytic torsor,
followed by a ruled bundle and bimeromorphic modifications. This excludes that specified repair;
it does not assert that every possible cusp normalization has this form.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.9; theorem 21.18;
proposition 21.11; (Buchdahl, 1999, Theorem 11, p.297); (Chen, 2026, Section 2.1, p.8).

Proof. Write p : E → C for the projective Jacobian. The calculation in 21.9 gives R1 p∗ OE =
OC (−∞), and g(C) = 3. The coherent Leray sequence therefore gives h1 (E , OE ) = 3. Projectivity
and Hodge decomposition imply b1 (E ) = 6. The topological Leray sequence with rational
coefficients is

         0 −→ H 1 (C; Q) −→ H 1 (E ; Q) −→ H 0 (C, R1 p∗ Q) −→ H 2 (C; Q) −→ H 2 (E ; Q).

The last arrow is injective because p has a section. The first arrow is an isomorphism of
six-dimensional vector spaces. Exactness thus implies H 0 (C, R1 p∗ Q) = 0.
    The local torsor identifications differ by translations. On a smooth elliptic fibre translations
act trivially on H 1 . On the I12 fibre they preserve the orientation of the component polygon and
therefore act trivially on its one-dimensional H 1 as well. These identifications commute with

                                                191
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


the local specialization maps. Hence, for π : V → C, they glue to R1 π∗ Q ≃ R1 p∗ Q on the whole
curve, including infinity. The same Leray edge sequence for V now gives H 1 (V ; Q) ≃ H 1 (C; Q).
Thus b1 (V ) = 6 is even. Buchdahl’s theorem (Buchdahl, 1999, Theorem 11, p.297) proves that
V is Kähler without an algebraicity hypothesis.
    Choose a Hermitian metric on O ⊕ M . The induced metric on the tautological relatively
ample line of its projectivization has a closed real (1, 1) curvature form θ positive in the vertical
direction. If ω is a Kähler form on V , compactness implies that θ + Aπ ∗ ω is positive in every
direction for a sufficiently large constant A. It is closed, so it is a Kähler form on the projective
bundle. A smooth compact bimeromorphic model is therefore in Fujiki class C and satisfies the
  ¯
∂ ∂-lemma;  the domination statement is recalled, with its precise reference to the ∂ ∂¯ theorem, in
(Chen, 2026, Section 2.1, p.8). Apply 21.18 for the final obstruction.

21.4    Nonexistence of a proper analytic filling
Corollary 21.14 (counterexample; the proposed global filling). The actual punctured S 6 family
has no proper Hausdorff complex-analytic filling after any finite cover of w = 0. In particular,
a proper flat filling with smooth total space and reduced normal-crossings centre does not exist.
There is no positive least semistable exponent, no equivariant analytic filling to descend, and no
central multiplicity data for such a descent.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.58; section 21.1;
section 21.2; proposition 21.40.

Proof. Theorem 21.58 below proves the stronger assertion allowing arbitrary singular central
spaces and multiplicities. A hypothetical filling after any initial cover remains proper after a
further cover; the theorem excludes that further cover as well. The local constructions in 21.1
and 21.2 and the partial filling 21.40 therefore cannot be completed to the requested global
object.

    The obstruction cannot be removed by citing H 1 (B, V) = 0 from theorem 3.8. That vanishing
solves an additive translation cocycle for a fixed nonzero parameter and its integer shifts. On a
finite overlap the translation contains
                                  log sj                    12
                                         Πc v j ,     c=−       log r.
                                   2πi                      2πi
Its vertical exponential contains a product of the two logarithms. No assertion in the cited
vanishing controls its growth at r = 0 or makes it a unit in the central toric charts. 21.6 proves
that at least one of those extension requirements must fail for the prescribed pieces. That local
failure alone would not rule out a different cap. 21.53–21.58 supply the additional global argument
which excludes every proper analytic filling of the actual family, including such alternatives.

Theorem 21.15 (fundamental-group obstruction). Let f : Y → ∆ be a proper holomorphic map
from a smooth complex manifold, with smooth connected fibres over ∆∗ and reduced normal-
crossings central fibre D. There is a continuous specialization map from a nearby fibre Yt to D
which induces a surjection
                                        π1 (Yt ) −→ π1 (D).
No Kähler hypothesis is needed. Hence the central fibre of any such semistable filling of S 6 is
simply connected. In particular it cannot be a simple pinching of a connected normalization along
one pair of disjoint nonempty conductor sections, whether its elliptic normalization base is split
or is a genus-one torsor.



                                                    192
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                             Paper I


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Nakayama and Ogus, 2010, Theorem
5.1, p.2226).

Proof. Equip Y and ∆ with their divisorial logarithmic structures from D and 0. Locally, after
absorbing a unit, the map is t = z1 · · · zk . Its monoid chart is the diagonal N → Nk ; it is fine,
saturated, exact and log smooth. Thus (Nakayama and Ogus, 2010, Theorem 5.1, p.2226) applies
in the complex analytic category. The induced map of real oriented logarithmic blow-ups is a
proper topological fibre bundle over [0, ) × S 1 . Fix θ = arg t. Trivializing this bundle along
the radial interval identifies Yt homeomorphically with the fibre Dθlog over (0, θ). Its natural
projection
                                           pθ : Dθlog −→ D
is proper and surjective. Above a point lying on k local branches, its fibre consists of the phases
(θ1 , . . . , θk ) whose product is the fixed phase θ, including the harmless phase of the local unit. It
is a torus (S 1 )k−1 , in particular connected.
      Here is a covering-space proof that pθ is surjective on fundamental groups; path lifting for
the collapse is not assumed. The normal-crossings space D is locally contractible and has a
connected universal cover D.      e Pull it back along pθ . The map from the pullback to D     e is still
proper, surjective and has connected fibres. Its total space is connected: a nontrivial separation
into open and closed sets would, by properness and connected fibres, give such a separation
of D.e On the other hand its connected components are indexed by the cosets of the image of
π1 (Dθlog ) in π1 (D). There is therefore only one coset. Composing pθ with the chosen radial
homeomorphism proves the claim.
     We give an independent elementary surjectivity argument. Put W = f −1 (∆ ) and W ∗ =
W \D. The negative gradient of |f |2 , for a Hermitian metric, retracts W onto D. For completeness,
in a product chart f = z1 · · · zk the arithmetic– geometric mean inequality gives

                                         k∇|f |2 k ≥ c |f |2−1/k .

A finite cover of compact D gives a common exponent α < 1 in k∇ρk ≥ cρα , where ρ = |f |2 ; for a
fourfold one may take α = 7/8. The remaining trajectory length is bounded by c−1 ρ1−α /(1 − α).
Hence trajectories converge uniformly to D, and parametrization by the level of ρ gives a
continuous strong deformation retraction fixing D. General position moves every loop of W off
the real-codimension-two normal-crossings strata, so π1 (W ∗ ) → π1 (W ) is onto. The smooth
proper fibration over the punctured disc gives

                                  π1 (Yt ) −→ π1 (W ∗ ) −→ Z −→ 0.

A small transverse meridian at a smooth point of a reduced component maps to the generator of
Z and bounds a disc in W . Thus the image of π1 (Yt ) alone generates π1 (W ) = π1 (D).
   For the last assertion, let R be the connected normalization and D0 , D∞ its two disjoint
conductor sections. Choose a continuous function h : R → [0, 1] equal to zero on D0 and one on
D∞ . The function exp(2πih) descends to the pinching. A path from a point of D0 to its paired
point in D∞ becomes a loop whose image has winding number one. Consequently the pinching
has a surjection of its fundamental group onto Z. This contradicts the preceding necessary
condition when Yt ≃ S 6 .

Theorem 21.16 (consequences with explicit derivation). Let g : Z → ∆s be a proper holomorphic
map from a smooth complex fourfold, smooth over ∆∗s , with reduced normal-crossings central fibre



                                                   193
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


D. Suppose its nearby fibres are biholomorphic to the six-sphere members of the specified family,
after any finite base change w = sN . Then

                                H 1 (D; C) = 0,         h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1.

Consequently the natural map H 1 (D; C) → H 1 (D, OD ) is not surjective. In particular, D cannot
be the analytification of a proper complex algebraic variety with normal-crossings singularities.
    If D has simple normal crossings, at least one of its nonempty closed strata fails the ∂ ∂-lemma.
                                                                                             ¯
In particular, no such simple normal-crossings filling can have all irreducible components Kähler
or all irreducible components Moishezon. These obstructions hold for every N ≥ 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; section P.12; theorem 21.58; Nishiguchi
(1988, Theorem 1.4 and Example 2.1); Istrati et al. (2022, Theorem 7.1).
    This is the stated application of the classical Euler and normal-crossing cohomology results; all
hypotheses and the independent derivation are retained in the appendix. A complete re-derivation
is given in Appendix P.12.
    This is an application of existing Hodge-theoretic results, not a claim of a new degeneration
theorem. Searches on 15 November 2026 for six-sphere semistable degenerations, normal-crossings
limits, Moishezon central fibres, and Conjecture 8.2 with Hodge theory did not locate this specific
application. We opened Chen’s version 2 and checked Definition 2.3 and Theorem 2.4(4), including
the condition inserted before parts (3)–(4); omitting that condition would make the statement
false. We also opened the original Graf–Kovács article and checked the proper Du Bois assertion
in Section 1.D. The separate source audit records the searches.
    The theorem prevents a repair made solely from compact Moishezon components in a simple
normal-crossings model. It does not prove that an arbitrary analytic filling must have such
components. In particular, no argument here makes an unknown three-dimensional component
over the cusp Moishezon. These Hodge arguments alone give conditional restrictions, not
unrestricted nonexistence. The latter is proved in 21.58 for every finite parameter cover, using
the actual affine clutching. The Hopf-component example of Nishiguchi (1988, Theorem 1.4 and
Example 2.1) shows why an analytic degeneration cannot simply be assumed to have class-C
strata. The toric-Kato construction of Istrati et al. (2022, Theorem 7.1) is another relevant
non-Kähler analogue. Neither source supplies the required cusp comparison for the six-sphere
family.

Theorem 21.18 (the obstruction on normalization components). Let D be a compact reduced
complex space with normal-crossings singularities, allowing self-intersections of global components.
Suppose that every connected component of its smooth normalization satisfies the ∂ ∂-lemma.¯
Then the natural map
                                   H 1 (D; C) −→ H 1 (D, OD )
is surjective.
    Consequently every smooth-total-space reduced normal-crossings filling of the specified six-
sphere family, after any finite base change, has a normalization component which fails the
  ¯
∂ ∂-lemma.   In particular its normalization cannot consist entirely of compact Kähler or Moishezon
manifolds. This conclusion includes normal crossings which are not simple.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.15; theorem 21.16.

Proof. We give a degree-one argument directly on D; no nearby Hodge-de Rham degeneration
theorem is needed. Let D[p] be the smooth compact branch space whose points are ordered
(p + 1)-tuples of distinct local branches through one point of D. Equivalently, we normalize
the loci where these branches meet, retaining their ordering. These are distinct local branches,
even when they belong to one global irreducible component. The finite holomorphic maps
πp : D[p] → D and their face maps are specified by forgetting one branch. The symmetric group
acts by reordering; we take the alternating summand, with the sign character, in each degree.
Averaging over this finite group is exact over C. Write δ for the alternating sum of the face
pullbacks.
    Both augmented complexes
                                         alt                         alt
                      CD −→ (πp )∗ CD[p] p≥0 ,    OD −→ (πp )∗ OD[p] p≥0

are resolutions. This can be checked locally without a global ordering. In a chart z1 · · · zk = 0,
the constant complex is the augmented cochain complex of the simplex on the k branches. For
the holomorphic complex, fix a monomial in the convergent power series ring. It survives on
exactly the intersections indexed by subsets of those i for which its zi -exponent is zero. If
there are no such indices it already vanishes on D; otherwise its coefficient complex is again
an augmented simplex complex. The usual contraction is a finite combination of coordinate
restrictions, so preserves convergence. This proves exactness for analytic functions, not just
for formal series. The descriptions agree under permutations of the local branches. The finite
simplex and permutation identities for the at most four branches in our threefold application are
checked exactly in code/b_nc_degree_one.py.
    Resolve the holomorphic terms by smooth Dolbeault forms and the constant terms by smooth
de Rham forms on the branch spaces. These compute the respective hypercohomologies. Indeed
finite pushforward is exact here, and partitions of unity from local ambient smooth functions pull
back to make the resulting sheaves fine. The ordinary de Rham lemma and Dolbeault lemma
apply on each smooth branch space. Projection to the (0, •) part defines the natural comparison
between the two total complexes and induces H 1 (D; C) → H 1 (D, OD ).
    Represent a coherent degree-one class by a total cocycle (α, f ), where α is a smooth (0, 1)-form
on D[0] and f is an alternating smooth function on D[1] . Choose the total-complex signs so that

    This strengthens the simple-normal-crossings obstruction in 21.16 by using only degree one.

prove that all possible analytic normalization components satisfy its hypothesis.
Proposition 21.19 (a restricted non-Kähler cap obstruction). Let D be a compact reduced
normal-crossings complex space. Suppose its irreducible components have been partitioned into
closed unions D0 , . . . , Ds , with their reduced induced structures. Assume that

                       H 1 (Di , C) −→ H 1 (Di , O)    is surjective for every i,           (B.46a)

and that the analogous map is injective for every pairwise intersection Di ∩ Dj . Then

                             H 1 (D, C) −→ H 1 (D, OD ) is surjective.                      (B.46b)

     In particular these hypotheses hold for the following specified cap assembly. The horizontal
block D0 is a two-section pinching of a ruled bundle over an analytic locally trivial torsor V → C
of 21.13, with conductor map A covering σ and A12 = t6P . The normalization may undergo the
modifications of 21.12, or any smooth bimeromorphic modifications for which the two conductor
restriction maps on H 1 are the same pullbacks as before. The other blocks are smooth hyperbolic
toric Kato threefolds or compact smooth spaces satisfying (B.46a), for example class-C spaces.
Assume every pairwise overlap is either a reduced union of invariant divisors of a hyperbolic
toric Kato threefold, or a compact normal-crossings surface whose normalized components and
normalized double curves are rational. No such assembly can be a semistable central fibre of the
S 6 family.
     This excludes the stated cap construction even when an invariant Kato surface in an overlap
kills a fundamental-group generator of a Kato component. It is not a classification of arbitrary
analytic cusp components or of their possible overlaps.

Proof. Write D[p] for the disjoint union of intersections of p + 1 distinct blocks. The augmented

by products in disjoint sets of variables. The ordinary alternating intersection complex is exact, as
one sees on each monomial, where it is the augmented complex of a simplex. The same contraction
acts coefficientwise on convergent power series. For constant sheaves, small intersections are
contractible unions of coordinate subspaces, and the same stalkwise simplex complex is exact.
This proves both resolutions also when the global blocks are self-crossing.
    Their hypercohomology spectral sequences have

shows that 1 − A∗ is invertible on both groups. The normalization sequence of the two-section

Both classes come from the same difference map on constant functions of the conductor. Their

computation is essential: on an individual conductor V , the comparison has dimensions six and
three and is not injective.

is injective, because a global section of dO is a closed holomorphic one-form. The two dimensions

     Finally let F be a reduced union of invariant divisors in a hyperbolic toric Kato threefold.

invariant curve is rational in the hyperbolic case (Istrati et al., 2022, Theorem 5.2). Use the
ordered-local-branch resolution from 21.18. The comparisons on component H 1 are isomorphisms,
and the groups on normalized double curves vanish. The same five-term argument shows that
H 1 (F, C) → H 1 (F, OF ) is an isomorphism. For an overlap with rational normalized components
and double curves, the argument is identical with zero component H 1 . Thus every pairwise
overlap in the statement has the required injective comparison, proving (B.46b) for the specified
assembly.
     For an actual semistable S 6 centre, 21.15 gives H 1 (D, C) = 0, while upper semicontinuity
and the nearby value h1 (O) = 1 in 21.16 give h1 (D, OD ) ≥ 1. This contradicts (B.46b). The
obstruction uses the cohomology maps on the overlaps; it does not assume that every Kato
component’s loop survives in the union.

Why automatic analytic comparison is not used. We also examined whether general
results on degenerations of tori would force an arbitrary filling into the excluded toroidal class.
The distinction between a construction theorem and such a comparison theorem is essential.
Kajiwara et al. (2008b, Theorem 5.1.3 and Sections 5.2–5.4) construct proper analytic models of
log complex tori without assuming a polarization. Their input is a specified log complex torus
and an admissible pairing; the theorem does not assert that every proper analytic filling is one of
these models. 21.45 constructs the actual local Jacobian log input and isolates its affine torsor
obstruction. 21.58 derives an associated torsor from traces in a hypothetical cap; it does not
identify that cap with a proper fan model.
     The classification in Kamenova (nd, Theorem 3.1) assumes a Kähler total space and trivial
canonical bundle. Those hypotheses have not been proved for a slice of an arbitrary filling
here. Schröer and Siebert (2002b, Section 3, Proposition 3.1) explicitly study normal-crossings
degenerations with Hopf normalization, but their smooth fibres are primary Kodaira surfaces.
This is a source of alternative analytic models to test, not a comparison with our punctured
family.
     Even extending the marked map in 21.17 does not extend a chosen punctured isomorphism
to a second model. Properness alone cannot justify that inference: the automorphism (s, [z0 :
z1 ]) 7→ (s, [e1/s z0 : z1 ]) of ∆∗ × P1 has no meromorphic extension across zero, although both
product families are proper over the disc. Its restriction to [1 : 1] has an essential singularity.
Thus an unrestricted proof needs additional information beyond a punctured isomorphism.
21.53–21.58 supply exactly such information: bounded differences of extending sections and
a global radial-loop invariant. Their contradiction proves nonexistence without extending an
individual punctured isomorphism meromorphically.

    For completeness, the two scalar Hopf surfaces used above are not biholomorphic. An
isomorphism lifts to an automorphism of C2 \ {0} that intertwines the two cyclic generators
or their inverses. Hartogs extension applies to the lift and its inverse; both fix zero and have
invertible derivative there. Differentiating the intertwining identity gives e−2π = (−e−π )±1 , which
is false. They have no rational curves, since a map P1 → Hα lifts to C2 \ {0} and is constant.
The usual resolution of a bimeromorphic map of smooth compact surfaces therefore also shows
that these two Hopf surfaces are not bimeromorphic. This agrees with the explicit scalar case of
Abasheva and Déev (2024, Section 2.2).
    There is an even shorter argument excluding a meromorphic extension of the punctured
product comparison. A sufficiently small closed semistable neighbourhood in H retracts onto
Y , by the monomial-gradient argument of 21.15. Its fundamental group is zero. The product
neighbourhood H− × ∆ has fundamental group Z. If the punctured comparison had a proper
meromorphic graph, resolving that graph would give a common smooth proper modification
of the two neighbourhoods. A proper bimeromorphic map between smooth complex manifolds
preserves π1 , by the codimension-two avoidance argument in 20.17. This is a contradiction.
Both models already have the indicated holomorphic map to the same P1 ; the example therefore
retains an extended base map while the total-space comparison fails.
    Finally take the product with P1 . Its central integral Betti numbers are
                                         (1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 3, 2),
and h1 (O) remains one. The nearby fibre is H− × P1 , of fundamental group Z and Euler number
zero. These explicit invariants prevent this example from being mistaken for a filling of S 6 .

Remark 21.21 (Primary literature and the scope of the auxiliary cap). The Cartier-divisor
cocycle above is established machinery, not a new logarithmic-transformation construction.
Fujimoto’s Definition 1.1 permits an arbitrary Cartier divisor; his Remark 1.4 attributes non-
Kähler torus degenerations to Ueno. His Proposition 1.14 extends principal elliptic bundles
across subsets of codimension at least three. Example 1.15 concerns failure of extension as a
principal elliptic bundle in codimension two and explicitly leaves general relative compactification
open there; it supplies no unrestricted nonexistence theorem for the present cusp (Fujimoto,
1990, pp. 85–86, 93–94).
    Hopf components in analytic semistable degenerations are already present in the original
work of Nishiguchi (1988, Theorem 1.4 and Sections 2–3). The explicit diagonal Hopf quotients,
elliptic conductor gluing and normal-line calculation in Schröer and Siebert (2002a, Section 3,
especially Propositions 3.1–3.4) give a closely related analytic model. Those are comparisons, not
smoothing theorems for the present threefold. The construction above supplies its own complete
proper family and does not invoke such a theorem by analogy.
    There are two concrete obstacles to directly inserting the product cap into B.3. The divisor
E × P1 in Hi × P1 has normal degree zero along the P1 ruling. The exceptional divisor obtained
by blowing up an elliptic curve in a horizontal normalization has normal degree −1 on its
exceptional P1 fibres. For a two-component attachment with no triple divisor on this interface,
these cannot be dual normal lines. In the general normal-crossings formula a triple divisor must
also be included: a section E × {p} has degree +1 on the ruling and could cancel this particular
mismatch. No obstruction to such a higher-intersection attachment is asserted. Moreover the
actual generic two-tori do not possess the elliptic fibration of a principal elliptic bundle, as the
following exact calculation shows.
    Fix an ordinary base point for which µ ∈   / Qτ + Q. Such points exist: otherwise the ordinary
base would be the countable union of the analytic loci where one rational relation µ = rτ +s holds;
Baire’s theorem would force one such relation identically, contradicting that P is a nontorsion
section. For integral vectors v = (a, b, c, d) and v 0 = (A, B, C, D), write
                                Πv = (6aµ + bτ + c, aβ + bµ + d).

                                                 202
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


The coefficient of β in det(Πv, Πv 0 ) is

                                      (Ab − aB)τ + (Ac − aC).

If it vanishes and one of a, A is nonzero, the first three coordinates of v, v 0 are rationally
proportional. The remaining determinant is (6aµ + bτ + c)(D − (A/a)d) after choosing a 6= 0; the
first factor is nonzero, so a zero determinant would make the two vectors dependent. The case
a = 0, A 6= 0 is the same statement with the vectors interchanged. If a = A = 0, the determinant
is
                              (bD − Bd)τ + (cB − Cb)µ + (cD − Cd),
and the rational independence of 1, τ, µ again forces all the minors to vanish. Thus every
independent integral pair spans a complex line for at most one value of β. There are countably
many pairs. For all other admissible parameters the two-torus is simple and contains no elliptic
subtorus. In particular the distinguished line Cδ meets the period lattice in Zδ, so its complexified
orbit is C∗ , rather than an elliptic curve.
    A principal elliptic-bundle construction may therefore describe a central cap, but cannot
by itself equal the entire prescribed punctured cusp family. It would need an additional affine
identification that destroys its generic elliptic fibration, together with the actual nodal q-interface
and the finite-place component rotations. The construction here establishes none of those
additional comparisons. 21.58 separately rules out a proper analytic filling of the actual global
family, without denying the auxiliary Hopf degeneration constructed above.

Remark 21.22 (Limits of automatic analytic comparison). The abstract identity Aut(X) = C∗
does not supply a meromorphic compactification of the action. On an ordinary two-torus the
distinguished orbit is a nonconstant holomorphic map from C∗ . If it extended meromorphically
across both ends to P1 , it would extend holomorphically: a meromorphic map from a smooth
curve to a compact complex manifold has a removable indeterminacy. Every holomorphic map
P1 → T 2 is constant, since it lifts to C2 . This is a contradiction. Thus an algebraic structure on
the abstract automorphism group is insufficient here.
    The compactification theorem of Biliotti and Ghigi (2021, Theorem 1.2) assumes Fujiki class
C; that hypothesis is unavailable. The local isomorphism theorem of Meersseman (2011, Theorem
3) assumes pointwise isomorphism on the whole base, including its central point, and constant
vector-field dimension. It cannot identify the unknown central fibre. The Hopf compactification
example of Katzarkov et al. (2025, Example 1) likewise illustrates that an analytic open part
need not determine a bimeromorphic compactification. Their definability-based comparison is
not used: no definability of our punctured comparison has been proved. 21.20 supplies a proper
family exhibiting the relevant failure directly. None of these automatic-comparison results proves
the conclusion of 21.58, whose argument instead uses extending-section differences and the global
affine loop invariant.
    Non-Kähler modifications of elliptic degenerations are established. The product case in
Fujimoto (1988, Section 3, Example 3.4(1)), using the preceding construction, already gives such
degenerations with elliptic abelian nearby surfaces. Its elliptic-bundle structure prevents a direct
identification with our generic simple two-tori. For the related codimension-two extension question,
Nakayama (2002, Theorem 7.1.3) proves an extension criterion for locally bimeromorphically
projective elliptic fibrations over a punctured polydisc: the fibration must be bimeromorphically
projective over that punctured base. It rules out the sectionless elliptic example discussed there.
Our regular fibres have dimension two and no asserted elliptic quotient, so that theorem does
not establish a nonexistence result for the present filling.

    The differential-geometric smoothing theorem of Doi (2009, Theorem 5.5, pp. 882–883) allows
non-Kähler components with dual normal bundles, anticanonical double divisors and compatible
residues. Its total space is a smooth real six-manifold and its map is smooth; the complex
structures on the surface fibres vary continuously in the stated sense. This is not a holomorphic
total-space filling theorem. Example 5.3 identifies the degree-zero elliptic ruled self-gluing with a
torus and the nonzero-degree cases with Kodaira surfaces. Neither result supplies the prescribed
holomorphic two-parameter comparison at our missing origin.

   Under q = sN ε(s) the degree becomes mN . The unit ε(s)m b(q(s)) has zero winding. Thus

                              (0, mN ) ∈ H 1 (Ea,q ; Z) ⊗ H 1 (Ss1 ; Z).

This is an integral calculation; no limiting logarithm or asymptotic estimate is involved.
    Suppose an extension C existed. Its central fibre is connected. Flatness and properness give
arithmetic genus one, and the normalization exact sequence gives
                                           X
                                       1=      g(Ci ) + b1 (Γ),
                                            i

where Ci are the smooth normalization components and Γ is the dual graph, including a loop
for a self-node. Consequently either there is a unique elliptic component and Γ is a tree, or all
components are rational and Γ has one cycle.
    The second case has nontrivial monodromy. This can be seen directly in the local plumbing
uv = s. Transport around s = 0 is a positive Dehn twist on its neck annulus. An edge outside
the unique graph cycle gives a separating neck and acts trivially on H1 . Each of the k ≥ 1 edges
in the graph cycle gives a nonseparating neck. These disjoint necks represent the same primitive
class up to sign on the smoothed genus-one surface. The transvection is unchanged by reversing
that class. Their product therefore has, in a symplectic basis, the matrix
                                                  
                                               1 k
                                               0 1

or its inverse under the opposite monodromy convention. It is not the identity. The given
punctured elliptic family has identity monodromy, so this case is impossible. This elementary
plumbing argument is all that is needed here; no algebraic stable-reduction or comparison theorem
for arbitrary analytic total spaces is being assumed.
    There is therefore an elliptic core C0 with rational trees attached at finitely many points.
Choose two oriented loops on C0 avoiding those points and with intersection number one. The
map p is a submersion near their union. Compactness of the loops and a smooth horizontal
distribution provide, after shrinking the disc, families of loops over the full disc. Each swept
torus on its boundary bounds the resulting solid torus in C. Hence the first Chern class of every
line bundle on C evaluates to zero on both such swept tori.
    The two transported loops form a basis of the nearby elliptic fibre’s H1 : cutting off the
rational trees adds only genus-zero pieces along separating necks, and their intersection number
remains one. Under the given punctured isomorphism, their swept tori therefore project to a
basis of the mixed group H1 (Ea,q ; Z) ⊗ H1 (Ss1 ; Z). They may differ from the marked swept tori
by integral fibre classes. This accounts in particular for an arbitrary loop of fibre translations
in the isomorphism. The fibre degree of Lm is zero, so these additional fibre classes do not
change either pairing. The nonzero covector (0, mN ) cannot vanish on both basis vectors. This
contradicts the bounding-solid-torus calculation and proves the assertion.
    Finally an extending tensor factor has zero pairing on both bounding tori by the same
argument. It cannot cancel the obstruction. Vertical divisors and any Cartier triple divisor on
such an extended interface are included among these harmless tensor factors.

Remark 21.24 (What a corrected cap must change). The obstruction concerns an individual
normal line, not just the tensor product of two normal lines in the T 1 condition. Opposite
windings can cancel in that tensor product while neither line extends on its own proposed smooth
branch. Thus cancelling the scalar q by q −1 is insufficient for this good-reduction interface. A
successful correction would have to change the interface or its punctured normal bundle outside
the class specified above. The constant-elliptic example 21.20 has no such winding and remains
consistent with 21.23.

Proposition 21.26 (an explicit parabolic family and its nonextending exceptional correction).
Fix an integer n ≥ 1 and holomorphic units a(s), κ(s) on a disc, with 0 < |a(s)| < 1. After
shrinking the disc there is a proper holomorphic submersion K → ∆s , with an embedded smooth
proper elliptic family
                               E = (C∗ × ∆s )/((v, s) ∼ (a(s)v, s)).
Its central surface is a parabolic Inoue surface Sn , with π1 (Sn ) = Z, b2 (Sn ) = n, and elliptic axis
of square −n. For s 6= 0, the surface Ks is obtained from the diagonal Hopf surface Hκ(s)sn ,a(s)
by n successive blow-ups at one axis point and its indicated infinitely near strict-axis points. In a
fixed annulus marking of E, its normal line has factor
                                      gs (v) = κ(s)(a(s)v + s)n .
This line extends across s = 0 and is isomorphic to the holomorphic family with factor κ(s)a(s)n v n .
For constant a, κ it is a constant family of degree −n lines.

                            NEs /Ks = Lκ(s)sn ⊗ OEs (−n[−s]),            s 6= 0.
Here n[−s] is the weighted total exceptional correction, not the intersection with the reduced
final exceptional locus. It has no Cartier extension on E, even after a finite base change or the
addition of a vertical component. Thus this construction does not contradict 21.23: the marked
divisor used to change the normal line fails to extend.
    For n = 8, the degree −8 axis normal can be chosen to be the inverse of OE (2) on any chosen
smooth elliptic complete intersection E = (2, 2) ⊂ P3 . This supplies the normal-line matching
with BlE P3 described below, including one positive triple section. It is an auxiliary construction
and first-order matching result. No attachment to the prescribed punctured S 6 family, compact

their tensor product would extend Lm , contradicting 21.23. Drifting translations cannot remove
both requirements. The present Kato family escapes exactly because Dexc = n[−s] has no such
extension.

Remark 21.27 (Auxiliary normal matching and the actual filling obstruction). Choose a smooth
quadric Q ⊂ P3 containing E. Its strict transform in A is still Q ≃ P1 × P1 : blowing up its Cartier
divisor E does not change Q. Its normal is OQ (2, 2)(−E) ≃ OQ , and it meets D in a section.
The matching surface S8 × {p} in B also has trivial normal. A third threefold would therefore
need divisors Q and S8 meeting along E, with normals OQ (−E) and OS8 (−E) respectively.
These are exactly the normal conditions for the central surface Q ∪E S8 in a semistable surface
smoothing. The surface smoothing is constructed in 21.28–21.29. Its topological Euler number
is 4 + 8 − 2χ(E) = 12 and its holomorphic Euler number is one. Its total space over an open
disc is not a compact third threefold, so that construction does not supply a compact threefold
assembly.
     A full assembly must also preserve the required coherent cohomology from 21.18; a lone
parabolic component attached to rational components can lose its H 1 (O) through the elliptic
overlap. Additional conductor surfaces meeting E would contribute further triple divisors
and must be included in the normal equation. Nor is a local change of the cusp parameter
automatically a permitted global base change of the prescribed family. These auxiliary matching
statements do not produce a filling of the actual family. 21.58 proves that no such proper analytic
filling exists after any finite parameter cover.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.28; proposition 21.29;
theorem 21.18; theorem 21.58.

Proposition 21.28 (globalization at the contracted parabolic elliptic axis). Let S = S8 (a, κ)
be the central parabolic surface in 21.26, let E ⊂ S be its elliptic axis, and put N = NE/S , so

singular point p. Its germ at p is the vertex of the affine cone over (E, N −1 ). In particular,

                                         H 2 (Y, ΘY ) = 0.

The restriction morphism from a semiuniversal deformation of Y to a semiuniversal deformation
of (Y, p) is regular. Consequently every prescribed analytic one-parameter deformation of this
isolated singularity is induced, after shrinking its parameter disc, by a proper deformation of
the compact surface Y . If the prescribed local deformation smooths the singularity, the global
deformation has smooth fibres away from the central value.
    This concerns globalization of a specified local deformation of an auxiliary compact surface.
It does not assert an attachment to the punctured S 6 family or a compactification of the resulting
threefold over the open parameter disc.

vector-field flow, which preserves the defining ideal. The flow preserves the unique singular point,
hence its maximal ideal. Functoriality of the blow-up of that ideal lifts the flow to the resolution,
preserving the exceptional curve. Its derivative is therefore a section of F. Conversely a section
of F differentiates pullbacks of holomorphic functions on Y and descends to a derivation, because
π∗ OS = OY . Both operations agree off E and are inverse there; uniqueness extends the equality
over E.
    The global-to-local cohomology map is surjective for a concrete reason. Write a = e2πiτ with
Im τ > 0, and vary τ to τ + u in the explicit Kato construction, keeping its translation parameter

                                                     213
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


zero. The same uniform collar argument as in 21.26 gives a proper holomorphic deformation of
the pair (S, E). Its Kodaira–Spencer class belongs to H 1 (S, F). Under the natural composite
                                                          ∼
                          H 1 (S, F) −→ H 0 (Y, R1 π∗ F) −−→ H 1 (E, ΘE )

it is the Kodaira–Spencer class of C/(Z + (τ + u)Z), which is nonzero. For example, differentiating
its second deck transformation z 7→ z + τ + u gives the usual nonzero period cocycle. This
argument works also at the elliptic curves with extra automorphisms; it does not differentiate
the coarse j-invariant. The target is one dimensional, so the first arrow is onto.
     The degree-two part of the Leray sequence is

                   H 1 (S, F) −→ H 0 (Y, R1 π∗ F) −→ H 2 (Y, π∗ F) −→ H 2 (S, F).

The first map is surjective and the last group is zero. Using π∗ F = ΘY proves H 2 (Y, ΘY ) = 0.
    We spell out the local-to-global criterion used in the final step, since the rational-cycle
contraction theorem does not apply to this elliptic contraction. For a compact complex space
with isolated singularities, H 2 (Θ) = 0 makes the restriction from global to local deformations
formally smooth. Here is the obstruction argument for the present single singularity. Take a
finite Stein cover with one small neighbourhood of p and all other members smooth. For a small
extension of Artinian bases, prescribe the lifted deformation on the singular member and take
smooth local lifts on the other members. Their pairwise identifications lift on the smooth Stein
intersections. The failure of the cocycle identity on triple intersections is a Cech two-cocycle
in ΘY tensored with the square-zero kernel. Its class vanishes by the proved H 2 -vanishing;
correcting the identifications by a one-cochain glues the desired lift. This proves the relative
infinitesimal lifting property.
    The analytic semiuniversal deformation theory turns this property into regularity of the
induced morphism of analytic base germs. The general criterion is Manetti (1991, Lemma 1,
p. 93), stated for reduced compact complex spaces with isolated singularities and proved by
the local-to-global spectral sequence of the cotangent complex. It is also used in Dloussky and
Teleman (2020, Section 3.2, Proposition 3.3 and the discussion preceding Proposition 3.4). There
is no hypothesis about the kind of exceptional curve in this criterion. A regular morphism of
analytic germs is locally a projection from a product with a smooth germ. Consequently a
specified analytic disc in the local deformation base lifts to the global base, without replacing the
prescribed local deformation by a different smoothing component. The global family is proper by
the compact deformation construction. Away from p its central fibre is smooth, and smoothness
is open; compactness permits one common shrinking of the disc. A local smoothing at p therefore
gives smooth global noncentral fibres, as asserted.

Proposition 21.30 (the second period does not lift to a finite marked Hopf modification). Fix
0 < |α|, |a| < 1, and put

                 H = (C2 \ {0})/h(x, v) 7→ (αx, av)i,      E = {x = 0} ≃ C∗ /aZ .

Let h be the automorphism induced by (x, v) 7→ (cx, bv), where b, c ∈ C∗ . Suppose p : Y → H is
a finite composition of point blow-ups, allowing infinitely near centres, and at least one point of
E is an image of its exceptional locus. If [b] ∈ C∗ /aZ has infinite order, there is no holomorphic
automorphism of Y which agrees, on the dense unmodified core, with the marked automorphism
h.
    The same obstruction holds for a finite collection of such marked modifications if the proposed
period permutes the collection and acts as h on each marked core. More generally, if a compact
smooth surface contains a preserved marked elliptic curve E of nonzero normal degree d, every
holomorphic automorphism restricting to translation by b on E must satisfy d b = 0 in E. The
latter assertion also excludes a finite cycle of such preserved marked cap axes when the cycle
composite is an infinite-order translation. These assertions apply to the direct attempt to lift
the second actual cusp period to the finite Hopf modifications in 21.26, for generic nonzero
parameters, after every finite base change. It concerns a holomorphic period action on these full
modifications. It does not exclude a meromorphic correspondence, a different connected unfolding
made from noncompact pieces, or a cap present only over the central parameter.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.26; theorem 20.2;
proposition 21.23.

Proof. Let S ⊂ H be the image of the exceptional curves of p. It is finite. Repeated infinitely
near blow-ups change the curves over a point but do not make S infinite. If e h were a lift, the
maps
                                      h, hp : Y −→ H
                                     pe
would agree on the dense core and hence everywhere, by the identity principle for holomorphic
maps to the separated complex surface H. The image under e      h of a curve contracted by p is
therefore again contracted by p. Applying the same argument to e     h−1 proves that the total
exceptional locus is preserved. Thus h(S) = S.
    The automorphism h preserves E, where it is translation by [b]. Consequently the nonempty
finite set S ∩ E would be invariant under that translation. The orbit of any one of its points is
finite, so for some k > 0,
                              [bk v] = [v],  equivalently bk ∈ aZ .
This says exactly that [b] is torsion, a contradiction. In particular, no choice of multiplicities
or infinitely near centres changes the obstruction: only their nonempty finite support on E is
needed.
    For finitely many modifications pi : Yi → H, a proposed deck map has biholomorphisms
Yi → Yσ(i) satisfying the same core comparison. The identity principle again gives equivariance
everywhere. The union of the finitely many exceptional image sets is h-invariant; its intersection

                                               217
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


with E gives the same contradiction. Equivalently, around a cycle of length ` the map h` would
lift to a single modification, while [b` ] still has infinite order.
     For the more general assertion no blowdown is needed. If an automorphism preserves E, its
derivative in the normal direction gives

                                         t∗b NE/S ≃ NE/S .

For a line bundle N of degree d on an elliptic curve, the homomorphism b 7→ t∗b N ⊗ N −1
is multiplication   byP−d under the usual identification Pic0 (E) = E. Indeed write N =
OE ( j nj [pj ]) with j nj = d; the Abel–Jacobi class of its translated divisor minus the original
     P
one is −db. Thus preservation of N forces db = 0. Taking a power proves the finite-cycle
version, since its composite preserves one axis and its nonzero-degree normal line. In particular a
nonzero-degree parabolic axis cannot carry the marked generic period translation even if no finite
Hopf modification is specified. The original finite-support argument also covers modifications
where that normal-degree test alone would give no information.
    We check the actual cusp rather than assume that torsion fails. The periods of 20.2 have the
form
                 g1 : (Z, W ) 7−→ (qc1 Z, c2 W ),  g2 : (Z, W ) 7−→ (c3 Z, r12 qc4 W ),
where the ci are nonvanishing holomorphic units near the cusp. Choose W or W −1 so that a = cε2

limiting unit has modulus different from one, as computed in 21.23. For q 6= 0 small, the partial
g1 quotient of (C∗ )2 is the dense core of the diagonal Hopf surface with multipliers (qc1 , a). The
second period induces the above h, with

                                     b(q, r) = (r12 qc4 (q, r))ε .

Fix a sufficiently small nonzero q. For each k > 0 and j ∈ Z, the equation b(q, r)k = a(q)j has
a discrete solution set in the punctured r-disc: its left-hand side has a zero or pole of nonzero
order at r = 0, while the right-hand side is a nonzero constant in r. Hence outside a countable
union of discrete sets, [b(q, r)] has infinite order. Under a finite base change in r the nonzero
order is multiplied by its ramification index and the same conclusion holds. A finite base change
in q does not affect this fixed-nonzero-q argument.
    To compare with 21.26, write qc1 = κ(s)sn after the chosen finite cover in the cusp variable.
Its generic Kato fibre is precisely a finite Hopf modification with nonempty axis centre [−s]. A
holomorphic extension of the actual second period to that whole fibre would therefore contradict
the result just proved. Allowing finitely many translated copies does not remove the contradiction,
by the finite-collection assertion.

Remark 21.31 (What an infinite unfolding must additionally prove). There is no corresponding
obstruction to merely indexing translated modifications by all integers and letting the deck
map shift the index. That construction alone has the wrong core. Indeed suppose pj : Yj → H
and e
    hj : Yj → Yj+1 satisfy pj+1e  hj = hpj . On the disjoint union of their unmodified cores, the
quotient by the shift is identified with the single core H ◦ by

                                       [(j, y)] 7−→ h−j pj (y).

It is not the required quotient H ◦ /hhi. Thus a useful unfolding must have additional connected
overlaps and must recover the original second-period identifications there.
     Nor can one simply glue several full compact Hopf modifications along the same dense
core and assume a Hausdorff space results. If two embedded compact spaces in a Hausdorff
space share an open subset dense in both, their images, being closed, both equal its closure.
They coincide. A construction by genuinely distinct compact copies with only that common

                                                 218
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


core consequently cannot be such a Hausdorff gluing. These observations alone do not classify
connected unfoldings of noncompact pieces with a new boundary geometry. Analytic transition
maps, proper discontinuity and the retained punctured quotient are not supplied by the auxiliary
compact family in 21.26. Independently of that restricted classification question, 21.58 rules out
any such construction giving a proper filling of the actual global family.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.26; theorem 21.58.

21.6    A local insertion into the prescribed simple-torus family
Proposition 21.33. Let q0 be a regular point of the elliptic base, and let ∆z , z = q − q0 , be a
simply connected disc avoiding 0, 1, ∞. After w = r6 , take the standard twelve-cycle model

                                          X −→ ∆z × ∆r

of the prescribed local two-torus family. There is a proper replacement X 0 → ∆z × ∆r , with a
specified isomorphism to X off (z, r) = (0, 0), whose total fourfold is smooth and whose divisor
r = 0 is reduced normal crossings. The composite map to ∆r is flat.
     The replacement has twelve new compact vertical normalization components. Six are P1 -
bundles over a scalar Hopf surface; the other six are the blow-ups of those bundles along two
disjoint elliptic curves. Every new component has fundamental group Z, and therefore fails the
∂ ∂¯ lemma. The punctured family is the actual prescribed family, so its generic simplicity is
preserved.
     This is a statement about a proper model over a bidisc, flat over the degeneration parameter.
It does not assert joint flatness over the bidisc, a one-parameter degeneration of compact surfaces
with Hopf components, or a global S 6 filling. All twelve component labels, and hence the obstruction
of 21.6, are unchanged.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.6; (Cartan, 1952); Fujimoto
(1990, Definition 1.1).

Proof. The actual action. Use the rank-three period subsystem

                       u(z) = (τ (z), µ(z)),     w = (1, 0),         δ = (0, 1).

It defines the analytic semiabelian group

   Gz = C2 /(Zu(z) + Zw + Zδ),         1 −→ C∗δ −→ Gz −→ Ez −→ 0,             Ez = C/(Z + τ (z)Z).

This is the punctured degree-zero line bundle determined by the actual µ(z). We make neither a
product assumption nor a torsion assumption on that line bundle. The formula
                                           log t
                                                    
                                χz (t) =         u(z)  (t ∈ C∗ )                    (B.4.15.1)
                                            2πi
is a single-valued holomorphic homomorphism: a logarithm change adds an actual lattice period.
It varies holomorphically with z. The r-monodromy fixes u, and the z-disc has no period
monodromy.
    Here the action extends to the entire twelve-cycle model, not just to its smooth fibres. Each
unfolded normalization is
                                            ∗
                                Rz = Gz ×Cδ P1 = PEz (O ⊕ Lz ).
Translation in Gz preserves both conductor sections. More explicitly, a class represented by (a, b)
acts before the closing quotient by

                                   (ξ, W ) 7−→ (ξ + a, e−2πib W ).                         (B.4.15.2)

It commutes exactly with the closing period, which is another translation of the same commutative
group and whose scalar factor contains r12 . The adjacent line directions are paired dually in
the local equation xy = r; the two scalar factors cancel. Scalar multiplication also preserves the
one-dimensional toric subdivision producing the twelve components. Thus (21.33.2) extends over
every node, preserves each branch, and changes a branch equation x by a unit times x. This
checks the required action using the actual semiabelian marking of B.1.

    The affine family itself admits the necessary local punctured comparison. On U = ∆z × ∆∗r its
lattice local system Λ has H 2 (U, Λ) = 0, since U retracts onto a circle, also for local coefficients.
Its relative Lie algebra V is a coherent vector bundle. The exponential sequence

                                       0 −→ Λ −→ V −→ T −→ 0

and Cartan’s theorem B on the Stein base give H 1 (U, T ) = 0 (Cartan, 1952). Consequently
the actual affine torsor has a holomorphic section on U , which supplies the stated punctured
comparison with its Jacobian. No extension of this section across r = 0 is asserted.
   The base blow-up and small resolutions. Blow up the base origin:
                   e = Bl(0,0) (∆z × ∆r ) −→ ∆z × ∆r ,

In the chart r = zs, the pulled-back node is xy = zs, with one further smooth elliptic coordinate.

branch, and blow up (x, z). This is globally the sum of the pulled-back invertible ideal of the
chosen central component and the ideal OBe (−F ). The ideals are G-invariant. Their non-Cartier

                                      z = xQ, y = Qs,          r = xQs,

They are smooth, and all three factors of r occur once. In the other base chart z = rζ, the node
is xy = r and the same ideal is (x, r) = (x), so no change occurs. Away from the indicated node
loci it is also invertible. The resulting total space is smooth and its r-central divisor is reduced
normal crossings.
    For the component identifications, before resolution put

                                 Vx = {x = z = 0}, Vy = {y = z = 0},
                                 Hx = {x = s = 0}, Hy = {y = s = 0}.

The V branches are vertical over F , and the H branches lie over the strict transform of r = 0.
On Vx , the two maps in (21.33.3) are

                       (Q, s) 7−→ (y, s) = (Qs, s),         (X, y) 7−→ (y, s) = (y, Xy).

These are exactly the blow-up charts of (y, s). Thus Vx is blown up along its elliptic curve over
y = s = 0; Vy is unchanged. Similarly Hy is blown up along the corresponding elliptic curve
and Hx is unchanged. Each even vertical component is therefore blown up at its two disjoint
conductor curves, whereas each odd vertical component is unchanged. The horizontal parities
are reversed.
    The Cartier logarithm and properness. Set M = OBe (F ). On a trivializing cover write its
transition units as gij . Glue the resolved pullbacks by χz (gij ). These are genuine automorphisms
satisfying the cocycle identity. This is the Cartier-logarithm construction of Fujimoto (1990,
Definition 1.1); the explicit semiabelian action above verifies its applicability here, without
assuming that the smooth two-tori are principal elliptic bundles. The invariant ideals show that
the action lifts to the resolutions; equivalently one may twist first and then resolve the descended
ideals.
    Over every base chart the glued space is a copy of the proper resolved pullback. It is Hausdorff:
two points over the same base point are separated in such a chart, and points over distinct base
points are separated in the base. Properness is local on the target, and composition with the

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                            Paper I


proper β proves properness over the original bidisc. The canonical divisor section of M is nonzero
off F and trivializes the twist there. The base blow-up and the resolutions are also isomorphisms
off the origin. This gives the specified isomorphism with the original family there, in particular
over every r 6= 0.
    The construction can be inserted into any larger model which is standard near q0 : the
preceding trivialization supplies the overlap map outside the origin. The cocharacter u is needed
only on this disc and is not extended around the special base points. Since the local rings of
the total space are regular and r is a nonzero divisor, they are torsion-free, hence flat, over the
one-dimensional regular parameter ring. This proves flatness over r. The new vertical threefolds
rule out joint flatness over the bidisc. Properness over the r-disc alone follows only when this
local replacement is inserted into a model with compact elliptic base.

Remark 21.34. For a generic arc z = kr through the blown-up base origin, the strict transform
meets F at an ordinary point. Its central surface remains a cycle of ruled surfaces over the
elliptic curve. The non-Kähler geometry in (21.33.4) is carried by the variation around the whole
exceptional P1 . Therefore a theorem only about one-parameter limits of simple two-tori would
not, by itself, exclude these vertical threefold components.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.33.

Proposition 21.35 (scope of the insertion operations). The local operation 21.33 attaches a
triangulated cylinder to the original twelve-cycle in the dual complex and admits an elementary


                                                  223
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


collapse back to that cycle. In a compact normal-crossings model, performing it at a regular place
consequently preserves the homotopy type of the global dual complex.
    The same conclusion holds for finite sequences of these insertions, twists by a connected
holomorphic group action preserving the prescribed normal-crossings model, and toroidal
subdivisions of its central cone complex. In particular, starting with a model whose dual complex
has a nonzero first integral cohomology class, these operations cannot produce a semistable S 6
centre. They also cannot change the component rotations in 21.6.
    This statement concerns the specified generated class of operations. It makes no assertion
that arbitrary analytic caps or arbitrary changes of the punctured comparison belong to that class.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.33; theorem 21.6;
theorem 21.15.

Proof. Write Hi , i ∈ Z/12, for the original component vertices and Vi for the new vertical ones.
At a node between an even component i and its odd neighbour j, the two charts (21.33.3) have
triple strata
                                  {Vi , Vj , Hj }, {Vi , Hi , Hj }.                   (B.4.16.1)
The square with horizontal edges Hi Hj and Vi Vj is thus divided by the diagonal Vi Hj . Over all
twelve nodes, (21.35.1) is exactly a triangulation of C12 × [0, 1], attached along the old horizontal
cycle C12 × {0}.
    There is a literal elementary collapse relative to the old cycle. First remove each triangle
containing a top edge Vi Vj , paired with that free edge. Next remove each remaining triangle,
paired with its now free diagonal Vi Hj . Finally remove each vertical edge Hi Vi , paired with its
free vertex Vi . What remains is precisely the original twelve-cycle. These are 36 elementary
collapses. Equivalently, the retraction sends Vi to Hi and is the identity on all old vertices and
edges.
    This description is valid inside a larger dual complex K. The only new strata lie over the
base origin, so the new complex is the mapping-cylinder attachment

                                     K ∪ f :C12 →K (C12 × [0, 1]).

It retracts onto K, regardless of possible global identifications among the local horizontal branches.
For self-crossings one uses the ordered local-branch dual complex, so no identification of distinct
local branches is silently discarded.
     A connected group acts trivially on the finite sets of component labels and connected
components of every stratum: its permutation is locally constant and is the identity at the
identity element. Cartier twists by such an action therefore keep this same incidence complex.
Toroidal subdivisions subdivide the corresponding central polyhedral complex and hence preserve
its underlying homotopy type. These arguments apply successively, proving the assertion for
finite compositions. Around each regular insertion point the relative component monodromy is
still the identity; no peripheral rotation is added to 21.6.
     For completeness, a compact normal-crossings space D has a natural injection

                                   H 1 (∆(D), C) ,−→ H 1 (D, C),                           (B.4.16.2)

where ∆(D) denotes its local-branch dual complex with connected strata. Use the ordered finite
branch spaces D[p] and take the alternating summand for the branch-permutation action. Over
C this is an exact direct-summand operation. Resolve the constant sheaf by this augmented
alternating branch complex. At a point its row is the augmented simplex complex, so it is exact,
including for self-crossings. The associated first-quadrant spectral sequence has

                         E1p,q = H q (D[p] , C)alt ,         E21,0 = H 1 (∆(D), C).

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                             Paper I


No higher differential enters or leaves (1, 0). Its filtration piece in total degree one gives (21.35.2).
Equivalently one can use the orientation local system on each unordered branch stratum; an
ordinary constant sheaf there would be incorrect if branches permute. A nonzero integral first
cohomology class of the finite dual complex remains nonzero over C, because first integral
cohomology is torsion-free. Thus a surviving circle class forces H 1 (D, C) 6= 0. By 21.15 every
semistable centre of a simply connected nearby S 6 is simply connected, which is incompatible
with this conclusion.
    The finite incidence and collapse certificates themselves are integral. They are saved in
code/ab_push_regular_cap_dual.py and its output. For the twelve-cycle the chain ranks are
24, 48, 24, the nonzero Smith entries of the two boundary maps are respectively 123 and 124 ,
and the integral homology is (Z, Z, 0). The explicit retraction pulls the integral angular cocycle

calculation supplies its analytic interpretation.

Remark 21.37 (Source audit and the valid remaining implication). The converse just disproved
is asserted in Honda and Viaclovsky (2025, Theorems 1.2 and 3.2, arXiv version 1). The published
primary PDF excerpt, printed p. 553, retains it as Theorem 1.1. The two versions and the precise
access record are distinguished in B_monodromy_source_audit.md. In the version read in full,
equation (3.9) establishes only

                                 b1 (Y ) ≤ dim H 1 (F ; R)T ≤ b1 (F ).

Identity of T gives equality in the second inequality; it does not give equality in the first. The
inequality and the implication from equality of the endpoint Betti numbers to identity monodromy
survive this counterexample. The irreducible-fibre argument in its Corollary 3.7 also survives:
the top-dimensional homology of an irreducible central fibre has rank one, forcing equality with
the invariant subspace in the displayed relative-homology sequence. No irreducibility is present
in the counterexample. This is a source correction relevant to possible non-Kähler completions,
not a nonextension theorem for the prescribed S 6 family.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Honda and Viaclovsky (2025, Theorems
1.2 and 3.2, arXiv version 1).

21.9    An embedded Tate interface at the missing corner
Proposition 21.41 (the other Kato axis). In the proper smooth Kato family K → ∆s of 21.26
there is a second relative effective Cartier divisor D ⊂ K, disjoint from the persistent elliptic
divisor E. The surface D is smooth and proper over ∆s . Its general fibre and central fibre are

               Ds = C∗ /(κ(s)sn )Z     (s 6= 0),    D0 = the reduced rational n-cycle.

At its nodes the relative local equation is uv = s. Its normal line in K is the multidegree-zero
Tate line whose factor on the closing collar is a(s). In particular it has degree zero on every
component of the central cycle. Scaling the first blowdown coordinate gives a holomorphic C∗
action on the pair (K, D) over the base.
    For n = 12 this constructs an embedded proper copy of the actual cusp’s elliptic root interface,
with its degree-zero normal line, after choosing the units κ, a to be the actual Tate and normal
multipliers. In the additive period convention u = (τ, µ), W = e−2πiζ2 , these multipliers are

κ(s)s12 = e2πiτ and a(s) = e−2πiµ . The elliptic translation by 6P is realized by first-coordinate
scaling a(s)−6 .
    This is an embedded Cartier and normal-line comparison, not an identification of relative
tubular neighbourhoods. No lift of the whole second period, attachment to the global partial filling,
or origin completion is asserted.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.26; (Istrati et al., 2022,
Example 9.10); theorem 21.58.

Proof. Use the modification, embedding and compact collar domains of 21.26. Write w for the
second blowdown coordinate and set, on the modified fundamental region,

                                           hs = πn∗ w − s.

The collar identification is σs πn , where σs (z, w) = (κ(s)z, a(s)w + (1 − a(s))s) in the last chart.
Consequently
                                        hs ◦ (σs πn ) = a(s)hs .                           (B.4.20.1)
Its zeros therefore glue to a relative effective Cartier divisor, and (21.41.1) is simultaneously the
normal-line transition. The divisor is closed in the proper family K → ∆s , so it is proper.
    For s 6= 0, the line w = s misses every blow-up centre. In the coordinate v = w − s the
contracting germ is
                               (x, v) 7−→ (κ(s)x(a(s)v + s)n , a(s)v).
Its restriction to v = 0 is x 7→ κ(s)sn x. The generic developing map of 21.26 restricts to the
identity in this coordinate, since its product Gs (v) has Gs (0) = 1. Thus this is precisely the
unmodified other Hopf axis, with the stated Tate multiplier and normal multiplier a(s).
     The divisor of πn∗ w is reduced. After the first blow-up, both the strict horizontal axis and
the exceptional curve have coefficient one. Every later centre is the intersection of the newest
exceptional curve with the strict vertical axis. It lies on no other component of the divisor of
πn∗ w. The new exceptional coefficient is therefore again one. Before the end collars are identified,
the divisor is a chain comprising the strict horizontal axis and the n exceptional pieces. The end
annuli join the two endpoint pieces, leaving the familiar rational n-cycle of the parabolic surface.
It is disjoint from its elliptic curve, as also described in the parabolic model of (Istrati et al.,
2022, Example 9.10).
     At a crossing of two adjacent pieces, ordinary blow-up coordinates give πn∗ w = uv up to a
holomorphic unit, which can be absorbed in u. Hence D has equation uv = s. It is smooth, and
its central fibre is reduced nodal. Away from these nodes its defining equation is a coordinate
minus s. This proves smoothness of the whole divisor and semistability over the disc. The
monomial transition charts are those of the unit-interval Tate model, and the closing on the
nonzero axis is exactly x 7→ κ(s)sn x. They identify the marked family with that Tate model, not
only its individual smooth fibres.
     The same local defining functions trivialize the normal line. Their only nontrivial closing
factor is (21.41.1), namely the holomorphic unit a(s). On each rational component the line has
degree zero; equivalently its two adjacent-node degree corrections cancel its self-intersection −2.
For n = 1 the same statement uses the two branches of the self-node. The factor a(s) gives the
retained gluing parameter around the cycle. This is exactly the multidegree-zero extension of
the line with factor a(s) on the smooth Tate curves.
     The first-coordinate scaling commutes with the modification and the collar maps and preserves
hs . One may equivalently descend the vector field x∂x and its local flow. Properness over the
base makes that flow complete on compact fibres, uniformly on compact parameter sets; its 2πi
period yields the stated holomorphic C∗ action. On the Tate axis it is ordinary multiplication of
x, so a holomorphic unit a(s)−6 realizes the marked translation by 6P .

                                            s = uv − h.                                 (B.4.20.2)

distinction, not only a possible global obstruction to linearization.

                                       r = f h = f (uv − s).                             (B.4.20.3)

the prescribed two-period Mumford cusp. This auxiliary proposition supplies neither global
plumbing data nor that period comparison. 21.58 subsequently excludes any proper filling of the
actual family.
    There is also a concrete obstruction to the most direct global use of this plumbing. For fixed
s 6= 0, all the n blow-up centres lie on the first Hopf axis x = 0, at [v = −s] and its infinitely
near strict-axis points. The other axis Ds is v = 0, x 6= 0. The axes are disjoint, and hence
every exceptional rational curve misses Ds . A plumbing that leaves the complement of a small
tubular neighbourhood of Ds unchanged retains these compact curves in its r 6= 0 fibres over
the same s. A complex torus has no rational curve: a holomorphic map from P1 lifts to its
vector-space universal cover and is constant. Thus this fixed-base localized plumbing of the
entire Kato surface cannot produce the prescribed ordinary two-tori. Further deformations or a
different map to the original base are outside this obstruction.
    The Cartier factor, Tate multiplier, reduced divisor multiplicities, scaling action and the two
local base-map comparisons are checked in code/ab_push_tate_interface.py and its saved
output. Properness rests on the explicit compact domains of 21.26.

nonzero monomial has nonzero derivative in a coordinate with positive exponent. Equivalently,
on F 6= 0 it is the displayed torus projection. Thus r = g(1 − F ) has two smooth transverse
branches in the third chart after resolution. The second chart has r = f (G − 1) independently of
the resolved surface coordinates, and the first was already checked. This proves smoothness and
reduced normal crossings over r for all n.
    For r 6= 0 in the third chart, g = r/(1 − F ), so the local fibre is the resolved threefold
uvF = sn with F 6= 1. For n = 1, its q divisor is uvF = 0, a literal three-branch normal-crossings
chart. For n = 12 the standard triangulation gives 144 unimodular charts above this one triple
point. This is the same local cyclic-cover count used earlier for each of the two actual cusp
triple points; it is not a new global Euler count. The other potential singularity, at f = −r, is
included in this construction: the first blow-up small-resolves it for n = 1, and the second is an
isomorphism there because f is nonzero.
    The equation arises from the actual repaired neighbourhood of 21.42. There h = uv − q in
the old node chart and H = h/q is holomorphic in the repaired collar. The unit inverse-normal
plumbing Hf = r is exactly

                              f (uv − q) = rq,         f uv = (f + r)q.

Putting g = f + r gives Xn . Thus the retained q factor has been derived from the actual
meromorphic function regularized by the modification, rather than inferred solely from an
abstract normal-line isomorphism. More precisely, the actual repaired collar, where H is small,
identifies with the third chart near F = 1 by

                        F = (1 + H)−1 ,      g = f (1 + H),         r = f H.

There uvF = sn is exactly the resolved equation uv = sn (1 + H) from 21.42. The charts near
F = 0 are additional local completion charts; their attachment to a complementary global Kato
piece has not been established.
    This local equation and its resolution do not supply the complementary Kato charts, their
second-period identification, the proper closure of the surviving exceptional-curve families,
or an origin cap for 21.40. In particular the fixed-base obstruction in 21.41 is not removed
by recognizing a local Mumford triple chart. 21.53 and 21.58 exclude the respective actual
origin completion and global proper filling; the local model above remains a proved auxiliary
construction. The exact chart identities, determinants, edge incidences and fan counts are saved
in code/ab_push_corner_resolution.py and its output.
    The full period action is a separate condition. The established first collar action is H 7→ aH
and f 7→ a−1 f ; the product r = f H is fixed. The product G(q, H) from 21.42 conjugates this on
a small collar, but this does not extend that conjugacy past its zeros H = −a−j . If an actual
marked period were to scale the test coordinate W = 1 + H = 1 + r/f by b, its required action
on f would be
                                                   rf
                                       f 7−→                ,
                                              (b − 1)f + br
not scalar multiplication. The test coordinate has not been identified with a marked period
coordinate, so this identity records a compatibility requirement, not an obstruction.
