Proposition 21.44 (exceptional-curve nonclosure and persistence in a semistable cap). Let
K∗ → ∆s be the repaired degree-one Kato family of 21.42, with q = s12 , and let E → ∆s be its
unchanged persistent elliptic axis. For s 6= 0 let Cs ≃ P1 be the exceptional curve of the single
Hopf blow-up.
    The union of the Cs has no proper analytic divisor closure in K∗ . Further finite proper
modifications cannot give these curves a proper analytic divisor closure: any such closure would
push forward to a forbidden one. In particular, the generic Hopf blowdown does not extend as a
relative proper holomorphic modification, or as a relative meromorphic contraction represented
by a proper analytic graph, across s = 0.
    There is also a deformation obstruction which does not assume a particular plumbing. Suppose
a smooth complex fourfold Y has holomorphic functions (Q, r), its divisor r = 0 is reduced normal
crossings, and one component K contains a neighbourhood of some Cs0 , s0 6= 0, agreeing with
the complementary Kato region and its ordinary base coordinate Q. Suppose this curve is disjoint
from every conductor branch of r = 0. Then every sufficiently nearby fibre (Q, r) = (Q0 , r0 )
contains an embedded rational curve. Consequently such a cap cannot have the prescribed ordinary
two-tori as its r 6= 0 surface fibres. The conclusion applies to the whole complementary Kato
component with these hypotheses; it makes no assertion about a different central component, a
curve meeting the conductor, or a replacement changing the holomorphic base map.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.42; proposition 21.26;
Dloussky and Teleman (2012, Section 1.2); Dloussky and Teleman (2012, Proposition 2.3 and its
proof, pp. 6–7 of the original preprint); Merkulov (1995).

Proof. We first use the exact marked blowdown of 21.26. The exceptional curve of the single
generic Hopf blow-up meets the persistent elliptic axis transversely at

                                   [v = −q] ∈ Ea(q) = C∗ /a(q)Z .

All modifications in 21.42 are disjoint from that axis. The intersection section in the repaired
family is therefore still
                                          p(s) = [−s12 ].                             (B.4.23.1)
The units a(q) obey 0 < |a(q)| < 1. Choose a holomorphic logarithm on the full parameter disc
and put

give a smooth trivialization of the elliptic family. A logarithmic lift of (21.44.1) is

                                                  log(−s12 )

On a positive loop around zero, τ returns to itself and z changes by 12. Thus the loop of
the section has class (12, 0) 6= 0 in the integral first homology of this trivialized family. A
continuous section over the disc would fill that loop. Hence p has no continuous, and therefore
no holomorphic, extension. A meromorphic section from a nonsingular curve would extend
holomorphically: its proper graph is generically degree one over the curve, and normalization
gives a finite degree-one map to that normal base. This is equally impossible. A finite base
change of degree d > 0 multiplies the winding to (12d, 0) and does not change the conclusion.
    Suppose an analytic divisor Z in K∗ , proper over the disc, restricted over the punctured
disc to the union of the Cs . Its horizontal irreducible part does not contain E, since the generic
intersection is the one transverse point (21.44.1). Both are Cartier locally in the smooth threefold,
so their intersection is an analytic curve, proper over the disc. Its reduced horizontal part has

                                                  239
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


generic degree one. An irreducible horizontal analytic curve cannot have a positive-dimensional
fibre without being contained in that fibre. Hence its normalization is finite of degree one over
the disc and is isomorphic to the disc. It extends p(s), a contradiction. Vertical components of
the intersection have no effect on this horizontal component.

would give such a Z, by the proper mapping theorem; the image has dimension two and the same
generic exceptional curves. The horizontal exceptional locus of a relative proper holomorphic
blowdown likewise gives Z. For a meromorphic contraction with proper analytic graph, resolve
the graph and apply the same argument to its horizontal exceptional locus and its proper image
in K∗ . This is a direct marked-intersection proof of a familiar nonproperness phenomenon for
exceptional curves in GSS surface deformations; see Dloussky and Teleman (2012, Section 1.2)
for the primary context. No classification of all central curves is used.
    We next prove the deformation assertion. Write C = Cs0 and S = K ∩ {Q = Q0 }. Near this
curve, S is a smooth surface and C is its exceptional curve, so

                                        NC/S ≃ OP1 (−1).

The base coordinate Q is submersive on K near C. Because C misses every other central branch,

Moreover (21.44.2) induces an isomorphism on global sections, since both H 0 (O(−1)) and

     Kodaira’s embedded-deformation theorem therefore gives a smooth two-dimensional local
parameter space T of compact embedded deformations of C, with tangent space H 0 (C, NC/Y ).
In precisely this relative surface setting one may apply the directly opened Dloussky and Teleman
(2012, Proposition 2.3 and its proof, pp. 6–7 of the original preprint): after shrinking the
neighbourhood of C, (Q, r) is a holomorphic submersion of relative dimension two, and C is a
compact simply exceptional divisor of its fibre. That proposition does not require the submersion
to be proper. The general completeness theorem is due to Kodaira; we use the exact statement
in the opening of Merkulov (1995). Shrink this family so its curves remain in the chosen
neighbourhood. Their genus remains zero, so all are isomorphic to P1 . The functions Q, r are
constant on every compact connected curve and thus define a holomorphic map

                                            T −→ C2 .

Its derivative at [C] is precisely the isomorphism on sections induced by (21.44.2). The
holomorphic inverse function theorem shows that the map covers a neighbourhood of (Q0 , 0). In
particular the nearby fixed pairs with r 6= 0 contain rational curves. A holomorphic map from P1
to a complex torus lifts to its vector-space universal cover and is constant. Thus those fibres
cannot be the prescribed ordinary two-tori.
    The conductor condition is essential. For example, if a further central component meets K
along the persistent elliptic axis, then its intersection number with C is one and NK/Y |C ≃ O(−1).
The normal sequence need no longer supply the r direction in (21.44.2). The proposition therefore
does not exclude such a changed central arrangement; its proper construction and comparison
with the prescribed family remain separate requirements.

21.11     The associated logarithmic torsor at the missing origin
Proposition 21.45 (obstruction in the fixed log-torus category). The actual local Jacobian
admits a nondegenerate logarithmic complex-torus extension over the full (q, r) bidisc and hence
has proper analytic models in the sense of Kajiwara et al. (2008b). After the normalized base
change q = Q12 , the two marked axial fan presentations of 21.38–21.40 determine a torsor under
its associated log-torus sheaf on the punctured bidisc. This torsor does not extend across the
origin as a torsor locally trivial for the usual analytic topology. The obstruction persists after
every further finite coordinate-root base change.
    Here the torsor is formed from the associated log-torus sheaves, not from the fixed proper
fan models themselves, which need not be group objects. The conclusion excludes an origin cap
obtained from a locally trivial torsor of this specified kind with the given axial identifications. No
implication from an arbitrary proper analytic cap with vertical threefold components to this torsor
category is asserted.

Proposition 21.46 (a one-eigenvalue Hopf boundary has no proper analytic completion). Let
α(q) = q m κ(q), where m ≥ 1 and κ is a holomorphic unit on a disc, and let β be holomorphic

                           Hq = (C2 \ {0})/h(z, w) 7→ (α(q)z, β(q)w)i.                     (B.4.25.1)

the full disc, even allowing singular or nonreduced central fibres and a singular total space. This
remains true after every finite base change ramified at zero.

one multiplier κ(q)q → 0 and the other tending to a nonzero contraction. This concerns that
specified auxiliary Hopf family. It is not a nonexistence theorem for a completion of the actual
two-torus family in 21.40.

     Now suppose an arbitrary proper analytic completion Z → ∆ exists. Pass to its reduction

and Milman (1995, Theorem 1.6 and the noncompact analytic extension immediately following
it). All singular points lie over zero, so the resolution is an isomorphism over the entire punctured

finiteness of the analytic resolution permits one shrinking of the disc; its dominating smooth
component is a smooth proper total threefold as in the preceding paragraph. Its map to the disc
is nonconstant, so the base function is a non-zero-divisor. No vertical component was retained
which could invalidate that assertion. The preceding contradiction applies. Reduction also shows
that nilpotent structure supported at zero cannot evade it.
     Finally, a finite base change replaces α by a holomorphic function of some positive vanishing
order and replaces β by a unit whose value at zero still has modulus strictly between zero and
one. The same proof applies verbatim.

Remark 21.47 (Scope and comparison with the classical toric Hopf degeneration). There is
no conflict with the degeneration in Oda (1978, Section 13, pp. 116–118). There the boundary
rays are generated by n and −n + an0 with a > 0, and the period is translation by λn . In the
                                                                                     0


universal-cover basis
                                                             v1 + v2
                         v1 = n,     v2 = −n + an0 ,    n0 =         ,
                                                                 a
the base change λ = ta makes this period act with eigenvalues (t, t), up to fixed torus units in
the indicated variant. Both eigenvalues tend to zero. 21.46 assumes instead a nonzero limit for
the second eigenvalue. The distinction is forced by the exact period marking of the candidate
Tate interface, and cannot be removed by citing the existence of some Hopf degeneration. The
blown-up Kato family of 21.26 is also consistent with 21.46: its generic fibres are blow-ups of Hq ,
so the anticanonical sections must satisfy the extra vanishing conditions at the marked blow-up
centre and are not the spaces in (21.46.5).

21.12    A necessary vertical fibre over the missing origin
Proposition 21.48 (every origin component is a threefold). Suppose the actual partial family
of 21.40 has a proper analytic completion f : Z → ∆q × ∆r with smooth pure four-dimensional

has dimension three. In particular, there is no equidimensional completion, and no completion
having even one two-dimensional component of the origin fibre.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                                  Paper I


meromorphic, a graph modification must first be supplied and its resulting geometry retained.
21.53 subsequently excludes even the permitted vertical-component completions of the fixed partial
family, and 21.58 excludes every proper filling of the actual global family.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.40; proposition 21.53;
theorem 21.58; proposition 21.45; Demailly (2012, Chapter II, Sections 7–8).

Proof. We first prove the finite-multisection consequence of the actual log-torsor obstruction
21.45, without assuming that the unknown cap is itself a log torsor. Make the normalized finite
base change q = Q12 . The resulting space Z 0 is normal and pure four-dimensional. Its restrictions
to the two punctured axes have the explicit normalized fan presentations used in 21.45. Write

               B = ∆ Q × ∆r ,      Bq = ∆∗Q × ∆r ,        Br = ∆Q × ∆∗r ,           U = Bq ∩ Br .

    Assume there is a finite surjective map p : V → B of positive generic degree d, together with a
holomorphic map V → Z 0 over B. We may normalize V and retain any collection of components
dominating B; its degree remains a positive integer. A normal surface is Cohen–Macaulay; finite
over the smooth bidisc, it is flat. Thus the finite holomorphic trace and the degree-d sum with
multiplicities are available also at branch points. On the ordinary locus, sum the d points of this
multisection, with multiplicity, in each of the two actual axial group origins of 21.45. This gives
two local expressions for the trace in the Jacobian group. We show that they extend as log-torus
sections on Bq and Br .
     Ramification away from the axes. Over the ordinary locus the torus family is a smooth
holomorphic group family. Near a branch point, choose small neighbourhoods of the finitely many
preimages in V and local Lie lifts of their maps to the torus. The trace of these holomorphic
functions under the finite map is holomorphic, and its exponential is the ordinary sum. Changes
of lifts add periods, which disappear in the group quotient. Thus the ordinary trace extends
across the ordinary branch locus. Equivalently this is the usual addition map on the relative
symmetric power, applied to the finite multisection.
     The explicit norm at an axis. After shrinking B, every component of the finite cover’s branch
divisor which is not an axis meets each punctured axis nowhere: its intersection with either axis
is an isolated analytic germ at the origin. At a point of a punctured axis choose coordinates
(x, y), with x the normal coordinate to that axis. Locally the normal finite cover is a disjoint
union of covers
                                          x = te ,   y = y,                              (B.4.26.1)
including e = 1 sheets. Indeed the complement of the axis in a small polydisc has cyclic
fundamental group; each connected unramified finite cover is the displayed root cover there,
and its normal finite extension is unique. No assumption that the whole finite cover is a
coordinate-root cover is being made.
    The map from such a root polydisc into the prescribed fan model gives a section of its
associated log-torus sheaf. It has a local bounded multiplicative log lift. This can also be seen
directly in a toric chart: the pulled-back characters are meromorphic functions with zeros and
poles supported on t = 0, hence are tk u(t, y) with k ∈ Z and u a holomorphic unit. The quotient
by the period lattice causes only the period ambiguity already retained in 21.45.
    The multiplicative norm of a character on (21.48.1) is explicitly
                         e−1                                          e−1

The last product is a holomorphic unit in (x, y). Thus the norm has an integral ghost vector

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


the first character has zero normal order and the second is unrestricted; on the Q axis both are

    The local extensions agree on overlaps because they agree on the ordinary locus. To see

    A two-dimensional fibre germ would supply one. Suppose an origin point of Z has local
fibre dimension two. Finite base change and normalization are finite maps and preserve that
local fibre dimension at points lying above it. At a resulting point of Z 0 , choose two generic
local linear sections in an analytic embedding. Their intersection with the fibre is isolated.
Intersecting with Z 0 gives a two-dimensional analytic germ whose map to B is finite. This is the
local finite-projection criterion from Weierstrass preparation; see also Demailly (2012, Chapter
II, Sections 7–8). Choose a component through the point. Its finite image has dimension two
and is therefore the whole base germ. A finite representative of this germ, after shrinking the
bidisc, is finite and surjective over the entire smaller bidisc. Its normalization is still finite and
maps to Z 0 , giving exactly the forbidden multisection of positive degree. Properness of this finite
representative prevents loss of sheets at its boundary.
    Every fibre component of a dominant map from a pure fourfold to a smooth surface has
dimension at least two. If a two-dimensional irreducible component existed, a generic point on it
would have local fibre dimension two, which we have excluded. Flatness over r makes r = 0 a
Cartier divisor of pure dimension three, so the origin fibre has no component of dimension greater
than three. All its irreducible components consequently have dimension three, as asserted.

Proposition 21.50 (maximal monodromy with trivial central dualizing bundle). Let p : X → ∆
be a proper holomorphic map from a smooth complex threefold, smooth over ∆∗ , whose nonzero
fibres are complex two-tori. Suppose that D = p−1 (0) is a reduced normal-crossing divisor and
assume in addition that ωD ≃ OD . If its monodromy on H1 (Xt , Q) satisfies

                                         rank(T − 1) = 2,                                (B.4.28.1)

then every normalization component of D is a smooth rational toric surface, its conductor is its
toric boundary, and the dual complex of D is a topological two-torus. In particular all normalized
components are Kähler.
    No Kähler hypothesis on X is used. The additional triviality of ωD is not inferred from the
neighbouring two-tori. The proposition does not produce a modification with this property from
an arbitrary analytic completion.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Friedman (2016, Definition 1.1 and
Lemmas 1.2, 2.2, 2.7); Dloussky (2005, Corollary 2.25, Lemma 2.26 and Proposition 2.27); Fujiki

Proof. Write Vi for the compact smooth normalization components and Ci for their reduced
conductor divisors. Adjunction gives

                                          KVi + Ci ∼ 0.                                  (B.4.28.2)

If D is smooth, the map is a proper submersion near its compact central fibre and its monodromy
is trivial. Otherwise every Ci is nonempty, by connectedness. Adjunction on a conductor branch
says that it is either a smooth elliptic curve disjoint from the other branches, or a rational curve
with two boundary points, counted on its normalization. The rational branches form cycles,
including the nodal irreducible and two-component cases.
     Nonnegative Euler contributions. A nonempty effective anticanonical divisor makes every
pluricanonical system empty: multiplying a nonzero pluricanonical section by the appropriate
power of the anticanonical section would give a nonzero holomorphic function with a nonempty
zero divisor. Thus the surface has Kodaira dimension −∞. Its minimal model is rational, ruled,
or of class VII. We spell out the consequences for the reduced anticanonical pairs here.
     On a rational surface, the conductor is connected, by 0 → KV → OV → OC → 0 and
H (KV ) = 0. For a rational cycle, the charge identity and positivity are
   1


 e(V \C) = 12−C 2 −#{cycle components} ≥ 0,           e(V \C) = 0 ⇐⇒ (V, C) is toric. (B.4.28.3)

Here e denotes compactly supported Euler characteristic. This includes the nodal irreducible
convention: Friedman (2016, Definition 1.1 and Lemmas 1.2, 2.2, 2.7). For a smooth elliptic
anticanonical curve, e(V \ C) = 2 + b2 (V ) > 0 instead.
    On a nonrational ruled minimal model, a conductor component dominating the base has
degree at most two and genus at most one. The base is therefore elliptic. The minimal conductor
is two disjoint elliptic sections or one unramified elliptic bisection. Its Euler contribution is
zero. The two section squares sum to zero, and the bisection has square zero, also directly from
KV + C ∼ 0 and KV2 = 0.
    A minimal class-VII surface with b2 = 0 and a curve is a Hopf surface. Its elliptic curves have
square zero, and a reduced anticanonical divisor has at most two elliptic components. For this
last assertion the exact sequence 0 → KV → OV → OC → 0 gives h0 (OC ) ≤ 1 + h1 (KV ) = 2.
The Euler contribution is zero. This also covers secondary Hopf surfaces; no primary marking is
required.
    For a minimal class-VII surface with b2 > 0, the reduced anticanonical divisor is a numerically
anticanonical divisor whose coefficients are all one. Dloussky (2005, Corollary 2.25, Lemma 2.26
and Proposition 2.27) imply that it is parabolic Inoue or Inoue–Hirzebruch. Half-Inoue has
only a nontrivially twisted anticanonical divisor and cannot satisfy (21.50.2). The remaining
possibilities are hyperbolic Inoue with two disjoint rational cycles, or parabolic Inoue with one
rational cycle and a disjoint elliptic curve. If n = b2 > 0, there are n rational cycle components
and e(V ) = n, so the contribution is zero. In the parabolic case the elliptic curve has square −n.
The curve configurations, anticanonical identities and underlying (S 1 × S 3 )#nP topology are
                                                                                     2

recorded in Fujiki and Pontecorvo (2010, Sections 3.2–3.3).
    These assertions extend to nonminimal pairs. An exceptional curve outside C meets it once,
transversely at a smooth point, since −KV · E = 1; its contraction reverses an interior blow-up.
An exceptional curve in C meets the rest at two points and its contraction reverses a corner
blow-up. The reduced anticanonical condition is preserved. Interior blow-up increases e(V \ C)

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


by one, whereas corner blow-up leaves it unchanged. Thus every contribution is nonnegative.
Equality permits only toric rational pairs, minimal elliptic ruled or Hopf pairs, and corner
blow-ups of hyperbolic or parabolic Inoue pairs. For these Inoue pairs the cycle count and
b2 increase together, and the fundamental group stays Z. Corner blow-ups do not touch the
parabolic elliptic curve, whose square remains strictly negative.

To see this without an invariant-cycle theorem, remove small tubes about the disjoint double

loop across one neck adds its oriented normal-circle class, with coefficient the signed crossing
number of that edge. Core loops have zero change. Crossing numbers of a closed loop form a
cycle of the dual graph. Thus T − 1 factors through its rational cycle space. The normal-circle

    The dual complex. All normalization pairs are now rational toric pairs. Every vertex link

21.14    What invariant forms do not control
Proposition 21.52 (full-rank periods do not bound an affine comparison). There is a proper
semistable family of two-dimensional complex tori over a disc, with smooth total threefold and
rank-two unipotent monodromy on H 1 , and a fibre-preserving automorphism over the punctured
disc with the following properties. It acts identically on all relative invariant one- and two-forms
and on the Gauss–Manin variation. Their coherent extensions supplied by the proper family
therefore give the same lattices under this identification. An absolute holomorphic canonical
form extending across the centre is also unchanged. Nevertheless, the automorphism has no
meromorphic extension to the total family.
    Thus these invariant-form and connection data do not alone control an affine origin or a
marked total-space comparison, even in the presence of a proper smooth semistable cap. This
statement does not refute a separate extension theorem for the difference of two sections which
both extend holomorphically into the same cap.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; Kajiwara et al. (2008b, Sections
1.1.1–1.1.3, pp. 73–74); proposition 21.53; proposition 21.54; theorem 21.58.

                                      Et = C∗ /tZ      (t 6= 0)

and reduced nodal rational central fibre. Its proper analytic model and node chart xy = t are
the explicit example in Kajiwara et al. (2008b, Sections 1.1.1–1.1.3, pp. 73–74). Form E ×∆ E.
Its only total-space singularity is the product of the two nodes, with local equations

                                xy = t,      uv = t,      xy = uv.

Blow up the ideal (x, u) in this conifold and take its strict-transform charts. They are

                                  u = xA,    y = Av,     t = xAv

with smooth coordinates (x, A, v), and

                                  x = uB,    v = By,     t = uBy

                                                253
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


with smooth coordinates (u, B, y). This is the standard proper small resolution, an isomorphism
away from the conifold point. Glue it to the identity on the complement of that point. The
resulting p : Y → ∆ is proper, has smooth total threefold, and has reduced normal-crossing
centre: its displayed equations are products of distinct coordinates. The resolution does not alter
the ordinary fibres Et × Et .
    For each elliptic factor choose period cycles wi , ui with ui 7→ ui + wi around t = 0. On the
direct sum the logarithm of monodromy has rank two and square zero. The same rank holds on
dual H 1 . Thus this example has the full-rank weight-one unipotent degeneration at issue, rather
than a constant elliptic factor.
    The nonextending translation. On the punctured disc use multiplicative coordinates (Z, W )
for the two factors and put

                          Th (Z, W, t) = e2πih(t) Z, W, t ,                             (B.4.29.1)
                                                         
                                                               h(t) = 1/t.

This is a holomorphic automorphism of the punctured family. The zero section e(t) = ([1], [1])
extends to the smooth torus locus of the central normalization. For positive integers j tending
to infinity,
                                tj = 1/j,     t0j = 1/(j + 1/2)
lie in the disc and tend to zero, whereas

                         Th (e(tj )) = ([1], [1]),      Th (e(t0j )) = ([−1], [1]).

In the Tate model these approach the distinct central smooth points with multiplicative
coordinates (1, 1) and (−1, 1). The small resolution is an isomorphism near both points. Hence
Th ◦ e has no continuous extension to the centre.
    This also excludes a meromorphic total extension, rather than only a holomorphic one. If
such an extension existed, let Γ → Y be its proper meromorphic graph and pull it back along
e : ∆ → Y. The resulting analytic space is proper over the disc and has a single point in each
noncentral fibre. Its unique component dominating the disc is a proper analytic curve, generically
of degree one. After normalization it is finite of degree one over the normal disc, hence is the
disc itself. Its map to the target Y would extend Th ◦ e holomorphically. This contradicts the
two distinct limits just found. Vertical components in the pulled-back graph do not affect this
dominating curve.
    Relative forms and their coherent extensions. On the ordinary locus the invariant relative
one-forms are
                           ω1 = dZ/Z,      ω2 = dW /W         (mod dt).
They and ω1 ∧ ω2 are unchanged by every Th . The holomorphic forms of a compact torus are
invariant, so this accounts for all relative holomorphic one- and two-forms on the ordinary fibres.
The relative log forms extend in the Tate model. Ordinary coherent relative forms also give
finite-order extensions: for example tω1 , tω2 , and t2 ω1 ∧ ω2 extend as ordinary relative forms. In
the first resolution chart the first two are explicitly

                              tω1 = Av dx,           tω2 = Av dx + xv dA;

the other chart gives the analogous regular expressions. At an isolated Tate node the same
identity is t dx/x = y dx.
    More generally, take the torsion-free image of each coherent direct image of relative forms in
its bundle on the punctured disc. Under the two punctured identifications id and Th , these are
identical coherent lattices, since the induced map on the entire ordinary relative-form bundle is
the identity. Coherence therefore gives no bound on h in this example.
    Gauss–Manin and an absolute form. Every fibre translation is homotopic to the identity
and acts identically on integral cohomology. Consequently Th induces the identity on the flat

                                                     254
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


Gauss–Manin bundle, its connection, and its Hodge subbundle. The logarithmic period growth
and regular singularity of that connection are unchanged. They concern the linear cohomology
variation, not the translated origin.

                                               dZ dW

    What a total differential would have to add. On a local multiplicative chart, an absolute lift
of the first relative form transforms by
                                  Th∗ (dZ/Z) = dZ/Z + 2πih0 (t)dt.                          (B.4.29.3)
This horizontal term is erased both on passing to relative forms and on wedging with the base

h(t) = e1/t makes that term essential, while leaving all the preceding relative and canonical
calculations unchanged. For this choice the two sequences tj = 1/ log j and t0j = 1/ log(j + 1/2)
give the same two distinct central limits. A condition imposing a regular extending affine
connection or specified absolute lifts could detect such growth, but it is additional data; properness
and the invariant forms above do not supply it.
    The example compares two markings of the same proper family. It does not identify either
with the actual six-sphere cap. Nor does it show that differences of two sections both extending
into a single cap fail to extend: a common essential translation cancels in such a difference. The
difference-extension bridge is proved in 21.53; 21.54–21.58 add the global meridian and loop
control needed for the actual family. They do not contradict this counterexample. Exact chart,
monodromy, and translation identities are checked in code/e_push_forms_translation.py.

21.15    Noncompletion of the prescribed partial filling
Proposition 21.53 (the fixed partial filling cannot be completed). The partial filling of 21.40
has no proper Hausdorff complex-analytic completion over its missing base point. This remains
true after finite coordinate roots of the two base coordinates and allows arbitrary additional
three-dimensional components of the origin fibre. No Kähler or projective hypothesis is imposed
on a putative completion.
    This is a statement about the prescribed partial filling, including its two punctured axial models.
This proposition alone does not exclude every filling over the r disc: a different completion along
r = 0, q 6= 0 need not have the axial model of 21.40. Resolving the graph in 21.17 does not by
itself supply that identification. 21.54–21.58 remove the need for it by controlling meridians and
the global affine loop class, and prove unrestricted nonexistence for the actual family.

21.16    Global elliptic monodromy constrains every central meridian
Proposition 21.54 (the global meridians have only the prescribed toric direction). Suppose
g : Z → ∆r is any proper complex-analytic filling of a finite parameter cover of the actual
six-sphere family. Retain its reduced main component, normalize and resolve it, extend its
intrinsically marked map to P1 by 21.17, resolve the graph, and resolve the support of its central
divisor. Denote the resulting smooth proper modification by Z,e and its holomorphic marked map
by h. All modifications can be chosen to be isomorphisms over r 6= 0. The central support has
normal crossings; its multiplicities need not be one.
    There is a finite subset Σ ⊂ P1 , containing 0, 1, ∞, with the following property. For every
q ∈ B ◦ := P1 \ Σ, every local angular vanishing circle of the r-central normal-crossings divisor,
viewed in the homology of the nearby ordinary two-torus, lies in

                                        Zδb ⊂ H1 (Xq,r ; Z).                              (B.4.31.1)

The same conclusion holds for the image of the entire local angular torus at a higher crossing over
B ◦ . Here δb is the primitive cycle in the audited period marking. The conclusion is unaffected by
any further finite cover of the degeneration parameter.
     This is a constraint on every hypothetical global filling. It does not assert that the unknown
rank-one axial completion is the prescribed model of 21.40, or that an affine origin in one model
extends into the other.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.17; proposition 21.40;
Bierstone and Milman (1995, Theorems 1.6 and 1.10 and the paragraph following Theorem 1.6);
proposition 21.25.

Proof. The global model and the finite exceptional set. The punctured total family is connected
and smooth, hence irreducible. Its closure is the unique reduced main component dominating the
parameter disc. Retain this component, normalize it, and resolve it properly, without changing
its smooth punctured part. The resulting total space is a smooth connected fourfold, proper over
the disc. The parameter is a nonzero divisor, so its map to the disc is flat. The proof of 21.17
requires no reducedness or normal-crossings condition at the centre: its torsion-free coherent bi-
anticanonical pencil and labelled critical-value argument apply to this smooth model. Its marked
graph is therefore a proper modification. Further analytic resolution and principalization of the

disc allows us to work over a compact central fibre throughout. The modifications have their
centres over r = 0, so neither the actual punctured family nor its marked map changes. Flatness
over r persists because r is a nonzero divisor in the smooth local rings. We do not infer that its
central multiplicities remain one.
    For possible self-crossings use the finite closed spaces of ordered local branch intersections,
with each local component normalized. Locally these are the coordinate intersections of the
central branches. In particular, the double-branch spaces are compact smooth surfaces and the
triple-branch spaces are compact smooth curves, even when two branches belong to one global
component. There are finitely many such components.
    Add to Σ the images of all branch-intersection components on which h is constant and
the critical values of h on every remaining branch-intersection component, including the
normalizations of the single branches. These sets are finite. Indeed the maps are proper;
on a component mapping nontrivially to the curve P1 their critical image is a proper analytic
subset of that curve. Zero-dimensional deeper strata contribute only finitely many further values.
    Thus, over B ◦ , the closed double-branch spaces form proper smooth families of compact
curves. The connected components of their fibres form finite covering spaces of B ◦ : this follows
either from proper submersion trivializations, or from their finite Stein factorizations. Removing
the finitely many triple points from one connected smooth curve leaves it connected. Branch
orderings, central multiplicities, and these connected fibre components therefore constitute finite
discrete data over B ◦ .

Remark 21.55 (Scope of the affine comparison). The finite-orbit mechanism uses the global

invariant-form counterexample 21.52 is consistent with this limitation. 21.58 uses the loop class,
rather than an extending comparison of individual origins, to prove unrestricted nonexistence for

matrices; an isolated rank-one degeneration over an ordinary base disc has no such constraint.

21.18    No proper analytic filling of the actual punctured family
Theorem 21.58 (nonexistence after every finite parameter cover). The actual punctured six-
sphere family has no proper Hausdorff complex-analytic filling after any finite cover of its
degeneration parameter. In particular, there is no positive integer N for which the cover w = rN
has a proper filling with smooth total space and reduced normal-crossings central fibre.
    The assertion permits an arbitrary singular central space, arbitrary additional components,
and arbitrary central multiplicities. It does not impose a Kähler, projective, or logarithmic
hypothesis on the putative filling. Its proof derives the specific logarithmic torsor needed for the
contradiction from differences of sections extending into that filling.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 21.52; proposition 21.56;
proposition 21.54; Bierstone and Milman (1995, Theorems 1.6 and 1.10); proposition 21.17;
proposition 21.45; proposition 21.53; proposition 21.49; proposition 21.40; proposition 21.48.

Proof. We distinguish an individual affine origin from its radial-loop class throughout. 21.52
prevents an argument based only on extending invariant forms from controlling an individual

                                                  266
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


origin. 21.56 is the additional global input that controls the loop class without making such an
assertion.
    Reduction of an arbitrary filling to a marked proper map. Suppose a filling exists. Its
punctured part is a connected smooth fourfold. Retain its unique reduced main component,
normalize, and resolve it properly, with every centre over the central parameter. The result is a
smooth connected fourfold proper over the parameter disc and unchanged over its puncture. The
parameter is a nonzero divisor, so its map to the disc is flat. The complex-analytic resolution
used here has the scope recorded in 21.54 and Bierstone and Milman (1995, Theorems 1.6 and
1.10).
    21.17 extends the intrinsically marked map to P1 meromorphically. Resolve its proper graph
and the support of the central divisor. We obtain a proper holomorphic map

                                      (f, r) : Z −→ P1 × ∆r                               (B.4.33.1)

with Z smooth, whose restriction over r 6= 0 is exactly the marked actual family. The central
support is simple normal crossing after further embedded resolution, but its multiplicities are
retained. 21.54 and 21.56 apply in this scope. There is no use of a semistable-reduction theorem
for threefolds.
    A hypothetical filling remains proper after any further finite base change, normalization, and
retention of its main component. A finite map of disc germs is a coordinate power after absorbing
a holomorphic unit into the source coordinate. We may therefore make a further cover so that
the actual parameter is w = r6 , followed, if necessary, by r = Rn with n > 0. This notation
includes every original positive cover degree: pulling w = ρN back by ρ = R6 gives w = R6N and
hence r = RN .

analytic filling. In particular the smooth reduced-NC filling requested in Part B does not exist
for any positive cover exponent.

    The final step uses two separate facts: a cap-derived origin has zero global radial defect by
21.56, and a section extending along the actual cusp has zero radial ghost class by 21.45. Neither
fact identifies the unknown central model with 21.40. A common essential translation with zero
loop class, as allowed by 21.52, is harmless in this comparison. The untwisted Engel family
provides a useful scope check: its identity closing has zero affine origins on both axial fan models,
hence F = 0. The nonzero clutching class used in (21.58.14) is specific to the actual twisted
family; the proof does not exclude the untwisted family’s known filling.

Corollary 21.59 (counterexample; the premise of a global central fibre). There is no central fibre
or descent resolution of the requested proper analytic filling of the actual S 6 family. Its proposed
integral homology, fundamental group, central Euler number and nearby-cycle comparison are
therefore undefined.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 21.58.

Proof. Theorem 21.58 excludes the underlying proper analytic space after every finite parameter
cover. An invariant of that nonexistent central fibre cannot be computed by assigning it the
topology of a local or auxiliary model. The local topologies and necessary degeneration conditions
proved above retain exactly their stated hypotheses. The punctured family’s smooth monodromy
is a different, well-defined invariant and is computed in Part C.

22     The boundary of the parameter disc
We use the standard twists throughout this section. Put H∗ = (3/π) log 6, fix a boundary
parameter c∗ = x + iH∗ , and set a = x + 3/2. The distinction between a single degenerate
fibre and the total quotient over its root disc is essential below. All topological group quotients
have their quotient topology; a Hausdorff reflection means a continuous quotient universal for
continuous maps to Hausdorff spaces.

    For completeness we reproduce the obstruction in proposition 5.9, rather than regard a

result, with the normalizing constant checked exactly.

Lemma 22.2. Let V be a connected Riemann surface and π : X → V a flat proper holomorphic
map of reduced complex spaces. Suppose that over a nonempty open subset V0 , the fibres are
smooth compact threefolds whose unique anticanonical divisor is 2Sv , where Sv is a smooth
connected surface with b1 (Sv ) = 2. Then there is an open subset V good ⊂ V , with at most
countable complement, on which the reduced support of the relative anticanonical divisor is a
smooth proper surface family. Its Albanese elliptic invariant is holomorphic.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Flatness and the smoothness of the fibres over V0 imply that π is a submersion there: the
local analytic smoothness criterion applies because the base is smooth. The relative nonsmooth
locus is a closed analytic subset, by the Jacobian criterion. Its proper image is analytic by
Grauert (1960, §7, Satz 1), the proper mapping theorem. It misses V0 , hence is discrete. We

                                                  271
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


remove it and work over the connected remaining curve V 0 . Removing a discrete subset from a
connected Riemann surface does not disconnect it. Thus X 0 → V 0 is a smooth proper map.
    Write L = KX−10 /V 0 . Grauert’s direct-image theorem (1960, §6, Hauptsatz I) makes F = π∗ L
and R1 π∗ L coherent. We prove the needed base change directly over the smooth curve; we do
not use the originally stated §7, Satz 2, whose claimed closed exceptional locus was corrected in
Grauert’s 1963 erratum. For a local base parameter t vanishing at v, smoothness and invertibility
of L give an exact sequence 0 → L −   → L → i∗ Lv → 0, where i : Xv ,→ X 0 is the closed embedding.
                                       t

Its direct-image sequence gives, at v,
                       0 −→ Fv /tFv −→ H 0 (Xv , Lv ) −→ (R1 π∗ L)v [t] −→ 0.
The last term denotes elements annihilated by t. The support of the torsion subsheaf of
the coherent module R1 π∗ L is closed discrete, by the structure theorem for finitely generated
modules over the local discrete valuation rings of the smooth base curve. Outside that support
the canonical base-change map is an isomorphism. Also F is torsion-free: multiplication by a
nonzero base function is injective on sections of L. It is therefore locally free. Its rank is one
by choosing an interior point outside the discrete torsion support. These statements concern
the canonical map, not merely equal dimensions. Locally a frame gives a relative section σ of L,
nowhere identically zero on a fibre. Its divisor is independent of the frame. Let D be its reduced
support. On V0 , the divisor is 2Sv and D is exactly Sv .
    The map D → V 0 is proper, since D is closed in a proper space. There is no vertical divisor
component: a vertical divisor in the smooth total space would contain a whole irreducible fibre,
contrary to the nonzero restriction of σ. Every horizontal component has proper image all of the
connected base. Since the interior fibre is irreducible, there is exactly one horizontal component,
and its multiplicity in div σ is two. Thus div σ = 2D on this base. In the smooth ambient space
D is Cartier. It is flat over the curve because its local rings are torsion-free over the base discrete
valuation ring. Restriction of the Cartier identity to an interior fibre gives 2Dv = 2Sv , whence
Dv = Sv with its reduced structure. Flatness and the smoothness of these fibres make D → V 0
smooth over V0 . Its analytic nonsmooth locus therefore misses V0 ; the proper mapping theorem
once more makes its image discrete. After deleting that image, D → V good is a smooth proper
family of connected surfaces. Each deletion is closed discrete in the then-current open curve.
Their finite union is at most countable, and the final good locus is open; we do not assert that
successive exceptional sets cannot accumulate at an earlier removed point.
    Ehresmann’s theorem identifies the smooth fibres along every path; in particular their first
Betti number is two. Buchdahl (1999, Theorem 11) then gives a Kähler metric on every fibre.
Hence h1,0 = 1, every holomorphic one-form is closed, and the integral period map has a rank-
two lattice image. Constant h1,0 , properness, and analytic base change supply a local relative
holomorphic one-form. Locally on a simply connected base disc, a relative one-form and a basis
of the free part of H1 give two holomorphic periods. Their ratio lies in one half-plane after
orienting the basis. To see holomorphicity directly, choose local primitives of the closed relative
form on simply connected fibre charts; their differences are holomorphic functions of the base,
and the finite sum around a transported cycle is its period. The modular invariant of the ratio is
independent of all choices and is holomorphic. This proves the last assertion without requiring a
global choice of section of the Albanese family.

Proposition 22.7. At the boundary, the construction over B \ {1} is a complex manifold, since
proposition 5.1 and theorem 5.5 makes every remaining finite period map invertible and the
cusp completion is unchanged. The order-four deck action descends continuously to T H . On its
rational central circle it is translation by −a/4; on the irrational central point it is trivial. Its
finite quotient is Hausdorff with central fibre a circle or a point, respectively. Neither quotient is
a complex space over the base compatible with the given holomorphic family off the centre. The
linear foliation by C(2, −1)t on the original central torus cover has compact elliptic leaves. For
rational a the leaves are closed; for irrational a the closure of a leaf is the set with its fixed value
of Im ξ.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 5.1 and theorem 5.5;
propositions 5.6 and 5.7.

Proof. The deck transformation is a biholomorphism of the original quotient, so the universal
property extends it uniquely to a homeomorphism of the Hausdorff reflection. The action on the
fixed product coordinate at the centre is ξ 7→ ξ − κ2 /4 = ξ − a/4. A finite group quotient of a
Hausdorff space is Hausdorff: finite orbits are separated by intersecting finitely many translated
open neighbourhoods. A finite rotation quotient of a circle is a circle.
    We verify properness of the reflected map, rather than assume it. On a closed small base disc
every noncentral torus point has a representative in the image of [0, 1]4 under its period matrix.
These representatives belong to a single compact subset of C2 . At the centre their images meet
every class of the circle or the point. The image of that compact parameterized parallelepiped is
therefore the full inverse image of the closed disc in the reflection. The reflected map is proper;
the same holds after the finite quotient. If it were holomorphic on a compatible complex space,
the central fibre would be analytic. A circle cannot be a complex analytic space: a positive-
dimensional analytic germ has real dimension at least two, and a compact zero-dimensional
analytic space is finite. A central point is also impossible here: upper semicontinuity of fibre
dimension, or the local dimension inequality at a point in the closure of the three-dimensional
smooth locus, forces a fibre dimension of at least two for a holomorphic map to a curve. Thus


                                                  275
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


this Hausdorff reflection cannot be glued as a complex-space filling to the remaining constructed
manifold.
    For the leaf assertion, the moving line is {ξ = 0}. At the centre the projection of the period
group to the ξ-line is Ga ⊂ R. Its intersection with the moving line is a rank-two lattice in Cη :
the periods are p + qi with (p + q)/2 + ka + ` = 0 for integers p, q, k, `. For irrational a this
is the index-two lattice p + q ≡ 0 (mod 2); for rational a it is either that lattice or Z[i]. Both
give intrinsic elliptic leaf manifolds isomorphic to Ei . In the irrational case their maps into the
non-Hausdorff central quotient need not be topological embeddings; “leaf” here means the image
with this intrinsic immersed topology. When Ga is discrete, the saturated leaf is closed. When it
is dense in R, its saturation has closure Cη × (Re ξ + R), with Im ξ fixed. This is a statement
in the original, possibly non-Hausdorff central fibre. Its own Hausdorffization is the rank-three
quotient described in propositions 5.6 and 5.7; it is not the central fibre of T H .

quotient limits. They are assertions about real topological and metric groups, not complex tori
of a varying complex dimension.

displayed expansion. The order-four deck action preserves it, acts freely on it, and the coarse
map t is a four-fold covering of its image. Since the punctured root quotient is a punctured
disc, that image is again a simple closed curve. The strict global maximum in proposition 5.1
and theorem 5.5, including the independent certificate in Part E.4, gives a uniform gap on the
complement of any fixed root neighbourhood; the cusp tends to minus infinity. Thus no other
zero-locus component exists for small enough .

Proposition 22.11. For any height H = Im c > H∗ , the zero locus is the well-defined modular-

It is compact away from the cusp, and is a real-analytic set in the finite root charts. At every

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; propositions 5.6 and 5.7; proposition 5.1
and theorem 5.5; propositions 3.1 and 3.2.

Proof. The formula for D in proposition 5.1 and theorem 5.5 gives the equation, and the theta
transformation law shows that it is independent of the modular and period representatives.
Compactness away from the cusp follows from Dpart → −∞. The analytic and regular-level
assertions follow in each root chart from the real-analytic implicit function theorem. On the
complement, the real period matrix is invertible. On compact subsets of that complement its
inverse is bounded, which proves uniform discreteness and proper discontinuity of the lattice
action. The quotient is therefore a complex manifold with compact torus fibres. The finite deck
action is free for the same invariant-coordinate reason as propositions 3.1 and 3.2: a nontrivial
power translates that circle by a noninteger fraction, regardless of the sign of D. Near the cusp
D < 0, so its existing holomorphic Mumford completion and its overlaps remain available. At a
zero with irrational kernel line, the fibre quotient is already non-Hausdorff. At a zero with rational
kernel choose a primitive integral kernel vector. Its holomorphic period vanishes at that root point
but is not identically zero nearby. Its first nonzero Taylor coefficient, multiplied by arbitrarily
large integer multiples and approached along suitable root directions, yields nonseparated central
points. Thus no neighbourhood of a zero in the naive quotient is a Hausdorff complex manifold.
This justifies the asserted maximal open base locus.
    For connectedness, in any holomorphic coordinate z with T = Im τ > 0, differentiation gives

                                               3 0       Im µ 0   2
                            ∂z ∂z̄ Dpart = −     µ (z) −     τ (z) ≤ 0.
                                               T          T

Thus the function is superharmonic on the root charts. This property and the minimum principle
descend under the finite quotient; one can equally apply the principle on a root cover of a putative
minimum. A component of the strict sublevel set not containing the cusp would have compact
closure with boundary at level −H, and would attain a smaller interior minimum. The strong
minimum principle excludes this. A sufficiently small cusp neighbourhood is contained in the
sublevel set, so all components reaching the cusp are the same one. Hence the sublevel set is
connected.

Proof. The last three period columns are real-linearly independent, so the rank is exactly three.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                      Paper I


the same annihilator characters, and characters separate closed subgroups of a real vector space
by putting such a subgroup into the form Rd × Ze . This proves the closure formula. Inside the
three-dimensional image hyperplane its connected part has dimension 3 − r, and its discrete
quotient has rank r. The one transverse real direction gives the displayed group.

such a generator to an integral basis for the converse; for necessity, a discrete subgroup of
a real three-space has rank at most three, forcing a nonzero integral kernel. A nondiscrete
finitely generated subgroup cannot be closed, since a nondiscrete closed subgroup contains an
uncountable vector group. Finally each fixed integral period converges to its limiting period; a
Chabauty limit is closed and therefore contains their closure. This does not identify it with that
closure.

Remark 22.15. This identifier recorded an open step at the earlier checkpoint: the minimum

Proposition 22.17. For every H > H∗ , the degeneracy locus ZH is exactly one embedded C 1
Jordan curve in the finite t-plane. It is real analytic unless H = H0 = 3 log 48/(2π); at that height
it is real analytic away from t = 0 and has the regular crossing described in 22.14. There are no
singular coarse levels at any supercritical height. The bounded complementary disc contains t = 1
and has Dc > 0; the complementary disc in P1 , containing the cusp, has Dc < 0. The point t = 0
is in the latter disc for H < H0 , on the curve for H = H0 , and in the former disc for H > H0 .
     The bounded discs are strictly nested as H increases, shrink to {1} as H ↓ H∗ , and exhaust
the finite plane as H → ∞. Their small-height boundary shape is the expansion in 22.10. The
maximal open base locus of the complex manifold construction consists of these two complementary
discs. Approaching their common boundary, the covolume of the marked root torus lattice is

                                  covol(Πc Z4 ) = Im τ |Dc | −→ 0.

At the boundary the period map has rank three and the exact quotient and Hausdorff reflection
are those of 22.12. Thus this statement classifies the locus and the local degeneration requested in
D.4.

     We now pass from these estimates to the coarse function. Away from t = 0, 1, the modulus
is a local holomorphic coordinate and P 6= 0: the Weierstrass equation gives P 2 = −g3 , and
g3 = 0 on a nonsingular elliptic curve gives j = 1728. Consequently 22.13 and the certificates

the punctured root neighbourhood of t = 1. At t = 0, 22.14 supplies a C 1 coarse extension with
nonzero differential. Hence

                                 f = −Dpart : C \ {1} −→ (H∗ , ∞)

is a C 1 submersion. It is proper: a closed bounded interval of values excludes a neighbourhood
of 1, because f (1) = H∗ , and excludes a neighbourhood of infinity, because f → ∞ there. Its

                                                 286
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


inverse image is therefore a closed subset of a compact annulus. The strict minimum at 1 is the
independently certified proposition 5.1 and theorem 5.5 maximum in E.4.
    We give the needed level transport also at t = 0, without assuming that this coarse function
is C 2 . Fix H∗ < a < b < ∞. On the compact band K = f −1 ([a, b]), the continuous covector df
is nowhere zero. At each point choose a constant real direction on which df is positive; it remains
positive in a neighbourhood. A finite smooth partition of unity gives a smooth vector field V on a
neighbourhood of K with df (V ) > 0 throughout K. Compactness gives a positive uniform lower
bound. The smooth flow of V , starting on f −1 (a), therefore reaches every intermediate level,
and then level b, in finite time. It cannot cease earlier, since before exiting the band it remains in
a compact subset of the vector field’s domain. The hitting time is unique by strict monotonicity
of f , and depends C 1 on the initial point and target height by the implicit function theorem.
Reversing the flow gives the inverse. Thus every two levels in the band are C 1 -diffeomorphic.
This argument applies to arbitrary finite bands and crosses H0 without a regularity gap.
    For a − H∗ small, 22.10 proves that f −1 (a) is one embedded circle. Transport proves that
every f −1 (H) is one embedded circle. The real-analytic implicit function theorem applies away
from t = 0, 1; the level never contains 1, and it contains 0 exactly when H = H0 . This proves
the regularity assertions, including the absence of singular coarse levels. By the Jordan curve
theorem there are exactly two complementary discs in the sphere. Continuity and the absence
of any other zero imply a constant sign on each disc. The values near 1 and infinity identify
their signs. Also Dc (0) = H − H0 , proving the claimed position of zero. The inequalities f < H,
together with the unique minimum and properness just proved, give strict nesting, shrinking and
exhaustion.

    The literature comparison concerns the exact function just classified. Chen, Kuo, and Lin
(2019, Appendix A, (A.1) and (A.3)) give the classical modulus derivatives of ℘ and g2 ; with their
η1 = π 2 E2 /3, these agree with our heat-equation calculation. Their Theorems 1.1–1.4 concern
different holomorphic simple-zero functions and Green-function degeneracy curves. Chen, Fu,
and Lin (2025a, Theorem 1.1; 2025b, Theorem 1.2) establish generic nondegeneracy for multiple
Green functions and nondegeneracy of the extra critical points of a fixed torus Green function.

theta norm at ℘ = 0, modulus critical points, and Green-function degeneracy curves, including
those primary papers and their references, did not locate this precise global classification. The
proof here consists of the stated analytic identities, finite interval certificate, and level-transport
argument.

    We justify the global analytic correction. Differences of allowed finite extensions are the
equivariant holomorphic vertical vectors on the complete root discs. The extra subgroup of order
k at the first point acts trivially on the vertical vector coefficients and rotates s; its invariant
holomorphic coefficients are exactly those in sk . The remaining order-three equivariance is the
original one. The argument at the second point uses sl and order four. Thus the coarse difference
sheaf is literally the same sheaf VB as for multiplicities (3, 4), not an assumed analogue. Its
first-coordinate quotient is OB (−p0 ): the modular frame has vanishing orders 2k, l on the two
enlarged roots and a simple cusp pole. Its fixed second-coordinate subline is OB . Finite averaging
provides local lifts, hence

                              0 −→ OB −→ VB −→ OB (−p0 ) −→ 0.

form a torsor under this sheaf: on each overlap their defects agree, so their difference is a
single-valued section of the indicated difference sheaf. Vanishing of its Čech class gives a global
middle translation. Its overlap equalities are exactly the two finite formulas and the cusp formula
just displayed. Consequently the local biholomorphisms glue, with their inverses, over B.
    For necessity the base is intrinsic even when its anticanonical pencil changes. If F : X → X 0 is
a biholomorphism, the pullback of the Fubini–Study form by f 0 F is exact because H 2 (S 6 , R) = 0.
Its restriction to a regular complex torus, wedged with a flat Kähler form, has zero integral.
Positivity forces f 0 F to be constant on that torus. The proper analytic image of (f, f 0 F ) is
therefore a curve of degree one over B; normalization and the inverse argument give a base
automorphism. Its three monodromy orders 3, 4, ∞ are distinct, so it fixes all three marked points
and is the identity. Multiplicities agree. On ordinary fibres the lift is affine. The simultaneous
rational centralizer of A1 , A2 is QI + QE, as follows by solving their entrywise commuting
equations. Comparison of the constant last two columns of Πc and unimodularity then gives
fibre-linear part αI, integer difference h, and lattice map αSh−1 . The normalized root base change
is functorial, so the lifted map commutes with the actual deck generator. Summing its defect
around that generator gives the two norm conditions above. A cusp map has an integral toric
winding: at a generic point of a toric component, its ratio of characters is tqc times a holomorphic
unit. Its class in Λ vanishes. The middle cocycle relation then gives p0 = αp. This proves all the
necessary conditions.
    Substitute 23.1. In the second congruence the extra term N10 − αN1 is divisible by 4l, and
hence drops out modulo 2l. We obtain exactly the statement’s two congruences. For fixed data
b 6= 0 excludes α = −1. The invertibility of N0 modulo k, of N1 modulo 2l, and gcd(k, 2l) = 1
give h ∈ 2klZ. For varying data the Chinese remainder theorem gives exactly one shift class
modulo 2kl, and all residue classes of ρ0 mod k, ρ1 mod 2l occur without changing b or freeness.
Finally a positive u-circuit sends c to c − 1. Its translation on Z/(2kl) is a generator.

    The preceding theorem answers Question 3 of (Viaclovsky, 2026a, Section 1.1). The original
return asserted the same arithmetic classification in proposition 4.8; the contribution here is the
explicit dictionary and the complete enlarged-root and collar argument.

Proposition 23.5 (local separation and canonical dimension). The multiplicity pair (3k, 4l) is
constant on every sufficiently small deformation of one of the preceding members. Distinct pairs
therefore determine disjoint open loci among these isomorphism classes. Moreover

Equality kl = 3k + 4l never occurs under gcd(3k, 4l) = 1.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 23.2; theorem 23.4.

Proof. Local miniversality identifies every small deformation with the fixed-data period family;
23.2 makes its multiplicity pair an intrinsic biholomorphic invariant. The canonical formula of
23.4 and connected fibres identify its pluricanonical sections with those of O(r(kl − 3k − 4l)) on
the root curve. Negative weight has no sections. Positive weight has linearly growing section
counts along multiples of 12kl, giving Kodaira dimension one. Equality would imply k | 4l;
coprimality forces k = 1, and then l = 3 + 4l is impossible.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                      Paper I


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 23.4; (Bănică and Stănăşilă,
1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.1).

Proof. For coprime m, n, the number of nonnegative solutions of mi + nj = N is N /(mn) + O(1)
as N → ∞: there is one permitted residue class of j modulo m, and its representatives lie between
0 and N /n. The canonical formula in 23.4 proves the displayed limit, with a negative value
when the anticanonical counts grow. Write 1/12 − s(X) = a/b in lowest positive terms. Since
gcd(m + n, mn) = 1, we have a = m + n, b = mn. Thus m, n are the two roots of T 2 − aT + b.
Their order is determined because only m is divisible by three and only n is divisible by four.
    For every fixed integer r, apply the finite-free-complex theorem of (Bănică and Stănăşilă,
1976, Chapter III, Theorem 4.1) to the relative canonical power, which is an invertible flat sheaf
for a holomorphic submersion. Its zeroth cohomology dimension has analytic jumping loci. On
an irreducible base any value constant on a nonempty open set is its generic value: a proper
analytic jumping locus has empty interior. Local miniversality in 23.4 makes these dimensions
constant near either of the two given fibres, since all nearby fibres have the same multiplicities
and their canonical formula is independent of the period parameter. Consequently the two fibres
have equal dimensions for every positive and negative r. Their limits s(X) are equal, and the
preceding arithmetic recovers the same pair. This proof uses relative cohomology only; it makes
no general invariance assertion for Kodaira dimension.

the canonical geometric-point comparison

is an isomorphism for q = 0, 1, 2, and the direct images are locally free. The trace induces the

Both comparisons descend on the analytic root-curve groupoid. These conclusions, and hence the

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem 23.4; theorem 3.9; Du et al.

    Grauert’s original direct-image theorem (Grauert, 1960, Section 6, Hauptsatz I, and Section

Complete construction and independent

The construction and standard cohomological conclusions are credited in the main text. We
retain the complete independent derivations, including the finite quotient maps and the affine
cusp origins.


A     Invariant and arithmetic notation in the family marking
Base, fibres, and the two peripheral orientations. We use B = P1t , p1 = 0, p2 = 1,
p0 = ∞, Σ = {p0 , p1 , p2 }, and D = W + S1 + S2 with reduced components. The full fibres are
f ∗ p1 = 3S1 , f ∗ p2 = 4S2 , and f ∗ p0 = W . A positive base loop is counterclockwise in a holomorphic
local coordinate. The analytic root deck generator is clockwise, sj (gj z) = e−2πi/mj sj (z), with
g1 g2 g0 = 1. The lifted positive base loop ends at the inverse deck translate; its endpoint
identification applies gj . Thus its homology action is Aj , not A−1      j . The clockwise boundary
orientation used in the collar integration is stated separately in proposition 10.6. References
there to a peripheral generator refer to this fixed analytic generator.

denotes its dual cohomology basis. The letter w in that cohomology basis is a covector, whereas
the scalar family parameter below is e−πic . In the ordered additive coordinates (ζ1 , ζ2 ),

B     The analytic threefold constructed in the candidate
This section audits the construction itself. It does not infer existence from the later topology.
The period family, the three local fillings, and the gluing are proved in that order. The notation
is the candidate’s: B ≃ P1 , B ◦ = B \ {p0 , p1 , p2 }, and the local monodromy orders at p1 , p2 are
m1 = 3, m2 = 4.

B.1    The period family
Let ∆ ≃ (Z/3) ∗ (Z/4) be the orientation-preserving (3, 4, ∞)-triangle group acting on a simply
connected Riemann surface hz , with elliptic generators g1 , g2 and g0 = (g1 g2 )−1 . Let t be the
affine coordinate on B with values 0, 1, ∞ at p1 , p2 , p0 , respectively. Write

                                           π : hz −→ B \ {p0 }

Lemma B.1 (simultaneous elliptic-orientation normalization). The generators may, and
henceforth do, satisfy
                       g10 (z1 ) = e−2πi/3 , g20 (z2 ) = e−2πi/4 = −i,          (103)

                                                     303
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


while g0 = (g1 g2 )−1 remains parabolic. More precisely, the Cayley coordinates
                                                        z − zj
                                             sj (z) =                                            (104)
                                                        z − z̄j

obey
                               s1 ◦ g1 = e−2πi/3 s1 ,        s2 ◦ g2 = −is2 .                    (105)
The two signs in equation (103) are a simultaneous orientation choice; they are not obtained by
shrinking a coordinate disc.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Beardon, 1983, Section 7.38 and
Section 10.6 (the latter checked in the 1986 translation)).

Proof. Realize ∆ as the orientation-preserving subgroup of the reflection group of a hyperbolic
triangle with counterclockwise vertices A, B, C, angles π/3, π/4, 0, and opposite sides a, b, c,
respectively. Let σa , σb , σc denote reflection in those sides and put

                               x = σb σc ,      y = σc σa ,       z = σa σb .

The product of reflections in two oriented geodesics meeting at angle θ is the rotation through
2θ. Hence x is the counterclockwise rotation about A through 2π/3, y is the counterclockwise
rotation about B through π/2, and z is parabolic at the ideal vertex C; this is the standard
triangle-group construction (Beardon, 1983, Section 7.38 and Section 10.6 (the latter checked in
the 1986 translation)). Moreover

                                      xyz = σb σc σc σa σa σb = 1.

Set
                         z1 = A,       z2 = B,          g1 = x−1 ,      g2 = y −1 .
Both finite rotations are thereby reversed, so their complex derivatives at their fixed points are
exactly those in equation (103). Since g2 g1 = y −1 x−1 = z, one also has

                                             g1 g2 = g1 zg1−1 ;

thus g1 g2 , and therefore g0 = (g1 g2 )−1 , is parabolic.
    This simultaneous reversal is forced once the orientation of g1 and the cusp conjugacy class
are fixed. Indeed, in hxi ∗ hyi ≃ C3 ∗ C4 every parabolic element is conjugate to a nonzero power
of the primitive cusp word z = y −1 x−1 = y 3 x2 . The two mixed choices would instead give

                       (x−1 y)−1 = y −1 x = y 3 x,         (xy −1 )−1 = yx−1 = yx2 .

Both words are cyclically reduced of length two. A nontrivial power z n has cyclically reduced
length 2|n|; hence a mixed word could be parabolic only for |n| = 1. But neither y 3 x nor yx2
is a cyclic permutation of y 3 x2 or its inverse xy. Thus neither mixed choice is parabolic. The
derivative selected at z1 consequently fixes the derivative at z2 as well.
     Finally, for an elliptic Möbius transformation g fixing z0 ∈ hz , the Cayley map s = (z −
z0 )/(z−z̄0 ) conjugates g to a disc automorphism fixing zero. Such an automorphism is s 7→ g 0 (z0 )s.
Applying this to g1 , g2 proves equation (105).

Proof. Normalize the modular function by j(q) = q −1 (1 + O(q)) and put JB = 1728(t ◦ π); the

                        h†z = hz \ JB−1 {0, 1728},         h†τ = h \ j −1 {0, 1728}.

Away from the deleted sets, the classical modular map j : h†τ → C \ {0, 1728} is an unramified
covering with deck group PSL2 (Z). The deleted set in hz is locally finite. Since hz is simply
connected, π1 (h†z ) is normally generated by small positive meridians about its points. At a
translate of z1 , JB has local degree three over 0; the corresponding meridian therefore has deck
image equal to the third power of the order-three modular generator. At a translate of z2 , JB
has local degree four over 1728; its meridian has deck image equal to the fourth power of the
order-two modular generator. Both images are the identity. The covering-space lifting criterion
gives a global lift τ with j(τ ) = JB .
    Near a deleted point, compose the lift with a biholomorphism χ : h → D. The bounded
map χ ◦ τ extends by the removable-singularity theorem. Its value at the puncture has modulus
strictly less than one: equality would give an interior maximum and force χ ◦ τ to be constant,
although its punctured values lie in D. Thus the extension still lands in h.
    Because JB is ∆-invariant, τ ◦ g and τ are lifts of the same map through the Galois covering
j on the punctured surface. Hence there is a unique deck transformation ϕ(g) ∈ PSL2 (Z) such
that
                                          τ ◦ g = ϕ(g) ◦ τ.                                 (106)

ϕ(gh) = ϕ(g)ϕ(h), so ϕ is a homomorphism.

Proposition B.3 (exact admissible period constants). Let τ, µ, β part be the cusp-regular functions

                                           {c0 ∈ C : Im c0 < −M }.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition B.2.

Proof. The preceding proposition proves continuity on B \ {p0 }, including its elliptic points, and
convergence Dpart → −∞ at p0 . Choose a base point b∗ . Outside a compact set containing b∗ ,

Since the exact ordered real determinant is Im τ D, these and only these excluded constants
make the period matrix singular somewhere.

Lemma B.10 (radial retraction and the finite-fibre stalk map). Under proposition B.9, the finite
local model Nj strongly deformation retracts onto its reduced central fibre Sj . After identifying a
nearby fibre with the marked real torus As = (Λ ⊗ R)/Λ by the flat coordinates Ξ, the specialization
map
                                     H r (Sj ; Z) −→ H r (As ; Z)
is the pullback πj∗ of the quotient covering

                                 (j)              (j)
                           πj : A0 −→ Sj = A0 /hx 7→ Aj x + vj /mj i.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition B.9.

Proof. Use the linearizing coordinate to define the radial contraction ru : ∆j → ∆j by

                             sj (ru (z)) = (1 − u)sj (z),        0 ≤ u ≤ 1.

Because sj ◦ gj = ζj sj , this contraction commutes with gj . In the global real-analytic marking

                                       Ξ(z, x + Λ) = [z, Π(z)x],

put                                          
                               Hu Ξ(z, x + Λ) = Ξ(ru (z), x + Λ).
Formula (2.8f) shows directly that Hu commutes with the logarithmic lift: it keeps x fixed while
both composites send it to Aj x + vj /mj . Hence Hu descends to a strong deformation retraction
of Nj onto Sj .
    Fix tj 6= 0 and one root s with smj = tj . Every orbit of the logarithmic lift meets the fibre
over s exactly once, so that fibre maps isomorphically onto fj−1 (tj ). Following the descended
radial retraction sends the marked point x ∈ As to the orbit of the same x in the central torus,
namely πj (x). The induced map from central-fibre cohomology to nearby-fibre cohomology is
therefore exactly πj∗ , with no unrecorded conjugacy or index.

Theorem B.11 (global analytic construction). Gluing the period family over B ◦ to N0 , N1 , N2
by the preceding punctured-disc biholomorphisms produces a connected compact Hausdorff complex
threefold X and a proper surjective holomorphic map

                                          f : X −→ B ≃ P1

with connected fibres. The fibre over p0 is exactly the reduced nonnormal surface W of theorem B.6;
those over p1 , p2 have scheme multiplicities three and four. The open embedding N0 ,→ X identifies
canonical bundles, so
                                        ωX |N0 ≃ ωN0 ≃ ON0 .                                  (111)

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem B.6; lemma B.8; theorem B.6
and proposition B.9.


                                                  320
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


Proof. Take the disjoint union of the four manifolds and identify the two copies of each punctured-
disc restriction by the displayed biholomorphism. The special discs are pairwise disjoint, so
every nonsingleton equivalence class has two points and meets each summand at most once. The
saturation of an open set is the union of that set with its images under finitely many overlap
biholomorphisms, hence is open. Each summand therefore embeds openly in the quotient, and
the only transition maps are biholomorphisms. This gives a complex threefold.
    Points over distinct base values have disjoint disc preimages. Points over one base value lie in
a common one of the four Hausdorff charts, so the quotient is Hausdorff. The images of countable
bases of the four open pieces give second countability. The local maps to the base agree on
overlaps. Moreover f −1 (Dj ) is exactly the embedded Nj , since every middle-piece point over Dj∗
was identified with its unique representative there; similarly f −1 (B ◦ ) = J. Each of these full
restrictions is proper, for the period-family piece by lemma B.8 and for the three fillings by their
local proper constructions. Explicitly, for compact K ⊂ B, choose finitely many open sets Va
covering K, with compact closures inside members Ua of this base cover. Each K ∩ V a is compact
in Ua , so its full inverse image is compact. Their finite union is f −1 (K); hence the global map is
proper. Since the base is compact, X = f −1 (B) is compact. All four pieces are connected and
every local filling meets the central period-family piece, so X is connected. The fibre statements
follow from theorem B.6 and proposition B.9; their fibres are connected, and surjectivity follows.
Because each summand embeds openly in the quotient, the restriction of the intrinsic canonical
bundle ωX to the open summand N0 is ωN0 . Equation (2.6a) proves equation (111).

What has and has not been discharged. The formulas above reconstruct the period
functions, both finite fillings, the toric cusp quotient, and all three punctured-overlap
biholomorphisms. Thus theorems B.6 and B.11 discharge existence, smoothness, properness, the
full central-fibre equation, and the normalization assertions used in the conductor calculation.
This promotion is local to the analytic construction: no collapse, Leray transgression, or
Mayer–Vietoris computation is used here. Integral cohomology and sphere recognition remain
separate below.
