Proposition C.6 (terminal degree-two lattice). Let A : Z6 → Z4 have columns
                       c1 = (2, −4, −2, 3)t , c2 = (1, −2, −2, 3)t ,
                       c3 = (3, 0, −4, 0)t ,    c4 = (0, 1, 0, −1)t ,     c5 = c6 = 0.
Then im A is saturated of rank three,
                                 im A = ker(4, 2, 3, 2),       coker A ∼
                                                                       = Z,                             (3.11)
and (4, 2, 3, 2) is the primitive left-kernel generator.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The row Φ = (4, 2, 3, 2) annihilates the four nonzero columns:
 Φc1 = 8 − 8 − 6 + 6 = 0,        Φc2 = 4 − 4 − 6 + 6 = 0,        Φc3 = 12 − 12 = 0,          Φc4 = 2 − 2 = 0.
It is primitive since the gcd of its entries is 1, so ker Φ ⊂ Z4 is a saturated rank-three lattice.
The 3 × 3 minor on rows (1, 2, 3) and columns (1, 2, 4) is 2, whereas the minor on rows (1, 2, 4)
and the same columns is −3. Consequently the ideal generated by all maximal minors contains
(2, 3) = (1). This proves that A has rank three and saturated image. We have im A ⊆ ker Φ
between rank-three lattices. The finite quotient ker Φ/ im A injects into the torsion-free group
Z4 / im A, so it is zero. Thus equality holds, and the primitive surjection Φ : Z4 → Z induces
(3.11).

Geometric boundary. The calculations in this section deliberately isolate the printed lattices,
presentations, and matrices. Their geometric realization is proved separately: the finite-band
and cusp maps are identified in proposition E.10, the based fundamental-group calculation is
verification record E.9, and the comparison with the intrinsic Leray transgressions is theorem E.14.

The extension transgression, including its sign convention. Here is a direct derivation
of the transgression used in proposition C.4. Write the cyclic quotient additively as Cm =
{0, . . . , m − 1} and choose its section s(a) = g a in Γ = hΛ, g | gλg −1 = Aλ, g m = vi. Since
Av = v, its factor set is
                                     
                                  a+b
                      c(a, b) =         v,    s(a)s(b) = c(a, b)s(a + b mod m).
                                   m

For an invariant integral covector ξ, extend its homomorphism on Λ to the one-cochain F (λs(a)) =
ξ(λ) on Γ. The inhomogeneous bar boundary (Brown, 1982, Chapter I, §5, equation (5.2)) gives

            (δF )(λs(a), µs(b)) = F (µs(b)) − F (λs(a)µs(b)) + F (λs(a)) = −ξ(c(a, b)).

It is inflated from the displayed cyclic two-cocycle. This is precisely the obstruction to extending
ξ to a cocycle on Γ, hence the transgression in the cohomological Hochschild–Serre sequence
(Brown, 1982, Chapter VII, §§5–6, Theorem 6.3). The carry cocycle b(a + b)/mc generates
H 2 (Cm ; Z) = Z/m: it is the connecting cocycle of the character a 7→ a/m mod Z for 0 → Z →
R → R/Z → 0. Indeed positive-degree cohomology with real coefficients vanishes by averaging
over the finite group, so the connecting map identifies Hom(Cm , R/Z) with H 2 (Cm ; Z). If the
generator of this last cyclic group is chosen as the negative of the carry class, the formula is

                                        d2 ξ = ξ(v) mod m.

This is the convention used in the finite-index proof. Reversing that generator reverses all these
transgression signs together. The image indices and the nonzero order-two value d2 (γη2 ) = ±[η2 ]
are unchanged. Multiplicativity and the derivation rule are the filtered cup-product construction
of (Brown, 1982, Chapter VII, §5, pp. 170–171).

C.5    Abelianization of a semidirect product
Lemma C.8 (Cited group formula, with a re-derivation). Let α : Q → Aut(K) be an action of
a group Q on a group K, and form G = K oα Q. Put

                            C = K ab /hα(q)[k] − [k] : q ∈ Q, k ∈ Ki.

The inclusion of K and the chosen section Q → G induce an isomorphism of abelian groups

                                Gab ≃ Qab ⊕ C,        C = (K ab )Q .                          (SD.1)

Thus the assertion applies to any split group extension once a splitting has been selected.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.
   This formula is Claude and Alpöge (2026, Section 10.5, Lemma 10.7, p. 90). We retain the
quotient argument of the working edition as the following independently worded re-derivation.
Uses: The definition of a semidirect product, a commutator subgroup, and the displayed
coinvariant quotient.


                                                328
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                                      Paper I


Proof. Write s : Q → G for the section. Define N to be the normal subgroup of G generated by

                              [k, k 0 ] and    s(q)ks(q)−1 k −1        (k, k 0 ∈ K, q ∈ Q).

Every generator lies in K ∩ [G, G], and this intersection is normal in G. Consequently N ⊂
K ∩ [G, G]. The relations defining K/N impose commutativity of K and identify the class
of k with that of α(q)k. They therefore give the canonical isomorphism K/N ≃ C. More
explicitly, the map K → C has a G-invariant kernel and kills all the displayed generators; in the
reverse direction K → K/N factors through K ab and through its Q-coinvariants. These two
factorizations are inverse on the images of every k ∈ K.
    The image of s(Q) in G/N still maps isomorphically onto Q, because N ⊂ K, and commutes
with K/N . Thus multiplication identifies G/N with C × Q. Finally, quotienting by a subgroup
of [G, G] does not change the abelianization: its commutator subgroup is [G, G]/N . Applying
this observation gives
                                G/[G, G] ≃ (C × Q)ab ≃ C ⊕ Qab ,
as claimed. Each map used here is induced by the original inclusion or section, so it gives the
asserted splitting.

C.6     Exact product covers, normalization branches, and peripheral kernels of
        the finite fillings

trivialization of the finite normal line. These calculations use no sphere identification, global
integral cohomology, or CDP theorem. The separate period and cusp constructions retain their
own proofs and are not inferred from these finite-local calculations.

Proposition C.11 (Smooth quotient charts and the exact multiplicities). The map qj : Jj0 → Nj

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem C.10; equation (FF25);

Proof. At sj = 0 the freeness is proved in theorem C.10. Away from zero, a power with
0 < k < mj has base coordinate multiplied by ζjk 6= 1, so has no fixed point. Equation (FF25)
shows that the mj -th power is the original lattice translation, hence is the identity on Jj0 . This
gives a free action of exact order mj .
    For y ∈ Jj0 , its finitely many distinct orbit points can be separated by pairwise disjoint
coordinate neighbourhoods. Intersecting their inverse translates and shrinking gives a coordinate
neighbourhood U of y with the Gaj U pairwise disjoint. Then qj |U : U → qj (U ) is a biholomorphism.
Two distinct finite orbits have disjoint saturated neighbourhoods by the same finite separation
argument. These charts prove the Hausdorff and smooth assertions, and the quotient is a finite
étale covering. They give directly the trivial-stabilizer case of the quotient analytic structure in
(Cartan, 1954, conditions (I)–(II), Theorem 1); smoothness is not inferred from a theorem about
arbitrary finite quotients.
    At a point of Sj , use the quotient chart to retain sj as a transverse coordinate, together with
two fibre coordinates. The full map is tj = sj j . Thus Sj is a smooth reduced Cartier divisor,

and its scheme multiplicity is exactly mj .
    For compact C ⊂ ∆j , the map induced by Ξ from C × [0, 1]4 onto the inverse image of C
in Jj0 is continuous and surjective, so that inverse image is compact. The actual power map
between the discs of radii rj and rj j is proper: the inverse image of a compact target set is
                                         m

closed, bounded, and stays strictly inside the radius-rj disc. For compact K ⊂ Dj , the inverse
image in Jj0 of all roots of its tj -values is therefore compact. Its finite quotient image is exactly
fj−1 (K), proving properness of the full restriction.

C.6.7    The finite-to-global analytic gluing interface

The global construction of theorem B.11 glues complete punctured restrictions of the original
middle family and the three local fillings. The finite identifications are precisely (FF36). The
special discs are pairwise disjoint, and a middle point over each punctured disc has exactly one
representative in its filling. Thus an equivalence class meets any given summand at most once.
Saturations of open subsets are open, because the overlap identifications are biholomorphisms,
so each summand embeds openly and injectively.
    Two points at one special base value have representatives in its same filling; two points at one
ordinary base value have representatives in the middle piece. They have disjoint neighbourhoods
in that Hausdorff open summand, and their images remain disjoint because no equivalence class
meets that summand twice. Points at distinct base values are separated by the base. This proves
the gluing’s Hausdorff assertion using the actual full restrictions, not an unrestricted gluing
principle.
    In particular f −1 (Dj ) is the entire corresponding filling: every middle point over Dj∗ is
identified with its unique filling representative. Thus the properness in proposition C.11 is
properness of the full inverse image. For a compact base set K, finitely many relatively compact
Va whose closures lie inside members Ua of the original four-piece base cover can be chosen to
cover K. The compact sets K ∩ V a have compact preimages under the corresponding full proper
restrictions, and these preimages cover exactly f −1 (K). This is the compact-cover argument
for global properness. The separate cusp and middle constructions supply their own full proper
restrictions; the finite-local proof neither replaces those constructions nor implies smooth sphere
recognition.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I

     For completeness, the cusp covering has no hidden fundamental group. The toric variety Y
is smooth, and its complement of the dense torus T = (C∗ )3 is a locally finite normal-crossings
divisor. A loop has compact image, hence meets only finitely many charts and divisor strata.
After a small transverse perturbation, fixing a chosen basepoint in T , it misses the divisor:
a real one-dimensional map transverse to a real codimension-two stratum has empty inverse
image. Hence π1 (T ) = N 0 → π1 (Y ) is surjective. For every primitive ray generator v ∈ N 0 , its
one-parameter subgroup extends to a map C → Y in the affine chart of that ray. Its unit circle
therefore bounds a disc in Y . The three rays (0, 0, 1), (1, 0, 1), (0, 1, 1) form an integral basis of
N 0 , so all generators of π1 (T ) die. Thus Y is simply connected. The one-parameter subgroup in

E     The alternate collapse and Mayer–Vietoris route
The nearby-cycle/Leray proof in section D gives one verified route to the topology of X. This
section audits the manuscript’s independent cellular-collapse/Mayer–Vietoris route. It now closes
the entire alternate certificate: the equivariant cusp retraction, its primitive integral cellular map,
equality with analytic nearby-cycle specialization, both geometrically realized Mayer–Vietoris
stages, and the comparison of their obstruction maps with Leray.
    We first correct a conflation in the earlier audit. For any two-set decomposition Y = A ∪ B,
our Mayer–Vietoris convention is

                       ∆q = (iA∗ , −iB∗ ) : Hq (A ∩ B; Z) −→ Hq (A; Z) ⊕ Hq (B; Z).          (TM.4.1)

The manuscript does not identify its printed αq with a one-shot map for three collars. It uses
two stages. First,

                        X ◦ = X1 ∪ X2 ,      X1 ∩ X2 ≃ F,       αq = (π1∗ , −π2∗ ).          (TM.4.2)

Second, it attaches the cusp through

          X = N00 ∪ X ◦ ,        N00 ∩ X ◦ = M,      Kq = ker Hq (M ) → Hq (W ) .            (TM.4.3)
                                                                               

The proof below realizes both stages by actual oriented inclusions and then also records the
equivalent one-shot degree-one collar matrix.

E.1    The abstract cusp-retraction lemma
Proposition E.1 (equivariant topological spine). Let A be a contractible manifold with boundary
and let A0 ⊂ ∂A be a contractible boundary component. Let a group Γ act freely and properly
discontinuously on (A, A0 ). Assume Q = A/Γ and H = A0 /Γ are manifolds, Q is compact,
H ,→ Q is collared, and the two quotient maps are connected coverings with deck group Γ. If the
inclusion identifies the two deck groups by the identity automorphism of Γ, then H ,→ Q is a
strong deformation retract. The retraction lifts uniquely from the identity lift to a Γ-equivariant
strong deformation retraction of A onto A0 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.5);
(Hatcher, 2002, Proposition 0.19 and Corollary 0.20).


                                                   349
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


Proof. Because A and A0 are contractible universal covers, πn (Q) = πn (H) = 0 for n ≥ 2,
while π1 (Q) ∼=Γ∼ = π1 (H). By hypothesis the inclusion induces the identity on Γ, so it is a
weak homotopy equivalence. Manifolds have the homotopy type of CW complexes; Whitehead’s
theorem (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.5) therefore makes the inclusion a homotopy equivalence.
     The collar makes (Q, H) an NDR pair, hence the inclusion is a cofibration. We record the
standard cofibration argument. Choose a homotopy inverse r0 : Q → H. Since r0 |H ≃ idH ,
the homotopy extension property modifies r0 through maps Q → H to a retraction r satisfying
r|H = idH . The relative homotopy-equivalence refinement of the homotopy extension property,
(Hatcher, 2002, Proposition 0.19 and Corollary 0.20), gives idQ ≃ i ◦ r relative to H. In the
standard proof one concatenates the boundary homotopy with its reverse, contracts this retracing
loop through homotopies fixing its endpoints, and extends the resulting square by the homotopy
extension property for (Q × I, H × I). The resulting homotopy is stationary on H and is therefore
a strong deformation retraction.
     Let P : A → Q be the covering. Lift the deformation homotopy from the initial lift idA .
Since the base homotopy fixes H and the initial lift fixes A0 , uniqueness of path lifting makes the
lifted homotopy fix A0 . For γ ∈ Γ, both H
                                         e t ◦ γ and γ ◦ H e t lift the same map and agree at t = 0;
uniqueness gives equality for every t. The lift is therefore Γ-equivariant and ends in A0 .

E.8    Complete recognition theorem
Lemma E.16 (cohomological closure in dimension six). Let X be a smooth, closed, connected,
oriented six-manifold. If

                           π1 (X) = 0,     H 2 (X; Z) = H 3 (X; Z) = 0,                 (TM.4.4)

then Hk (X; Z) is Z for k = 0, 6 and zero for 1 ≤ k ≤ 5.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. The Hurewicz map in degree one identifies H1 (X; Z) = π1 (X)ab = 0. The universal
coefficient sequence

                  0 −→ Ext(H1 (X), Z) −→ H 2 (X; Z) −→ Hom(H2 (X), Z) −→ 0

shows that Hom(H2 (X), Z) = 0, so the finitely generated group H2 (X) is torsion. The next
universal coefficient sequence contains an injection

                               Ext(H2 (X), Z) ,→ H 3 (X; Z) = 0.

For a finitely generated torsion group A =      i Z/ni , one has Ext(A, Z) =   i Z/ni ; hence
                                              L                              L
H2 (X) = 0. Poincaré duality gives

             H3 (X) ≃ H 3 (X) = 0,    H4 (X) ≃ H 2 (X) = 0,     H5 (X) ≃ H 1 (X) = 0.

Finally connectedness and orientation give H0 (X) = H6 (X) = Z.

Theorem E.17 (sphere recognition from the exact inputs). Let X be a smooth, closed, connected
six-manifold. If                                   (
                                                     Z, k = 0, 6,
                      π1 (X) = 0,     Hk (X; Z) ∼=                                   (TM.4.5)
                                                     0, 1 ≤ k ≤ 5,
then X is diffeomorphic to the standard S 6 .

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.32);
(Hatcher, 2002, Corollary 4.33); (Smale, 1961, Theorem A); (Smale, 1962, Corollary 1.2); (Kervaire
and Milnor, 1963, opening table and following Remark, pp. 504–505).

Proof. A closed smooth manifold has the homotopy type of a finite CW complex. We first prove
successively that πi (X) = 0 for 1 ≤ i ≤ 5. The case i = 1 is assumed. Suppose 2 ≤ n ≤ 5 and
πi (X) = 0 for i < n. Then X is (n − 1)-connected, so the Hurewicz homomorphism

                                     hn : πn (X) −→ Hn (X; Z)

is an isomorphism by the Hurewicz theorem (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.32). The target vanishes
by (TM.4.5), hence πn (X) = 0. Induction proves the assertion.
    Now X is 5-connected. Hurewicz in degree six gives π6 (X) ∼ = H6 (X; Z) ∼= Z. Choose a map
g : S → X whose homotopy class maps to a chosen orientation generator. It has degree one.
     6

Hence g∗ is an isomorphism in degrees zero and six; in every other degree both integral homology
groups vanish. Thus g is an integral homology equivalence. Both spaces are simply connected
CW complexes, so the homological Whitehead theorem (Hatcher, 2002, Corollary 4.33) makes g
a homotopy equivalence. Therefore X is a smooth homotopy 6-sphere.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                      Paper I


    Smale’s generalized Poincaré theorem in dimensions greater than four (Smale, 1961,
Theorem A) identifies the underlying topological manifold with S 6 . The smooth endpoint
is stated directly by Smale: every homotopy 6-sphere is diffeomorphic to S 6 (Smale, 1962,
Corollary 1.2). Equivalently, smooth homotopy 6-spheres up to oriented h-cobordism form Θ6 ;
Kervaire–Milnor’s opening table gives |Θ6 | = 1, and their following remark identifies h-cobordism
with diffeomorphism in dimension six (Kervaire and Milnor, 1963, opening table and following
Remark, pp. 504–505). Hence there is no exotic smooth structure in dimension six, and X is
diffeomorphic to the standard sphere.

F     Elementary integral chain constructions
These classical constructions are included as rederivations of the singular-chain prerequisites;
they make no novelty claim.

F.1    Chains, pairs and homotopies
Let Cm (X) be the free abelian group on the continuous maps σ : ∆m → X, with Cm = 0 for
m < 0. Write σ[i0 , . . . , ik ] for its restriction to the indicated ordered face. The differential is
                                               m
                                               X
                                       ∂σ =           (−1)i σ[0, . . . , bi, . . . , m].
                                                i=0

    Each twice-deleted face appears with opposite signs in ∂ 2 σ, so ∂ 2 = 0. Homology is
Hm = ker ∂/ im ∂. For A ⊂ X, the relative complex is C∗ (X, A) = C∗ (X)/C∗ (A). It is free on
the simplices not entirely contained in A. With an abelian coefficient group G, use C∗ (X, A) ⊗ G
for homology and Hom(C∗ (X, A), G) for cohomology; its coboundary is δa = a∂. Maps of pairs
induce the evident chain maps and contravariant cochain maps.

Lemma F.1 (homotopy invariance). Homotopic maps of pairs induce the same homology and
cohomology maps, with every coefficient group.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. For a homotopy H : X × I → Y , triangulate ∆m × I into the m + 1 ordered simplices

                       [(v0 , 0), . . . , (vi , 0), (vi , 1), . . . , (vm , 1)],       0 ≤ i ≤ m.

   Apply H(σ(−), −) to their sum with coefficients (−1)i , defining P σ. Adjacent internal faces
cancel. The bottom and top faces remain with signs minus and plus, and the side faces are
−P ∂σ. Hence ∂P + P ∂ = H1∗ − H0∗ . If H(A × I) ⊂ B, this formula descends to relative chains.
Tensoring the homotopy, or precomposing cochains with it, proves the assertion.

    The point complex has one generator in every nonnegative degree; its differential is zero in
odd degrees and the identity in positive even degrees. Therefore a point has homology Z in
degree zero and zero elsewhere. By lemma F.1 the same is true of a contractible space. Moreover
H0 (X) is free on the path components: the boundary of a path equates its two endpoints, and
these are exactly the relations imposed by paths.

F.2    Making singular chains small
For an open cover U of X, let C∗U (X) be generated by simplices whose image lies in one cover
member. Local arguments require the inclusion of these chains to be a chain homotopy equivalence,
rather than just an intuitive subdivision picture.

Lemma F.2 (small-chain lemma). There is a chain map ρ : C∗ (X) → C∗U (X) and a homotopy
D with

                                       ρι = 1,            1 − ιρ = ∂D + D∂.

    Both preserve every subspace of X, so the assertion also holds for relative complexes.



                                                             365
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. First construct subdivision S on the affine chains in each standard simplex. If b is its
barycentre, define Sσ = b ∗ (S∂σ) inductively, starting with vertices. Here the affine cone with
apex first satisfies ∂(b ∗ c) = c − b ∗ (∂c) for a positive-dimensional cycle, and the corresponding
reduced formula for dimension zero. It follows inductively that ∂S = S∂. Composing these affine
subdivisions with a singular simplex defines a natural chain map on singular chains.
     Construct a subdivision homotopy T by induction too. On an m-simplex, the chain z =
σ −Sσ −T ∂σ is a cycle by the already established lower-dimensional identity. It has augmentation
zero when relevant. Cone it to the barycentre and set T σ = b ∗ z. Then ∂T + T ∂ = 1 − S. All
chains constructed remain inside the original simplex image. Thus subdivision and its homotopy
preserve small chains and chains in any subspace.
     A barycentric subsimplex has vertices that are barycentres of nested faces. If a face of size `
lies in one of size k, their barycentre difference has norm at most (k − `)/k times the old diameter,
at most m/(m + 1) times it. The diameter of a Euclidean simplex is the maximum of its vertex
distances. Iteration therefore makes the mesh tend to zero. For the inverse-image open cover of
the compact standard simplex, choose at each point a ball whose doubled ball lies in one cover
member. Finitely many of the smaller balls cover the simplex; the minimum of their radii is
positive. Every subset of smaller diameter, by choosing one of its points in a smaller ball, lies in
the corresponding doubled ball. This is the required Lebesgue number. Every singular simplex,
and every finite chain, becomes small after sufficiently many subdivisions.
     Put TN = N     j=0 S T ; then ∂TN + TN ∂ = 1 − S . Now construct ρ, D inductively on the
                 P −1 j                                   N

basis of singular simplices. Given their values on the boundary of σ, put z = σ − D∂σ, so
∂z = ρ∂σ is small. Choose N such that S N z is small and define

                              ρσ = S N z + TN (ρ∂σ),      Dσ = TN z.

   The second term of ρσ is small because TN preserves smallness. The displayed identities give
∂ρσ = ρ∂σ and σ − ρσ = ∂Dσ + D∂σ. If σ is already small, its faces have D = 0 by induction;
choose N = 0, obtaining ρσ = σ, Dσ = 0. Every operation remains in the original image, which
proves the subspace assertion.

Corollary F.3 (excision). If Z ⊂ A ⊂ X and Z ⊂ intX A, the inclusion (X \ Z, A \ Z) → (X, A)
induces homology and cohomology isomorphisms with every coefficient group.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; lemma F.2.

Proof. Use the open cover int A, X \ Z of X. After quotienting small chains by those in A, the
first summand disappears and the quotient is C∗ (X \ Z, A \ Z). The restricted cover of X \ Z
gives the very same quotient: its first member is (int A) \ Z, whose chains again disappear.
lemma F.2 identifies both ordinary relative complexes with these quotients up to chain homotopy.
Tensor and dualize the equivalences.

F.3    Exact sequences and local gluing
A degreewise exact sequence of complexes 0 → K → L → M → 0 has a long exact sequence in
homology. Its connecting map sends a cycle m to the class of ∂` in K, where ` lifts m. Changing
the lift changes this by a boundary; changing the cycle by a boundary does likewise. Exactness
follows directly: a cycle of L maps to a boundary of M exactly when, after subtracting the
boundary of a lift, it lies in K; a cycle of M has zero connecting class exactly when its lift can be
corrected by a chain in K to a cycle of L; a cycle of K becomes a boundary in L exactly when it

                                                366
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                             Paper I


is the connecting image of the projected bounding chain. These three arguments prove exactness
at all the repeating positions. The same lifting argument, with δ, proves the cohomological
version and its naturality.
    The pair sequence comes from 0 → C∗ (A) → C∗ (X) → C∗ (X, A) → 0. It is degreewise split
on the simplex bases, so it stays exact after tensoring or dualizing.
    For an open cover X = U ∪ V , the sequence

                                 c7→(c,−c)                      (a,b)7→a+b    {U,V }
               0 → C∗ (U ∩ V ) −−−−−−→ C∗ (U ) ⊕ C∗ (V ) −−−−−−→ C∗                    (X) → 0

    is degreewise split exact: each simplex belongs to U , to V , or to both. lemma F.2 replaces the
last complex by C∗ (X). We obtain the Mayer–Vietoris sequences. For cohomology the middle-
to-intersection map is the difference of restrictions. Dividing throughout by the corresponding
chains in a subspace A gives the relative sequences for (X, A), with pieces (U, U ∩ A), (V, V ∩ A)
and (U ∩ V, U ∩ V ∩ A). Splitting is again obtained on the simplices outside A.
    We will use the following precise form of the five lemma. In a commutative diagram of exact
five-term sequences, if maps at positions one, two, four and five are isomorphisms, the middle
map is an isomorphism. For injectivity, an element with zero image maps to zero at position
four, so comes from position two; lift its image-zero condition through position one and use the
isomorphisms there to correct its preimage to zero. For surjectivity, map a target middle element
to position four; lift there, note its image at position five vanishes, and lift back to a source
middle element. Their difference lies in the image of position two, whose isomorphism provides
the required correction. This proves the lemma and applies equally to homology and cohomology
segments.
    For example, cover S m , m ≥ 1, by slightly enlarged hemispheres. Each is contractible, and
their intersection retracts to S m−1 . The reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence gives H     e j (S m ; G) ∼
                                                                                                     =
Hj−1 (S
 e       m−1 ; G). Starting with two points, this yields Hm (S ; G) = G and zero in other degrees;
                                                         e     m

the same argument gives reduced cohomology. The generator obtained by orienting the two
hemispheres compatibly is the fundamental class of the oriented sphere. Concretely triangulate
it as the boundary of an m + 1-simplex, radially projected from an interior point. Each ray
meets the boundary once, and its intersection distance is continuous face by face, so this is a
homeomorphism. The alternating sum of oriented faces is a cycle because shared faces cancel.
Its image at a point inside one face is the positive local disk generator by excision. Since
the sphere homology group in degree m is infinite cyclic, that value one proves the cycle is a
generator. To verify the same local value at any point, choose a different centre or a rotated
simplex whose face interior contains that point; the radial projections are related through
orientation-preserving rotations, which are homotopic to the identity by the following elementary
plane-rotation argument: an orthogonal orientation-preserving matrix is reduced to the identity
by successive rotations in coordinate two-planes, each connected to the identity by its angle
parameter. This gives the fundamental class [S m ], with local value one in every oriented chart.

F.4    Products, signs and evaluation on fibres
For cochains of degrees p, q with values in a commutative ring R, define the Alexander–Whitney
cup product by

                           (a ^ b)(σ) = a(σ[0, . . . , p])b(σ[p, . . . , p + q]).

   Expanding boundaries, terms deleting vertices strictly before the joining vertex give δa ^ b,
those after it give (−1)p a ^ δb, and the two joining terms cancel. Thus

                                δ(a ^ b) = δa ^ b + (−1)p a ^ δb.


                                                   367
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


    The formula is natural. It is associative: the same three face intervals occur in either order of
multiplication. The constant zero-cochain 1 is its unit. It descends to cohomology. An absolute
class can multiply a relative class for every pair; cochains on the subspace vanish in the relative
factor.
    We supply the chain comparison that explains external products and graded commutativity.
On the total tensor complex use ∂(c ⊗ d) = ∂c ⊗ d + (−1)deg c c ⊗ ∂d. Define
                         X
                 Aσ =           σX [0, . . . , p] ⊗ σY [p, . . . , m],   σ : ∆m → X × Y.
                        p+q=m

     Conversely define S(c ⊗ d) by triangulating ∆p × ∆q along all lattice paths from (0, 0) to
(p, q). Give a path the sign of the permutation of its horizontal and vertical steps relative
to all horizontal steps followed by all vertical steps. Compose its affine simplex with (c, d).
Internal faces from paths interchanging adjacent unlike steps cancel; boundary faces give precisely
∂c ⊗ d + (−1)p c ⊗ ∂d. For A, deleting a nonjoining vertex gives the matching tensor boundary
and joining-vertex terms telescope. Hence both maps are chain maps, preserving augmentation.

Lemma F.4 (product chain equivalence).
  The two maps are inverse up to natural chain homotopies, preserving products of subspaces.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Here is an explicit inductive construction of the needed homotopies. Chains in a convex
set have a contraction to any fixed vertex: cone each singular simplex to that vertex by linear
interpolation. The cone boundary identity gives ∂K + K∂ = 1 − i, where  is augmentation and
i inserts the vertex. Tensoring two such contractions gives a contraction of their tensor complex
to Z: the homotopy is K ⊗ 1 + (i) ⊗ L, with the tensor sign (−1)deg c in the second term. The
first identity and then the second verify this formula; its boundary sum is 1 − (i) ⊗ (j).
     For 1 − SA, assume a homotopy h is already defined on lower-dimensional simplices. On the
universal diagonal simplex ∆m → ∆m × ∆m , form z = (1 − SA)σ − h∂σ. It is an augmented
cycle. Cone z in the convex product to fill it. For an arbitrary σ, push this filling forward by
σX × σY . This defines h naturally and gives ∂h + h∂ = 1 − SA.
     For 1 − AS, repeat on a universal tensor generator 1∆p ⊗ 1∆q . The residual cycle is filled
by the tensor contraction just constructed, then pushed forward by the two singular simplices.
Induction on p + q gives the other homotopy. If either simplex lies in a subspace, every filling
still maps into the corresponding product subspace.

   The same induction compares A with the map obtained by swapping the two coordinates and
then applying A and the signed tensor swap cp ⊗dq 7→ (−1)pq dq ⊗cp . They agree on augmentation,
and the tensor contraction fills the residual cycles exactly as in lemma F.4. Evaluate a ⊗ b on this
homotopy after the diagonal X → X × X. For cocycles the resulting difference is a coboundary.
Therefore

                                       [a] ^ [b] = (−1)pq [b] ^ [a].

    No assertion of cochain commutativity was used.
    The equivalence also descends to C∗ (X, A) ⊗ C∗ (Y, B) and the product complex modulo
C∗ (A × Y ) + C∗ (X × B). When A, B are open, small chains in their union identify this quotient
up to chain homotopy with C∗ (X × Y, A × Y ∪ X × B). If one subspace is empty the assertion
holds for the other subspace without openness. For classes, define the external product by
a × b = pr∗1 a ^ pr∗2 b; its cochain formula is evaluation of a ⊗ b on A. This defines external


                                                       368
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


products on all pairs used here. Cup products of two relative classes likewise take values relative
to their union when its two subspaces are open, by the same small-chain comparison.
    For an integral relative cocycle u of degree r, define a right cap operator on an m-simplex,
m ≥ r, by

                            Ru σ = u(σ[m − r, . . . , m]) σ[0, . . . , m − r],

    and set it to zero when m < r. Boundary expansion and δu = 0 give ∂Ru = Ru ∂; the faces
at the cut cancel by the cocycle equation on the last r + 1 vertices. Thus it is a degree-−r map
commuting with the unshifted differentials. If u vanishes on a subspace, this map descends from
relative chains to absolute chains. For a cocycle a of degree m − r, its defining identity is

                                       a(Ru σ) = (a ^ u)(σ).

    We use this convention throughout. Reindexing chain groups here keeps their differential
unchanged; it is not the alternative signed convention for suspended chain complexes. Replacing
u by u + δv changes the cap map by a homotopy: on Cm set h = (−1)m−r+1 Rv . The cup-product
differential identity gives ∂h + h∂ = Rδv . Products and this cap identity also make sense with an
abelian coefficient group in the first factor and an integral cochain in the second, using integer
multiplication on the group.


G     Actual CW models and the first Hurewicz map
The singular-chain prerequisites, sphere generators and prism calculations are proved in section F.
The first Hurewicz theorem is the classical result of (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.32); the following
is our complete expanded proof.

     with the second argument of the minimum interpreted as +∞ at v = 0. The first choice of
the minimum puts the result on the bottom; the second puts it on the side. Its time coordinate
lies in [0, t], and its radial coordinate has norm at most one. On the bottom and sides λ = 1, so
R fixes them. It is continuous, including at v = 0, because the bounded first term supplies the
minimum throughout a sufficiently small neighbourhood of that point. Thus (125) retracts the
cylinder onto its bottom and sides.
     A simplex is radially homeomorphic to a disk, from its barycentre, so this proves the same
extension statement for simplex cylinders. In particular a map on the bottom and a compatible
homotopy on the boundary extend to the cylinder by composition with R.
     Let Y be path connected with basepoint y0 , and suppose q ≥ 2 and

                                      πi (Y, y0 ) = 0         (1 ≤ i < q).                       (126)

     For every singular simplex of dimension at most q − 1, choose a homotopy to the constant
simplex at y0 , coherently on all faces. At vertices, choose paths to y0 , with the constant path at
y0 . Suppose the lower-dimensional choices have been made. On the boundary of an i-simplex
cylinder, prescribe its original simplex on the bottom, its constant map on the top, and the
chosen face homotopies on the sides. They agree on intersections. This boundary is an i-sphere;
for 1 ≤ i < q, (126) makes its based class zero after transport to y0 . A null-homotopy extends it
across the cylinder. Choose that extension. For a simplex constant at y0 , choose the constant
extension.
     For every q-simplex σ, use (125) to extend its bottom map and these chosen side homotopies.
Its top σ 0 then has constant boundary. The quotient ∆q /∂∆q , with the original orientation, is
S q . Thus the top defines

                                         a(σ) = [σ 0 ] ∈ πq (Y, y0 ).                            (127)

    The group is abelian for q ≥ 2. Indeed concatenate cube representatives in either of two
coordinate directions. The interchange law follows by dividing the square of those two coordinates
into four rectangles. Both operations have the constant map as unit; applying interchange with
two of the four entries equal to that unit proves that the operations agree and commute. Extend
(127) additively to singular q-chains.
    We use the following finite sphere-pinch fact. If a triangulated q-sphere has its (q − 1)-skeleton
mapped to the basepoint, its class is the sum of the classes of its oriented q-simplices. Here is
a geometric proof. On each simplex collapse a collar of its boundary, and concentrate its map
on a smaller interior disk; radial reparametrization gives a homotopy relative to the boundary.
There are finitely many disjoint supporting disks. Remove the basepoint of the source sphere
and use its Euclidean chart. For q ≥ 2, the complement of finitely many disjoint small disks is
path connected: a polygonal path can detour around each disk on its connected boundary. Move
one sufficiently small support at a time along such a path to a prescribed sequence of disjoint
slabs. A smooth vector field equal to the path’s local translation near the moving support and
cut off away from the other supports gives this isotopy on each short path segment; compactness


                                                        372
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                       Paper I


divides the path into finitely many such segments. Radial shrinking and expanding supplies the
required small radii. These isotopies preserve orientation. The final map is the concatenation of
the individual disk maps, so its class is their sum, with the original simplex-orientation signs.
The abelian law just proved removes any dependence on the chosen order.

G.4      The first Hurewicz theorem, with inverse maps
Define

                         h : πq (Y, y0 ) −→ Hq (Y ; Z),           h([f ]) = f∗ [S q ].       (128)

    The prism identity gives homotopy invariance. Under the two-disc pinch, the fundamental
class of the sphere maps to the sum of the two positive disc generators. This follows from their
local values and excision. Hence h is a homomorphism. It is natural under maps of based spaces.

Theorem G.1. Under (126), h is an isomorphism and H
                                                  e i (Y ; Z) = 0 for 0 ≤ i < q.

equation (129); equation (127); equation (131); equation (132).

Proof. Apply the chosen simplex homotopies to the q-faces of a singular (q + 1)-simplex τ . They

   by the proved pinch fact. This sphere bounds the top (q + 1)-simplex, so (129) is zero.
Therefore a(∂τ ) = 0, and the additive map (127) induces

                                    A : Hq (Y ; Z) −→ πq (Y, y0 ).                           (130)

    Triangulate each chosen simplex cylinder by the ordered prism triangulation. Its chain
boundary is top minus bottom minus the corresponding face prisms. On a singular cycle z, the
face-prism terms cancel exactly: the homotopies of repeated singular faces are the same choices,
and their coefficients are those of ∂z = 0. The top chain is consequently homologous to z.
    For the top maps work in the actual relative chain complex C∗ (Y, {y0 }; Z). All constant
simplices at y0 vanish in this quotient. The pair sequence identifies its positive-degree homology

top q-simplex has constant boundary and represents exactly h(a(σ)) under this comparison, since
the identity simplex is the positive disk-relative generator. Thus the prism argument proves

                                           hA([z]) = [z].                                    (131)

    Equations (131)–(132) prove the isomorphism. If i < q, the coherent homotopies take an i-

    For completeness, in degree one the Hurewicz map identifies H1 (Y ; Z) with the abelianization
of π1 (Y, y0 ). Choose paths py from y0 to each point y. An edge σ from x to y determines
           y . Sum these classes in the abelianized group over a cycle. The boundary of each
px ∗ σ ∗ p−1
singular triangle gives zero, since that triangle fills its edge loop and the inserted paths cancel.
Changing the chosen paths contributes only endpoint terms, which cancel on a cycle. This defines
the inverse: a based loop returns its original abelianized class, and the inserted paths cancel in

H     Path fibres and integral homotopy equivalences
The CW and Hurewicz inputs are proved in section G; singular chains, excision, products and
prisms are proved in section F. These are expanded classical proofs; the homological Whitehead
conclusion is (Hatcher, 2002, Corollary 4.33). All homology below is integral unless a coefficient
group is displayed.

H.1    Paths, lifting and the exact homotopy sequence
For a space B, give its path space B I , I = [0, 1], the compact-open topology. Its subbasic sets
are

                                        [K, U ] = {γ : γ(K) ⊂ U },                                (136)

   where K ⊂ I is compact and U ⊂ B is open. Evaluation is continuous: if γ(t) ∈ U , choose a
compact interval neighbourhood J of t, relative to I, with γ(J) ⊂ U . The product [J, U ] × intI J
maps into U . A map Z → B I is continuous exactly when its adjoint Z × I → B is continuous.
For the reverse implication, a compact K is covered by finitely many product neighbourhoods on
which the adjoint lies in U ; intersect their neighbourhoods in Z. This proves continuity on (136),
without a local-compactness assumption on Z.

H.3    The fibration filtration and both actual edges
Let p : E → B be a fibration, with B a path-connected, simply connected CW complex and

          E2p,q = Hp (B; Hq (F ; G)),           dr : Erp,q −→ Erp−r,q+r−1      =⇒     Hp+q (E; G).    (157)

                                                       378
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


    The coefficient system is constant because of (141) and simple connectivity. Convergence has
exactly the meaning (155)–(156).
    First, a compact subset of a CW complex is contained in a finite subcomplex. Otherwise
choose one point in each of infinitely many distinct cells met by the subset. The closure of
any cell meets only finitely many cells, by closure finiteness. Its intersection with any subset
of the chosen points is therefore finite and closed. The weak topology says that every subset
of those points is closed in B. They form an infinite closed discrete subspace of the original
compact subset, which is impossible. The finitely many cells that remain, together with their
finite collections of boundary cells, give the asserted finite subcomplex.
    Put Ep = p−1 (B p ) and

                             Fp C∗ (E; G) = C∗ (Ep ; G),            E−1 = ∅.                    (158)

    The projected image of a singular simplex is compact, so the preceding argument puts it in
some finite skeleton. Thus (158) is exhaustive. The first page of section H.2 is Hp+q (Ep , Ep−1 ; G).
    We calculate these relative groups with the actual attaching disks. In B p , let N be B p−1
together with the regions kvk > 1/3 of its characteristic p-disks, and let N0 use kvk > 2/3. They
are open in B p by the weak topology. The skeleton together with the regions kvk ≥ 2/3 is closed,
contains N0 , and lies in N , so N0 ⊂ N . Expanding each annulus radially to its outer sphere gives
a deformation of N onto B p−1 , fixed on that skeleton. It is continuous on characteristic disks

a topological disjoint union: a union of closed subsets of these cores is closed in B p , as can be
tested on every characteristic disk. Its pullback has the same disjoint-union description. The

    Here is the local degree calculation of each of its components. For p ≥ 2, put m = p − 1
and fix a target open m-cell. Choose concentric balls V0 b V1 b V2 inside its coordinate chart.
Triangulate the compact attaching S m finely enough that stars meeting the inverse image of V2

piecewise affine.

many points in invertible affine pieces. Outside small neighbourhoods of those points the compact
source has image missing the chosen point. A sufficiently small target ball therefore has inverse
image precisely a disjoint union of source disks, each mapped homeomorphically onto that ball,
with sign +1 or −1. The sum of the signs is the cellular incidence coefficient: excision maps the
attaching sphere to the target relative disk group and counts its oriented generators. This also
proves this local description of degree, rather than requiring a smooth transversality assertion.
    Lift the homotopy of the attaching map with the fibre as additional parameter. It does not
change (161), because it is a homotopy within Ep−1 . Over each of the resulting source disks, use
the two fibre homotopy trivializations. The map takes the form

                                       (v, z) 7−→ (ϕ(v), ψv (z)).                               (163)

    Contract v in the second coordinate of (163), retaining its first coordinate. This is a homotopy
of pairs: its relative boundary condition depends on the first coordinate alone. Its effect on
relative homology is thus the local sign of ϕ multiplied by the homology map of ψv0 . That map is
the transport comparison on the two fibres. To verify it, apply the map of pullback fibrations to a
chosen lifted path and compare it with the other chosen lift by the relative square in section H.1.
Under transport to the reference fibre it is the identity. A different choice inserts a loop of B,
which is null-homotopic, so (141) removes that ambiguity. Summing the local signs proves that
(161) is the cellular incidence coefficient times the original fibre class.
    For p = 1, the boundary of the oriented interval is its terminal point minus its initial point.
Transport identifies the two coefficient maps with the identity and gives precisely those two
signed vertex terms. For p = 0 the differential is zero. Hence

    The cellular complex with any constant coefficient group A computes singular homology.

H.4    From weak equivalences to inverse maps
A weak equivalence is a map inducing a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on
all based positive homotopy groups. We prove the inverse-map assertion for connected CW
complexes without changing the original map to a cellular one.
    First suppose (Y, D) has D path connected, every component of Y meeting D, and all relative
homotopy groups zero. Every map u : (K, L) → (Y, D) from a CW pair can be homotoped,
relative L, into D. Choose paths into D for the vertices outside L. Extend their homotopy
over all higher cells using the cylinder retraction of section G.2. Suppose the preceding relative
skeleton already maps into D. A characteristic j-disk has boundary in D; its zero relative
class supplies a relative null-homotopy, and (146) turns it into a homotopy into D fixing its full
boundary. For j = 1, the same relative path statement applies. Perform this on all j-cells and
extend it to the rest of K, again by cylinder extension.
    Use the time interval [1 − 2−j , 1 − 2−(j+1) ] for the j-dimensional step, starting with j = 0.
Later steps fix each earlier relative skeleton, and fix L throughout. On a fixed characteristic
d-disk the homotopy is stationary after the d-dimensional step. Its restriction to that disk times I,
including time one, is therefore continuous. To verify continuity of the whole homotopy, take its
adjoint K → Y I . The restrictions to all characteristic disks are continuous by the compact-open
adjunction; the weak topology makes the adjoint continuous on K, and evaluation makes the
original homotopy continuous. Its time-one map lies in D. This proves the assertion also for
infinite-dimensional K.
    Now let f : A → B be a weak equivalence of path-connected spaces. Form its actual mapping
cylinder

                                                                                               (167)
                                                        
                       Mf = (A × I) q B / (a, 1) ∼ f (a) ,       j(a) = [a, 0].

    The retraction r : Mf → B sends [a, t] to f (a) and fixes B. Moving t to t + u(1 − t) gives a
deformation retraction onto B. Thus rj = f makes j a weak equivalence. Exactness of (145)
gives πk (Mf , j(A)) = 0 at every positive degree, with the path statement at degree one as well.
The preceding compression consequently shows, for every CW complex K, that
                                                   ∼
                                                                                               (168)
                                                   =
                                      f∗ : [K, A] −−→ [K, B],

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


    where brackets mean unbased homotopy classes. Surjectivity follows by viewing a map K → B
in Mf , compressing it into j(A), and retracting the resulting homotopy by r. For injectivity,
a homotopy between f a0 and f a1 in B, together with the two cylinder paths in (167), gives a
homotopy between ja0 and ja1 in Mf . Apply compression to the CW pair (K × I, K × ∂I),
fixing both endpoint maps. The compressed homotopy lies in j(A) and proves a0 ≃ a1 . The
product is a CW pair because I has its finite interval cell structure; its characteristic prisms give
the product weak topology by the same adjunction argument.
    When A and B are CW complexes, apply surjectivity of (168) with K = B to obtain
h : B → A with f h ≃ 1B . Then f (hf ) ≃ f , so injectivity with K = A gives hf ≃ 1A . This
constructs a homotopy inverse to the given f .

H.5    The integer comparison and the original sphere maps
Theorem H.1. Let f : A → B be an integral homology equivalence between path-connected,

H.6    Two worked checks of the mechanism
Example H.2 (Worked Exercise 6.1). Fix n ≥ 2 and an integer m. Take the free chain complex

                 C0 = Ze,     Cn = Zb,    Cn+1 = Za,        da = mb,      db = de = 0.           (184)

   Put e, b in filtration zero, a in filtration n + 1, and use the increasing filtration they generate.

an algebraic model of the edge calculation; no fibration realization is assumed.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; equation (151); equation (185);
theorem H.1.

Solution. The first and second pages have Z at (0, 0), (0, n), (n + 1, 0) and zero elsewhere. The
boundary da drops filtration by n + 1, so every differential before page n + 1 is zero. Formula
(151) then gives exactly

                                dn+1 : Z[a] −→ Z[b],      [a] 7−→ m[b].                          (185)

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


    The final entries are ker(m : Z → Z) at (n + 1, 0), Z/mZ at (0, n), and Z at (0, 0). These
agree directly with the homology of (184).
    The quotient has Hn+1 (C/Zb) = Z[a] and Hn (C/Zb) = 0. Its degree-n + 1 map has image
ker m, precisely the bottom-row subgroup. If m 6= 0, that image is zero and is not surjective. If
m = 0, it is surjective and the incoming differential is zero; but the degree-n map has kernel Z[b]
and is not injective. For m = 1 or m = −1, the nonzero fibre-row entry is killed completely by
the incoming differential. For all other nonzero m, its surviving group is exactly Z/mZ, retaining
the full integer m and its sign in (185). This verifies why both adjacent-degree arguments in
theorem H.1 are needed.

I   The orientation generator and the path-fibration proof
The homotopy-sphere conclusion is classical; the following argument retains our original map and
gives the distinct path-fibration proof of the course. The complete elementary constructions used
below are printed in sections G and H. The first Hurewicz theorem and homological Whitehead
theorem are also stated in (Hatcher, 2002, Theorem 4.32 and Corollary 4.33); we use their
integral, simply connected forms.

c 6= 0, then µ ≡ 1, whereas the order-four law would give 1 = µ ◦ g2 = 1 + 1/τ , an impossibility.
Hence c = 0, then b = d = 0, and finally a = 0. Thus the five functions

                                     1,     τ,   µ,    β,    6µ2 − τ β

are linearly independent over C.

Lemma J.3 (meromorphic descent). Let f : X → B be a proper surjective holomorphic map
from a connected complex threefold to a connected compact Riemann surface, with connected
fibres, and a submersion over B ◦ = B \ Σ, where Σ is finite and B ◦ 6= ∅. If g ∈ M(X) is
constant on the fibres over an uncountable subset of B ◦ , then there is a unique ϕ ∈ M(B) such
that g = f ∗ ϕ.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and
calculations in the proof.

Proof. Let P be the polar divisor of g, and put Ω = f −1 (B ◦ ) \ |P |. A proper analytic subset
of a connected complex manifold has real codimension at least two and does not disconnect it.
First note that f −1 (B ◦ ) is connected. Indeed, each of its connected components is open, and
its image is open because f is a submersion and closed because the base change f −1 (B ◦ ) → B ◦
is proper. Since B ◦ is connected, every component would meet every fibre; connectedness of
the fibres therefore permits only one component. Removing |P | now leaves Ω connected. Only
finitely many fibres are components of |P |. For every other b, the complement Fb ∩ Ω of a proper
analytic subset in the connected manifold Fb is connected.
     On Ω, define the analytic set

                                      Z = {dg ∧ f ∗ (dt) = 0},

where t is any local coordinate on B. If g|Fb is constant, then Fb ∩ Ω ⊂ Z. If Z 6= Ω, then,
because Ω is second countable, Z has at most countably many irreducible components. Each

                                                    389
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                        Paper I


irreducible two-dimensional fibre contained in Z is one of those components, and distinct fibres
give distinct components. This contradicts the uncountable hypothesis. Therefore Z = Ω.
    It follows that dg annihilates ker df . Connectedness of Fb ∩ Ω, together with local holomorphic
sections of the submersion, gives g = ϕ ◦ f on Ω, for a holomorphic ϕ away from finitely many
points of B.
    Fix such a point t0 . Choose a general holomorphic curve germ κ : (∆, 0) → (X, x), not
contained in |P |, with
                                f ◦ κ(s) = t0 + sk u(s),     u(0) 6= 0.
If g ◦ κ has pole order at most M , then |g ◦ κ(s)| ≤ C|s|−M . After shrinking the disc, boundedness
above and below of |u| gives constants c, C1 > 0 such that

                                 c|t − t0 |1/k ≤ |s| ≤ C1 |t − t0 |1/k

on each local inverse branch. Therefore

                                     |ϕ(t)| ≤ C2 |t − t0 |−M /k

away from the image of a discrete exceptional set, and then everywhere on the punctured disc
by holomorphy. For any integer N > M /k, the function (t − t0 )N ϕ(t) is bounded and extends
holomorphically. Thus ϕ is meromorphic at t0 . Repeating at the finitely many exceptional points
produces ϕ ∈ M(B). Equality on the dense open set Ω gives equality of meromorphic functions
on X, and surjectivity of f gives uniqueness.

Theorem J.4 (algebraic dimension and algebraic reduction). For the global holomorphic family
of theorem B.11,
                       M(X) = f ∗ M(P1 ) = f ∗ C(t),     a(X) = 1,                   (AD.9)
and f is the algebraic reduction.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; theorem B.11; proposition J.2;
lemma J.3.

Proof. By proposition J.2, all but countably many smooth fibres have algebraic dimension zero.
Let g ∈ M(X). Only finitely many fibres are components of its polar divisor, so on uncountably
many of the preceding fibres the restriction of g is a meromorphic function on a torus of algebraic
dimension zero and is therefore constant. By lemma J.3, g = f ∗ ϕ for a unique ϕ ∈ M(P1 ). The
reverse inclusion is immediate, and (AD.9) follows. Since f is proper, surjective, has connected
fibres, and induces the equality of meromorphic function fields, it is the algebraic reduction.

L     A second root-bundle derivation of the Kuranishi statement
We re-derive Theorem 3.9, credited to Du et al. (2026a, Theorem 6.12 and Proposition 6.16).

Proof. We confirm the particular implication used here from the root-bundle and cusp-
normalization data proved above. On B = P(3, 4), both vertical and structure-cohomology
bundles are E = G = O ⊕ O(−1). The vertical subline is generated by the invariant translation
field; its quotient has twelfth power O(−p0 ) by the discriminant’s simple cusp zero, hence is
O(−1) in the torsion-free root Picard group. The extension splits because H 1 (O(1)) = 0. For G,
relative duality and the normalization complex of the hexagon give det G = R2 f¯∗ OX = O(−1);
the invariant integral cocycle γ is nonzero on every ordinary fibre and on the dual-graph cycle at
the cusp. It gives the same split extension. This checks the nonvanishing at the cusp required by
the structure-sheaf calculation.
     The horizontal logarithmic line is O(−5). Projection and Leray applied to 0 → f¯∗ E →
TX (− log W ) → f¯∗ O(−5) → 0 give logarithmic tangent cohomology (1, 1, 0, 0): every nontrivial
root line appearing is one of O(−1), O(−2), O(−5), O(−6), whose coarse direct image is OP1 (−1),
while the two surviving trivial summands lie in degrees zero and one. The branch-normal sequence
has quotient η∗ KdP6 , with cohomology (0, 0, 1); the local map sends each ambient vector field
to its separate normal coefficient on each branch. Hence its exact cohomology sequence gives
(1, 1, 1, 0) for TX .
     The parameter derivative is nonzero. The fixed real marking of the torus lattice gives the
constant Beltrami class
                       1                                 Im µ                     6(Im µ)2

A nonzero constant Dolbeault tensor on a torus is not exact, because integration of every
derivative of a periodic coefficient is zero. A first-order trivialization of Xc would preserve the
relative complete pencil | − 2K|. Its induced infinitesimal automorphism of P1 fixes all three
critical values: the equations t = s3 , t − 1 = s4 , and q = xyz make each critical value a constant
section over the dual numbers. An infinitesimal projective transformation fixing three distinct

    Write the Kuranishi local algebra as C{z}/I in its one-dimensional tangent space. The
existing proper period family defines a local classifying map z 7→ φ(s) with φ0 (0) 6= 0. The
analytic inverse-function theorem makes C{z} → C{s} an isomorphism. Since it annihilates I,
necessarily I = 0. This verifies smoothness and reducedness as well as miniversality, and every
sufficiently small deformation is a member of that period family.

M     Independent normalization and analytic Picard proofs
M.1     The cusp structure sheaf
M.1.1    structure-sheaf cohomology of the cusp fibre

The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of proposition 8.1.

Proof. Let D1 , D2 , D3 ≃ P1 be the double curves and P, Q the two triple points, with the branch
order fixed in the proof of theorem D.1. The normalization complex is
                                                3
                                                                                                      (WBA.9.10)
                                           δ0                δ
                                                M           1
               0 −→ OW −→ ν∗ OdP6 −→                   ODk −→ CP ⊕ CQ −→ 0,
                                                 k=1

where δ0 is the difference of the two branch restrictions and

                 δ1 (g1 , g2 , g3 ) = (g1 (P ) − g2 (P ) + g3 (P ), g1 (Q) − g2 (Q) + g3 (Q)).

For completeness, exactness is stalkwise. At a generic double point it is the fibre-product sequence

                       0 → C{x, y, z}/(xy) → C{y, z} ⊕ C{x, z} → C{z} → 0.

At a triple point it is the augmented branch complex for C{x, y, z}/(xyz): three branch rings,
three pairwise intersection rings, and the common residue field, with alternating differences. The

                                                       395
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                            Paper I


augmented two-simplex complex is exact; successively lifting compatible power series proves
exactness of the analytic rings. Away from the singular locus the first arrow is an isomorphism.
    The same formulas give an exact complex with C in place of O. Since dP6 is rational and
each Dk is a rational curve, the positive structure-sheaf cohomology of every term on the right
of (WBA.9.10) vanishes. Hypercohomology therefore reduces to

                                                                                          (WBA.9.11)
               0       d
             → C3 −→
            C−     1
                     C2 ,         d1 (a1 , a2 , a3 ) = (s, s),   s = a1 − a2 + a3 .

Its cohomology has dimensions 1, 2, 1, proving proposition 8.1.
    For the constant-sheaf complex, the row of degree zero is again (WBA.9.11), the row of
degree one vanishes, and the remaining degree-two row begins with H 2 (dP6 ; C). The comparison
induced by CW ,→ OW is the identity on (WBA.9.11) and zero on the positive rows of the target.
It follows that the degree-one comparison of proposition 8.1 is an isomorphism, while in degree
two it maps the dual-complex summand ker ν ∗ isomorphically onto H 2 (W, OW ).
    Choose the basis γW , uW ∈ H 1 (W ; Z) whose intrinsic specializations are γ, u, respectively; it
exists and is unique by theorem D.1. Their cup product is nonzero, because its specialization
is γ ∧ u 6= 0 ∈ H 2 (F ; Z). Its pullback to dP6 is zero since H 1 (dP6 ; C) = 0. The degree-two
comparison therefore sends it to a nonzero element of H 2 (W, OW ). The images of γW , uW form a
basis by the degree-one comparison of proposition 8.1, and both sides of the cup-product assertion
of proposition 8.1 are one-dimensional. Hence the cup-product assertion of proposition 8.1 is an
isomorphism.

M.2     Direct images, base change, and the Picard line
M.2.1    structure-sheaf direct images

The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of proposition 8.1.

Proof. The proper map has connected fibres and B is normal, so Stein factorization gives

N.2.2    the complete Frölicher page

The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of proposition 10.1.

Proof. Frölicher’s original construction identifies E1 with Dolbeault cohomology and E∞ with the
associated graded de Rham cohomology (Frölicher, 1955, p. 643, Lemmas 1–2 and Theorem 3).
The table in proposition 8.9 leaves only the displayed q = 1 and q = 2 row complexes between
the endpoint classes. Since HdR k (X; C) = 0 for 1 ≤ k ≤ 5, every middle E p,q is zero. There is
                                                                              ∞
only one a priori possible higher differential between middle positions, d2 : E20,2 → E22,1 , but

dimensions.

    The theorem explains why neither topology nor the Frölicher sequence alone can select a
value of m: the two exact row complexes exist numerically for every m ≥ 0. The singular-fibre
calculation below supplies the missing analytic information.

N.4.2    the logarithmic Kodaira–Spencer divisor

The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of proposition 8.5.

calculation supplies the locally split logarithmic sequence (WBH.11.2) (Deligne, 1970, Chapter II,
§3.3). Taking a local splitting and a Čech representative, the connecting cochain is the difference
of the two splittings. Since exterior product of cochains obeys

                               δ(α ∧ β) = δα ∧ β + (−1)deg α α ∧ δβ,

the two displayed connecting maps extend across every logarithmic chart and satisfy the same

N.6.2    exact Hodge diamond

The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of proposition 8.9.

Proof. Put K = ker κ1 . Since
                                                                   κ

and the global map has rank one, its restriction to the two trivial summands is a nonzero constant

                                          K ≃ O ⊕ O(−1)⊕2 .

    Nontriviality for the complete threefold. Suppose its first-order deformation were trivial, with
an isomorphism XA ≃ Xc∗ × Spec A reducing to the identity. Intrinsic relative canonical bundles
and their complete spaces of sections are preserved by that isomorphism. By (PD18), it would
therefore identify fA with aA ◦ fc∗ for a projective linear change aA ∈ PGL2 (A) reducing to the
identity.
    This change fixes all three distinguished points even to first order. Here is a scheme-sensitive
check. In the finite covering charts fA is tj = sj j , so its relative critical ideal is (sj j ), and its
                                                        m                                    m −1

restriction to that critical scheme has tj = 0. The map from the parameter ring A to this critical
scheme is injective; it contains a constant-parameter section given by sj = 0 and the zero section
of the covering torus. At the cusp, in a chart containing a triple point, tc = z0 z1 z2 and the
critical ideal is (z1 z2 , z0 z2 , z0 z1 ). Again tc = 0 in its ring and A injects, using z0 = z1 = z2 = 0.
At a double chart the same assertion follows from tc = z0 z1 ; a smooth chart has no critical
point. These critical ideals are intrinsic to the differential of the map over A, and the charts
are local biholomorphisms onto XA . Away from the three distinguished base values the map
is a submersion, so it has no critical point. Consequently the scheme-theoretic critical-value
sections are exactly the three constant sections p1 , p2 , p0 . An automorphism reducing to the
identity cannot permute these three distinct closed points. Its value at each is therefore the same
point over A, not a nonzero infinitesimal displacement: such a displacement would be a nonzero
element of C in an injective copy of A on the just displayed critical chart.
    For completeness write aA (t) = t + (b0 + b1 t + b2 t2 ). Fixing 0 gives b0 = 0, fixing 1 gives
b0 + b1 + b2 = 0, and fixing infinity, in u = 1/t, gives b2 = 0. Hence aA is the identity. The
hypothesized trivialization thus preserves f , and restricting it to any regular base value would
trivialize the torus deformation (PD4). Its nonzero class (PD5) excludes this.
    Finally, the zero Kodaira–Spencer class is precisely the condition for such a first-order
trivialization. One may see the needed direction directly: choose local product charts for the
holomorphic submersion π and differentiate their transition functions at c∗ . The resulting
tangent-valued overlap functions form a Cech 1-cocycle. If its class vanishes, after refinement it
is the coboundary of local holomorphic vector fields. Changing each chart by that vector field
times  cancels the first-order overlap terms, producing the identity-reducing trivialization. This
is the usual Kodaira–Spencer connecting class (for the standard deformation-space interpretation
see (McMullen, 1996, Section 67, p. 15)); the explicitly recorded conversion from the plus-graph
convention in (PD5) changes its sign, not its vanishing. The contradiction proves the final
assertion.

    The theorem establishes a genuinely varying analytic family with its original marked fibration
and its intrinsic degree-two canonical pencil. It does not assert that every two distinct parameters
give nonisomorphic unmarked manifolds, or that this family exhausts their deformation space.
The global integral topology and the CDP argument are not inputs to this deformation calculation.
    The global identifications within this retained family are computed in theorem 3.8: they are
precisely c0 − c ∈ 2Z, including the finite-filling obstruction and every cusp overlap.

    For the geometric assertion, a holomorphic map between two compact complex tori lifts to
their universal covers. The derivative of the lift is periodic, so its entries descend to holomorphic
functions on the compact source torus and are constant. The lift is consequently affine, with a
complex-linear part L. In a holomorphic family these linear parts vary holomorphically. Their
lattice maps are integral and locally constant, hence give an isomorphism of the two marked
local systems. Because the map is over the identity of the base, that integral map H commutes
with both Aj . Thus H = aI + bE, with a, b ∈ Z. Its determinant is a4 ; invertibility over Z gives
a = 1 or a = −1.

Its third and fourth columns give L(z) = aI2 . Its first column then gives a(c0 − c) + b = 0.
Therefore c0 − c = −b/a ∈ Z, and the asserted two linear parts exhaust the possibilities.

O.9.4    The global additive correction and all overlap identities

We give the global correction explicitly as an additive gluing construction and prove its solvability.
Let B  e ◦ be the universal cover of the three-punctured base. Its fundamental group is free on the
original two negative peripheral generators. Pull back the original Πc , R to this cover. Assign
`1 , `2 from (PS13) to its free generators and extend by (PS20). Freeness makes this an actual
integral cocycle; its third peripheral value is precisely (PS21). The maps

                                (z, y) 7−→ (gz, Rg (z)y + Πc (gz)`g )                         (PS23)

form an affine action. To check the action law, covariance gives Rg (hz)Πc (hz) = Πc (ghz)Ag ;
substituting this equality in the composition gives exactly (PS20). The quotient is an affine
holomorphic bundle over B ◦ , since the deck action on the base is free and properly discontinuous
and one may use evenly covered base opens as affine charts.
    On a finite punctured disc, (PS16) says that aj is a section of this affine bundle. On the cusp
punctured disc, (PS21)–(PS22) say the same for a0 . Define a sheaf Hn on B as follows. Away
from the special points it is the sheaf of sections of (PS23). Near pj , a section is required to have
the form aj + ηj , where ηj : ∆j → C2 is holomorphic and obeys ηj (gj z) = Rgj (z)ηj (z). Near the
cusp it is required to have the form a0 + η0 , with η0 (tc ) holomorphic on the full cusp disc. These
are compatible definitions on the punctured overlaps by the equal affine cocycles just proved.
They also prove local nonemptiness, including at all three special points.
    The differences of these local sections form a vector sheaf V . Its ordinary sections have
covariance η(gz) = Rg η(z); at the two finite points and the cusp its extensions are precisely
the holomorphic extensions specified above. Projection to the first coordinate gives an exact
sequence on the original compact base

                        0 −→ OB e −→ V −→ L −→ 0,              L ≃ OB (−p0 ).                 (PS24)

Here L is exactly the homogeneous period sheaf from proposition B.2, not a newly chosen
extension. Indeed the first diagonal entries in (PS4) are its factors −1/τ and 1/τ , and at the
cusp both extensions require ordinary holomorphicity. The original function

                                          (E4 ◦ τ )2 (E6 ◦ τ )1/2

has those exact factors, orders two and one in s1 , s2 , and a simple pole in tc . Dividing by Θ
identifies the ordinary and finite stalks with OB , and the cusp stalk with mp0 . This recovers the
displayed L with its original cusp condition. These transformation and order calculations are the
ones used to construct the retained µ; no topological conclusion about Xc is involved.
    For completeness, exactness on the finite stalks in (PS24) retains the off-diagonal entry of
Rg . Given an equivariant first component u(z), begin with the vector (u(z), 0)t and average it
under the finite group action on vector-valued holomorphic functions. The resulting vector is
equivariant, and its first component is still u. Thus projection is surjective there. Its kernel is
exactly the invariant second-component functions, which are holomorphic functions of sj j = tj ,
                                                                                             m

multiplied by e. The ordinary and cusp stalks are immediate. This also proves that V is locally

    Both H 1 (B, OB ) and H 1 (B, OB (−p0 )) vanish. One can compute these two groups without
a degree approximation: on the two standard affine charts of P1 , split a holomorphic Laurent
series on their overlap into its nonnegative and negative powers. For OB these are the two
coboundary contributions, and for OB (−p0 ) its transition factor shifts the second contribution

O.9.5    Intrinsic necessity and the resulting parameter space

The analytically computed complete linear system |ωX    −2
                                                         c
                                                           | is the original map fc , by theorem O.1. A
biholomorphism preserves its canonical bundle, the complete space of sections, and its evaluation
map. Consequently it induces α ∈ PGL2 (C) with fc0 F = αfc . The three special fibres have
distinct intrinsic types: the cusp is reduced and nonnormal, while the other two have multiplicities
three and four. All remaining fibres are smooth reduced tori. Thus α fixes p0 , p1 , p2 individually.
In the original coordinate, a fractional-linear map fixing ∞, 0, 1 has zero lower-left and upper-right
entries and equal diagonal entries; hence α = idB .
    Now lemma O.3 forces c0 −c = n ∈ Z and linear part ±I2 . Equations (PS10)–(PS11), obtained
on the original normalized finite covers, exclude −I2 and then exclude odd n for +I2 . Conversely
(PS27)–(PS28) construct the global map for every even n. This proves theorem 3.8 without
converting a failed particular map into a nonisomorphism assertion.
    As a complex parameter space for the isomorphism classes represented by this retained family,
the quotient P/(2Z) has the explicit coordinate

                            w = exp(−πic),        0 < |w| < exp(−πM ).                         (PS29)

Indeed |w| = exp(π Im c), and two complex numbers have the same value of this exponential
exactly when they differ by an even integer. Every point in the displayed punctured disc has
a logarithm giving a c ∈ P. The exponential has nonzero derivative, so these local inverse
logarithms give the claimed quotient complex structure. The integer-period quotient seen by
the middle family instead has coordinate w2 ; it is covered two-to-one by (PS29). Its two lifts
are distinguished by the exact order-two summand in (PS12). This statement classifies the
parameters of the retained family; it does not assert that the family exhausts all deformations or
all complex threefolds with the same singular-fibre types.
