P.6    Re-derivation of Theorem 6.6
Proof. We apply the Appell–Humbert correspondence and the Riemann projectivity criterion
in (Schnell, 2019, Theorems 4.1 and 4.4); the reduction to the present explicit periods is as
follows. The real vector-space isomorphism Π : R4 → C2 transfers E to the actual alternating
form E(v,
      e w) = E(Π−1 v, Π−1 w) on the tangent space. Equation (4) gives J-invariance. The
explicit comparison is
                                           e Jw) − iE(v,
                               HE (v, w) = E(v,       e w).

Direct substitution gives HE (Jv, w) = iHE (v, w) and HE (w, v) = HE (v, w). Its associated real
Chern form is − Im HE = E,   e since (i/2)(HE (v, w) − HE (w, v)) = E(v,
                                                                     e w). Thus the Appell–
Humbert integrality condition is exactly integrality of the given E, with its sign fully specified.
The complex-oriented square computed in 6.4 shows that Pf(E) < 0 is equivalent to definiteness
of this Hermitian form. Its sign can be chosen positive. The cited projectivity criterion then
gives precisely the asserted abelian locus, in both directions.
    For nonzero E with Pfaffian zero, its real rank is two. Its nullspace KR ⊂ R4 is a rational
plane because it is the kernel of an integral matrix. J-invariance makes ΠKR a complex line,
and K = KR ∩ Z4 is saturated. The maps

                            (ΠKR )/ΠK ,→ Ft −→ C2 /(ΠKR + ΠZ4 )

are holomorphic group morphisms; the first is a closed embedded elliptic curve and the second is
its quotient onto an elliptic curve, with connected kernel. A basis of the saturated K extends to
an integral basis of Z4 . The other two periods project to real-linearly independent vectors in
the one-dimensional complex quotient, because Π is a real isomorphism. They therefore form a
discrete lattice there. Compactness follows by taking the image of its compact real fundamental
parallelogram. Conversely any elliptic quotient pulls an integral positive area form back to a
nonzero rank-two integral (1, 1) form. This proves the characterization of Ec . Equivalently all its
kernels can be found by saturated rank-two lattices with a basis v, w satisfying detC (Πv, Πw) = 0
and real independence. This is a second exact integer test, with explicit inclusion and quotient
morphisms.


                                                 439
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                         Paper I


    For the algebraic-dimension assertion, an effective divisor on a torus has a semipositive
Hermitian form: averaging its integration current under translations gives that constant form.
A nonzero semipositive form has rank one or two. Rank two gives the abelian case. Rank
one gives the elliptic quotient just constructed. In the absence of a definite form, there cannot
be two different such kernel subtori. Indeed addition from their product onto Ft would be a
surjective holomorphic homomorphism with finite kernel, and the product polarization would
descend after multiplication by an integer, giving a definite form. Thus there is a single kernel
Kt in this case. Every effective divisor is a sum of its translates: its intersection number with
Kt is zero, whereas a curve mapping nonconstantly to the elliptic quotient has strictly positive
intersection with a general quotient fibre. Every meromorphic function therefore factors through
this quotient. One can check the last statement on a fibre avoiding its polar divisor, where it is
a holomorphic function on a compact elliptic curve and hence constant; analytic continuation
then gives the factorization. The quotient supplies nonconstant meromorphic functions, so the
algebraic dimension is exactly one. If neither locus occurs, a nonconstant meromorphic function
would have a polar divisor of one of the two forbidden ranks. This proves dimension zero. Finally
monodromy acts by integral determinant-one changes of basis, preserving (4) and its Pfaffian.
Thus the stated unions descend without any marking ambiguity. Each individual matrix and
every locus is specified; no expected identification is left in these formulas.

The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                          Paper I


canonical map from singular cohomology to coherent cohomology is surjective in every degree.

P.16    Re-derivation of Proposition 16.7
Proof. We use Waldschmidt (1979, Theorem 1 and Corollary 1), whose complete proof was
opened in the translation hosted by its author. Its Theorem 1 states that, for algebraic invariants
g2 , g3 , algebraic elliptic points expE u, expE v, and β ∈ Q, the number

                                    σ(u + v)
                                             exp((β − ζ(v))u)
                                    σ(u)σ(v)
is transcendental if expE v is nontorsion and u, u + v are not lattice points. Here “algebraic
elliptic point” means that the Weierstrass coordinates are algebraic; it does not mean that its
logarithm is algebraic. Take v = u and β = 0. All hypotheses hold because P is nontorsion. The
sigma duplication formula identifies the displayed number with

                                       −℘0 (u)σ(u)2 e−uζ(u) .

The factor −℘0 (u) is nonzero and algebraic. Therefore σ(u)e−uζ(u)/2 is transcendental, as also
stated explicitly after Corollary 1 of the cited paper.
     For the second assertion we apply the analytic subgroup theorem in Huber and Wüstholz
(2023, Theorem 6.1). In the algebraic universal vector extension E   e a logarithm of an algebraic
lift of P has coordinates (u, ζ(u) − b), where b is an algebraic fibre coordinate, with a possible
algebraic linear change of the second coordinate. If b = ζ(u) − s2 u were algebraic, this logarithm
would belong to the algebraic line {(z, s2 z) : z ∈ C}. The theorem applies to the connected
commutative algebraic group E     e over Q and this line, defined over Q by 16.6; its exponential
contains a nonzero algebraic lift. It would provide a connected one-dimensional algebraic subgroup

                                                  446
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                                   Paper I


whose Lie algebra is that line. Its projection to E is nontrivial. A one-dimensional affine algebraic
group has no nonconstant algebraic-group homomorphism to an elliptic curve, so the subgroup is
an elliptic curve isogenous to E. Its inclusion would split the universal vector extension after that
isogeny. This is impossible: the nonzero extension class in Ext1 (E, Ga ) = H 1 (E, OE ) remains
nonzero under isogeny, since pullback is invertible in characteristic zero.

P.17    Re-derivation of Proposition 16.8
Proof. We use the exact theorem reproduced as Theorem A.1 in Rubin’s appendix to Agboola
and Howard (2006), attributed there to Bertrand (1984): for a number field F and a point of
infinite order in E(F ), its height hF,p is nonzero. We retain the standing hypotheses of that
appendix, including the sign assumption, rather than infer a wider theorem from the abbreviated
statement. The height takes values in the one-dimensional Qp -space attached to the unique
Zp -extension unramified outside p. Taking F = K proves its nonvanishing. The polarized height
of a rational point has zero anticyclotomic projection: complex conjugation fixes the point and
acts as −1 on that projection. Lemma A.2 of the same appendix states that if two of the
cyclotomic, anticyclotomic and p projections vanish, then the third vanishes. It follows that the
cyclotomic projection is nonzero as well. This argument asserts nonvanishing on this point, not
nondegeneracy of a height pairing on an arbitrary Mordell–Weil space tensored with Qp .
    For the displayed curve, propositions 13.6 and 13.7 prove nontorsion and analytic rank one,
hence sign −1. Its CM order has discriminant −19, which is maximal, and its class number is
one: the reduced positive binary forms of that discriminant give only (1, 1, 5) up to the usual
boundary convention. The discriminant of the minimal curve is −193 , so reduction at 5 is good.
Counting directly over F5 gives seven points, hence a5 = −1 and ordinary reduction; equivalently
−19 is a nonzero square modulo 5. Every hypothesis of the cited theorem therefore holds in this
concrete unresolved archimedean example.

We retain the standard filling data (`0 , `1 , `2 ) = (0, 1, −1) and an arbitrary admissible c. All

                                Mn = OX n(S1 − S2 ) ,           n ∈ Z.

We set g = gγ . Thus, in the positively normalized exponential coordinate of 10.6, Mn = exp(ng).

Proposition Q.1 (The root base and its explicit cohomology). Let ρ : B → B be the analytic
root curve with orders 3 and 4 at p1 , p2 . Write R1 , R2 for its tautological root line bundles. Its
Picard group is infinite cyclic, with generator R = R1 ⊗ R2−1 , and

                         R1 = R4 ,     R2 = R 3 ,      ρ∗ OB (1) = R12 ,   KB = R−7 .

Proof. The divisors Sj and their canonical sections give root data OX (Sj )mj = f ∗ OB (pj ), hence
the indicated map to the root curve. Over its order-mj chart the fibre product is the original

Jj0 → X is finite etale; in particular pullback is faithful and the stated local comparisons descend.
Away from the two root points the map is the original f . Properness and flatness may be checked
after this atlas: properness is the properness of the original fillings, and flatness holds because a
nonconstant base parameter is a non-zero-divisor in every smooth total-space local ring. Fibres
have dimension two, including the cusp.
    On a smooth torus chart a vertical field is a holomorphic linear combination of the translation
fields. Its coefficients are constant on each compact fibre and therefore depend only on the
base. The vertical derivative of an affine transition is its linear part Rg ; the translating part,
including the logarithmic regluing, has vertical derivative the identity. At the cusp the two fields

derivative fixes both coefficient directions. The exponential overlap sends ∂ζi to 2πixi ∂xi . These
transitions depend only on the base and define E; they prove the actual bundle identity V = f¯∗ E.
     We check the kernel and surjectivity at every type of cusp point. At t = xy, the kernel of df
is freely generated by x∂x − y∂y and ∂z . At t = xyz it is generated by x∂x − y∂y and x∂x − z∂z .

Actual-gluing Kodaira–Spencer calculation for Theorem 3.9. All line bundles other than the
trivial summands in Rq f¯∗ V = E ⊗ Rq f¯∗ OX are acyclic: they have weights −1, −2. Hence

f¯∗ O(−5) have weights −5, (−5, −6), and −6, all acyclic by Q.1. Consequently (D.3) induces an
isomorphism in every cohomology degree. Sequence (D.10), whose quotient has no cohomology
in degrees zero and one, then gives the claimed isomorphism H 1 (V) → H 1 (TX ).
     We use the Cech convention in which the derivative of a transition arrow is composed with
the inverse of the central arrow. A lattice transition is translation by Πc λ, and its derivative
in c is γ(λ)ξ. The linear deck matrices are independent of c. On the finite charts the affine
translations contribute γ(vj )ξ/mj ; their mj th iterates give γ(vj )ξ, precisely the lattice cocycle.
On the overlap with the smooth part the derivative of the logarithmic translating section is
γ(vj )(log sj )ξ/(2πi). Its Cech coboundary accounts for the difference of these representatives.
On the cusp the deck multiplier differentiates to γ(λ)ξ in logarithmic coordinates, and the
exponential overlap identifies it with the same cocycle. Thus the global Kodaira–Spencer class is
[ξ ⊗ γ], with a minus sign if the tangent-lift convention [∂h]
                                                             ¯ is used instead. The sign is recorded;
nonvanishing does not depend on it.
     Nonvanishing can also be checked on a regular torus. In the quotient description of H 1 (O)
used above, [γ] 6= 0; the first coefficient of (D.5) is zero, so ξγ cannot be a scalar multiple of the
base Kodaira–Spencer class. Its image in H 1 (TX |F ) therefore remains nonzero. Since H 1 (X, TX )
is one-dimensional by 3.9, this proves the asserted isomorphism.

Kuranishi ideal calculation for Theorem 3.9. Let α be the generator in 3.9. The constructed
holomorphic family gives an actual convergent deformation tangent to α. Differentiating its
integrability equation to second order gives ∂α
                                             ¯ 2 = −[α, α]/2, so the cohomology class of [α, α] is
zero. Bilinearity proves that the bracket H 1 (TX ) × H 1 (TX ) → H 2 (TX ) vanishes on every pair.


                                                453
The (3, 4, ∞) family                                                                           Paper I


This argument alone would not exclude higher obstructions, so we make the analytic argument
as well. A Kuranishi germ is a closed analytic subgerm of its tangent space H 1 (TX ) = C. Its
classifying map from the actual parameter disc has nonzero derivative by 3.9. Composing with
this embedding gives a holomorphic map of discs with nonzero derivative; the inverse function
theorem makes its image contain a neighbourhood of zero in C. Every equation of the Kuranishi
germ vanishes on that neighbourhood and is therefore zero. The germ, including its analytic
structure, is the smooth line. The same inverse-function argument makes the classifying map
an isomorphism of germs. Pulling back the semiuniversal deformation therefore realizes every
sufficiently small deformation in the c-family. This is semiuniversality; the positive-dimensional
automorphism group is not being discarded or interpreted as a fine-moduli assertion.

   The original-source comparisons and exact proof hashes are retained in the inventory. A
nonoperative unverified bibliography entry is not a source check. Historical gaps and partial
arguments are not erased by a subsequent proof: the former and the repair are both recorded,
and the complete mathematical arguments are printed at their indicated statements.


S    Programs, certificates and reproducible commands
All paths are relative to the companion archive’s root. For each row, change to the stated
working directory and execute the displayed command. Python programs use Python 3, SymPy,
mpmath and, where imported, python-flint 0.9.0. The latter’s retained dependency directory is
code/invariants_arithmetic/dependencies; it may be placed on PYTHONPATH. The PARI/GP
calculations use PARI 2.15.2 with its elliptic-curve data. MPFR programs use directed rounding
and explicit tails; their build commands are displayed below. A numerical diagnostic is labelled as
such and supplies no rigorous inequality. The proofs specify the exact identity, interval separation
or exhaustion established by each certificate.
    The rational cover contains 19,701 norm boxes; the independent Arb pass certifies all of them.
The gradient argument’s refinement has 19,755 leaves. The original parallel runner is retained,
while its scheduling is not an additional proof step. The obsolete initial global-meridians assertion
is not used: the corrected program and independent quotient fixed-space check are the operative
certificates. All original failed setup outputs and their successful dependency-ordered reruns
remain in the verification archive.

T    Limits and open points: the coefficient atlas
Remark T.1 (what is and is not explicit). Choose global ∂-closed
                                                        ¯        forms

                                 G ∈ A0,1 (X),              Q ∈ A1,1 (X)                     (256)

representing g and q. Proposition 8.10 says that i∗b [Q]∂¯ is the Dolbeault class of the explicit
translation-invariant form displayed in equation (207); it does not say that an arbitrary
representative Q restricts literally to that form. A literal global coefficient formula would
require additional C ∞ gauge choices and horizontal correction forms on the disc–pair-of-pants
cover, compatible with the two affine cyclic conjugacies and the toric cusp. Those choices are not
part of the canonical data. No such literal gauge is needed for the class and product calculations
below.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 8.10; equation (207).

Remark T.2 (literal global gauge boundary). The Bott–Chern algebra proposition 10.7 and
the fibre-coordinate restrictions displayed in equations (202), (203), (205) and (207) to (209)
are complete. The canonical data do not select a preferred literal global coefficient atlas for the
smooth forms G and Q. Such an atlas would require explicit smooth local trivializations and
horizontal correction functions through both finite affine fillings and the cusp. After fixing g
and one coherent-Leray lift q, changing those smooth gauges changes G and Q by Dolbeault
coboundaries but changes none of the cohomology classes, nonvanishing arguments, or products
proved above. This is a limitation only on a preferred global coefficient presentation, not on the
representatives as cohomology classes or on the Bott–Chern algebra.

Uses: the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; proposition 10.7; equations (202),
(203), (205) and (207) to (209).

Question T.3 (Open: A literal global coefficient atlas for the generators). The invariant
computations and all the metric types named above are settled for X. The real restriction map
                                       1,1            1,1
                                 rb : HA   (X; R) −→ HA   (Fb ; R)

has image Rη by 8.10 and 10.11. Its source has real dimension two and its target has real
dimension four. This concerns cohomology classes and does not assert literal equality of arbitrary
smooth representatives with an invariant fibre form.
   The formula (25) supplies a global G after a metric choice. For the standard primitive
marking, Gγ = G0 /12 represents gγ by 10.6. There is a precise operator construction of Q as well.
Fix a Hermitian metric on X and a regular fibre F , identify η with its real invariant form on F ,
and choose an orthonormal basis e1 , e2 of the Dolbeault-harmonic (1, 1) forms for ∆∂¯. Define

                       `(e) = −          i∗F e ∧ η,         Q=                         .
                                12   F                           |`(e1 )|2 + |`(e2 )|2

                      ¯         and has fibre Dolbeault class η. Indeed the image of fibre

    These two formulas fix global smooth representatives by explicit elliptic operators and a finite

U     Unconditional arithmetic of the normalized norm
Statements 16.1–16.5 do not decide the unconditional arithmetic nature of N at a nontorsion
point. An explicit small instance is

        E : y 2 = x3 − 140x + 784,      P = (0, 28),     j = −3375,       N (P ) = 2e−h(P ) .
                                                                                       b


Here P is a primitive generator modulo the rational 2-torsion and

             h(P ) = 0.46736567718147128000752020126284678363562034370331 . . . .
             b

The exact unresolved assertion is that 2e−h(P ) is transcendental. The corresponding example of
                                            b

conductor 361, y 2 + y = x3 − 38x + 90, P = (0, 9), has N = e−h(P ) and no finite local contribution.
                                                              b

The relative-period proof isolates its obstruction: an unconditional theorem excluding (87) for
the positive diagonal central direction. A theorem about linear 1-period relations does not supply
that exclusion. The attempted approaches and the exact CM theta comparison are printed in
the preceding period and CM-normalization sections; their source checks and computational
records are retained in the audit files. These arguments do not resolve the stated exclusion.

Appendix R identifies every source result and its printed statement. A recorded independent proof
reading counts as a check; a producing run’s status does not. We compared the retained source
arguments with the printed proofs, including the moved re-derivations and all distinct methods.
An exact-arithmetic rerun checks its stated algebraic assertions; a ball-arithmetic rerun checks
its inequalities and explicit analytic tails. Neither is treated as a check of unrelated geometric
steps. Source checks match the theorem actually used, its edition, and all its hypotheses.
     The current full readings, derivations, original-source checks and certificate reruns were
performed by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, ChatGPT Pro mode, effort Pro), 17 November 2026. The
per-result record preserves the earlier readings by Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic), effort high or
effort max as recorded, 12–16 November 2026, and Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), effort max,
12–16 November 2026. The complete machine-readable verification record is included with the
programs and logs; proofs are printed in this paper.
     The citations to Bertrand’s algebraicity theorem, the original Tate–Silverman specialization
sources, Rubin’s CM work and the sigma-value survey are retained only at the expressly qualified
comparisons. Their unverified entries support no implication in a proof. The rejected algebraicity
implication, the absence of a general unconditional norm transcendence argument and the
distinction between an exact leading factor and a full Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer assertion are stated
at their points of use.
